All 66 books of the Bible are written on rolls and then retained and presented in the library of the installation. “bios [bible]” focuses on questions of faith and technical progress. The installation correlates two cultural systems that are fundamental for societies today—religion and scientific rationalism. In this context scripture has always had an elementary function, as holy scripture or as formal writing of knowledge. In computer technology the “basic input-output system” (bios) designates the module which basically coordinates the interchange between hardware and software. So it contains the indispensable code, the essential program writing, on which every further program can be established.

Links: http://www.robotlab.de/bios/bible.htm
129576.biography: robotlab (DE) was founded by Matthias Gommel, Martina Haitz and Jan Zappe in 2000. The group develops experimental installations with industrial robots. Robotlab is associated with the Institute for Visual Medial at the ZKM - Center for Art and Media Karlsruhe, http://www.robotlab.de

129592.name: Natural History of the Enigma
129592.authors: Neil Olszewski, Neil Anderson, University of Minnesota, Eduardo Kac
129592.description:
The central work in the “Natural History of the Enigma” series is a plantimal, a new life-form I have created and that I call “edunia”, a genetically engineered flower that is a hybrid of myself and a petunia. The edunia expresses my DNA exclusively in its red veins.
Developed between 2003 and 2008 and first exhibited from April 17 to June 21, 2009, at the Weisman Art Museum [1], in Minneapolis, “Natural History of the Enigma”also includes a large-scale public sculpture, a print suite, photographs and other works.
The new flower is a petunia strain that I invented and produced through molecular biology. It is not found in nature. The edunia has red veins on light pink petals and a gene of mine is expressed in every cell of its red veins, i.e., my gene produces a protein only in the veins [2]. The gene was isolated and sequenced from my blood. The pink background of the petals, against which the red veins are seen, is evocative of my own pinkish- white skin tone. The result of this molecular manipulation is a bloom that creates the living image of human blood rushing through the veins of a flower.
The gene I selected is responsible for the identification of foreign bodies. In this work, this is precisely what identifies and rejects the other that I integrate into the other, thus creating a new kind of self that is partially flower and partially human. “Natural History of the Enigma”is a reflection on the contiguity of life between different species. It uses the redness of blood and the redness of the plant’s veins as a marker of our shared heritage in the wider spectrum of life. By combining human and plant DNA in a new flower in a visually dramatic way (red expression of human DNA in the flower veins), I demonstrate the contiguity of life between different species.
This work seeks to instill a sense of wonder in the public about this most amazing phenomenon we call “life”. The general public may have no difficulty in considering how close we truly are to apes and other non-human animals, particularly those with which it is possible to communicate directly, such as cats and dogs. However, the thought that we are also close to other life forms, including flora, will strike most people as surprising.
Thus, the key gesture of “Natural History of the Enigma” takes place at the molecular level. It is at once a physical realization (i.e., a new life created by an artist, tout court) and a symbolic gesture (i.e., ideas and emotions are evoked by the very existence of the flower).
I had a sample of my blood taken and subsequently isolated a genetic sequence that is part of my immune system—the system that distinguishes self from non-self, i.e., protects against foreign molecules, disease, invaders—anything that is not me. To be more precise, I isolated a protein-coding sequence of my DNA from my immunoglobulin (IgG) light chain (variable region).[3]
To create a petunia with red veins in which my blood gene is expressed I made a chimeric gene composed of my own DNA and a promoter to guide the red expression only in the flower’s vascular system. In order to make my blood-derived DNA express only in the red veins of the petunia, I used Professor Neil Olszewski’s CoYMV (commelina yellow mottle virus) promoter, which drives gene expression only in plant veins. Professor Olszewski works in the Department of Plant Biology at the University of Minnesota, St. Paul, MN. [4] My IgG DNA is integrated into the chromosome of the edunia. This means that whenever the edunia is propagated through seeds my gene is present in the new flowers.
In anticipation of a future in which edunias can be distributed socially and planted everywhere, I created a set of six lithographs called “Edunia Seed Pack Studies”. Visually resonant as they are with the flower and the work’s theme, these images are meant to be used in the actual seed packs to be produced in the future. In my exhibition at the Weisman Art Museum, I exhibited a limited edition of edunia seed packs containing actual edunia seeds.
Notes
[1] The exhibition comprised the actual edunias, the complete “Edunia Seed Pack” set of six lithographs and a limited edition of edunia seed packs with actual edunia seeds.
[2] The gene of mine that I used is an IgG fragment extracted from my chromosome number 2. Immunoglobulin G (IgG) is a kind of protein that functions as an antibody. IgG is found in blood and other bodily fluids and is used by the immune system to identify and neutralize foreign antigens. An antigen is a toxin or other foreign substance, such as viruses, bacteria and allergens, that provokes an immune response in the body. More precisely, my DNA fragment is from my immunoglobulin kappa light chain (IGK) [see diagram]. In “Natural History of the Enigma”, the fusion protein, produced exclusively in the red veins, is a fusion of my IgG fragment with GUS (an enzyme that allowed me to confirm the vascular expression of the gene).
[3] For her assistance in taking my blood, isolating my IgG and cloning it, I owe a debt of gratitude to Bonita L. Baskin, who at the time I carried out this work was CEO of Apptec Laboratory Services, St. Paul, MN. The blood was taken for “Natural History of the Enigma”on May 13, 2004, on the premises of Apptec Laboratory Services.
[4] With the assistance of Professor Neil Olszewski, I obtained positive confirmation that my IgG protein was produced only in the edunia veins by detecting the activity of the enzyme GUS (beta glucuronidase), which is fused to the IgG sequence. The detection was carried out through a staining technique.

Links: http://www.ekac.org/nat.hist.enig.html

Ohlendorf, Professor of Biochemistry, Molecular Biology and Biophysics, College of Biological Sciences/Medical School; Rebecca Krinke, Associate Professor and Director of Graduate Studies, Department of Landscape Architecture. At the Weisman Art Museum, thanks to Lyndel King, Director and Chief Curator; Diane Mullin, Associate Curator; and Craig Amundsen, Public Art Curator and program manager. In my studio I would like to acknowledge Wonbin Yang. Also, a very special thanks to Shelly L. Willis, who, when I started to develop "Natural History of the Enigma", was the Public Art Coordinator at the Weisman Art Museum, and now is the Public Art Administrator for the city of Sacramento, CA.
129592.biography: Eduardo Kac (BR) is internationally recognized for his telepresence and bio art. Kac’s work is exhibited internationally and is in the permanent collection of the Museum of Modern Art in New York, the Museum of Modern Art of Valencia, Spain, the ZKM Museum, Karlsruhe, Germany, and the Museum of Modern Art in Rio de Janeiro, among others, and has received many awards. http://www.ekac.org.

129629.name: The New York Times Special Edition
129629.authors: Because We Want It, Steve Lambert
129629.description:
On November 12, 2008, one week after the election of Barack Obama, a special edition of “The New York Times” hit the streets announcing the end of the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, a maximum wage, a new national public transit system and 14 more pages of “all the news we hope to print.” The paper was distributed throughout New York City as well as Boston, Los Angeles, San Francisco, other cities around the country, and on the website nytimes-se.com.
The project was a collaborative effort nine months in the making written by over 30 writers and distributed by hundreds of volunteers. When people were presented by this reality—it was literally put it into their hands in the form of the national paper of record—their critical faculties kicked into gear. Sadly, after seven years of ongoing war, truly imagining what peace could feel like is more difficult than one expects. The possibility of peace strikes one more powerfully because the paper makes the theoretical ideas and possibilities something one is actually holding in one’s hand, studying, and experiencing for a moment.
Inventor Dean Kamen once said that science already has solutions to all the world’s problems. There are incredibly informative studies buried in research journals and amazing but little known books that lay out step by step policies to solve global warming. Indeed, for many of the world’s problems, solutions do already exist. What we lack is vision and an articulated demand from an overwhelming majority of people. What the “NYT Special Edition” did was to explain this type of material in everyday language and as if it had already happened. A policy paper that was accessible, and, as Bill Moyers described it, “presented in a way that people would actually want to read.”
The response to the paper was overwhelmingly positive, reaching newspapers, magazines and television stations around the world. Readers seemed to understand that the paper, dated nine months in the future, was a vision; a plan for what was possible. A plan that doesn’t rely on powerful hero politicians to save the public, but a plan detailing the rewards of everyday people organizing together and pressuring, working, and demanding a more just world.

Links: http://nytimes-se.com
129629.credits: Supported by: Eyebeam, Cultures of Resistance, The Electronic Frontier Foundation, CODEPINK, Wooster Collective, and others.
129629.biography: Steve Lambert (US) is the founder of the Anti-Advertising Agency, lead developer of Add-Art (a Firefox add-on that replaces online advertising with art) and has collaborated with numerous artists including the Graffiti Research Lab, and the Yes Men. Steve’s projects and art works have won awards from Rhizome/The New Museum, Turbulence, the Creative Work Fund, Adbusters Media Foundation, the California Arts Council, and others. He is a senior fellow at the Eyebeam Center for Art and Technology in New York and teaches at Parsons/The New School and Hunter College.

129630.name: ReConstitution
129630.authors: Justin Manor, John Rothenberg, Eric Gunther
129630.description:
“ReConstitution” was a live audiovisual remix of the 2008 United States Presidential debates. There were three performances in three cities, each coinciding with the live broadcast of the debates.
We designed software that allowed us to sample and analyze the video, audio and closed captioned text of the television signal. Through a series of visual and sonic transformations we reconstituted the material, revealed linguistic patterns, exposed content and structures, and fundamentally altered the way in which the debates were watched.
The transformed broadcast was projected onto a movie screen for a seated audience. Over 1500 people attended our three performances in Boston, New York and Washington DC. The legibility of the underlying debates was maintained throughout the performance—we didn’t want the audience to miss a word of it.

Links: http://reconstitution2008.com
129630.biography:
Eric Gunther (US) has worked with at Small Design Firm as art director, designer, and programmer. He has created unique interactive installations and commercials for clients including Cirque du Soleil, the Nobel Peace Center, the Denver Museum of Art, Monticello, the Boston Museum of Fine Arts, and L’Oreal. He is part of the media performance group Sosolimited.

Justin Manor (US) is a designer and artist. He studied under John Maeda at the MIT Media Lab. He now works with the Small Design Firm to build custom installations that allow for easy navigation of large amounts of information. Founding member of Sosolimited.

John Rothenberg (US) is a designer and programmer. He studied at MIT. For the past four years he has been working at Small Design Firm, building electronies and programming graphics for interactive installations. Co-founder of Sosolimited.

129643.name: the idea of a tree
129643.description:
“The idea of a tree” is an autonomous production process which combines natural input with a mechanical process. It is driven by solar energy and translates the intensity of the sun through a mechanical apparatus into one object a day. The outcome reflects the various sunshine conditions that occur during this day. Like a tree, the object becomes a three-dimensional recording of its process and time of creation.
The machine starts producing when the sun rises and stops when the sun goes down. After sunset, the finished object can be “harvested”. It slowly grows the object by pulling threads through a coloring device, a glue basin, and finally winding them around a mould. The length/ height of the resulting object depends on the hours of sunlight during the day. The thickness of the layer and the color depends on the amount of solar energy (more sun = thicker layer and paler color; less sun = thinner layer and darker color). This correlation between input and output makes the changes visual and readable. The product becomes a three-dimensional “photograph” of the time and the space in which it is produced and communicates certain characteristics of locality. The process does not just react to different weather situations, but also to shadows occurring in the machine’s immediate surroundings. Each object represents one day at one spot where it was produced.

Links: www.mischertraxler.com
129643.biography: Thomas Traxler (AT), born 1981. From 2006 to 2008 took an IM masters course (conceptual design in context) at the Design Academy Eindhoven/NL. 2003-2006 BA (hons) in product and furniture design at Kingston University, in St. Pölten / Austria and Kingston / UK. He tries to combine his technical and experimental approach with conceptual thinking to design and create things and systems.

129653.name: Cosmic Revelation
129653.description:
“Cosmic Revelation” is a minimalist light-art projectand a scientific experiment as well. In a field of 16 flashing mirror sculptures connected to the Kascade detector field at the Forschungszentrum [Research Center] Karlsruhe (Germany) the impact of high-energy cosmic rays on the earth can be experienced at first hand.
“Cosmic Revelation” is presented directly in the detector field, but also remotely in other places. As a new kind of land art, the flashing field not only refers to the physical processes in matter, but also indicates the protecting and moderating qualities of the atmosphere as basic condition for the existence of a biosphere on earth.

Links: http://www.imachination.net/cosmicrevelation/
129653.biography: Tim Otto Roth (DE), born 1974. Studied philosophy and politics in Tübingen from 1994 to 1995. From 1995 to 2000 studied arts at Kunsthochschule Kassel. In 2004 in Kassel completed his diploma on the theory of visual communication; 2004-05 lectureship at Kunsthochschule Kassel. 2007 artist in residence at the Center for High Performance Computing (ZIH), TU Dresden. Since 2008, doctorate at the Academy of Media Arts Cologne. Roth is known for his large art and Science projects in public space.

129683.name: Common Flowers - Flower Commons
129683.description:
The “Common Flowers” project is based on the first commercially available genetically modified flower, the blue “Moondust” GM carnation developed and marketed by Japanese beer-brewing company Suntory. But although Suntory applied for and was granted permission to grow this GM plant in its key markets, it has chosen not to. Instead the blue GM flowers are grown in Columbia, harvested, and shipped as cut flowers to the worldwide markets.
With “Common Flowers” we reverse the plantgrowing process, by growing, multiplying and technically “cloning” new plants from purchased cut flowers using plant tissue culture methods. The blue GM carnations are brought back to life using DIY biotech methods involving everyday kitchen utensils and easily purchasable and ready materials.
And because the plants are officially considered “not harmful” and therefore legally permitted to be grown outside, we took the next logical step and released the blue GM carnation into the environment. This action is intended ask questions about the state of intellectual property, ownership and copyright issues surrounding the bio-hacking and bio-bending of plants. Our goal is to make these flowers available as shared “common flowers” and to create the free spaces where they can grow and prosper, in a “flower commons”.

Links: www.common-flowers.org
129683.biography:
Georg Tremmel (AT/JP) studied Visual Media Art at the University of Applied Art in Vienna and Interaction Design at the Royal College of Art in London, where he started his ongoing collaboration with Shiho Fukuhara.

ShihoFukuhara (JP) received a BA (Hons) in fine art from Central St. Martins College of Art and Design in London and continued her studies with an MA in interaction design at the Royal College of Art. They formed the artistic collaborative research framework BCL in to explore the relations, congruences and differences of biological and cultural codecs through artistic interventions and social research.

129711.name: Tantalum Memorial
129711.authors: Richard Wright, Graham Harwood, Matsuko Yokokoji
129711.description:
“Tantalum Memorial” is a series of telephony-based memorials to the more than four million people who have perished in the complex wars that have gone on in the Congo since 1998, often referred to as the “Coltan Wars”.
Coltan ore is mined for the metal tantalum, an essential component of mobile phones, which is now more valuable than gold and therefore coveted by dozens of international mining industry and warring militias.

The first thing that visitors see is a towering rack consisting of electromagnetic Strowger telephony switches. The switches are triggered by a computer, which is tracking calls from Telephone Trottoire, a “social telephony” network designed for use by the international Congolese diaspora. The audience can see the dialing progress of the calls on a nearby monitor and can hear the messages that are being passed around through headphones (spoken in Lingala). The movement and sound of the switches create a concrete presence in real time for this intangible network of conversations, weaving together the ambiguitiesof globalization, migration and our addiction to constant communication.
“Telephone Trottoire” was designed by the artists in collaboration with the London radio program “Nostalgie Ya Mboka”. The project builds on the traditional Congolese practice of “radio trottoire” or “pavement radio”, the passing around of news and gossip on street corners to avoid state censorship. 90 percent of Congolese people in the UK are refugees and their mistrust of official media has made them a particularly hard-to-reach community. Yet “Trottoire” has proved very popular—this version has already grown to 1,800 users and archived over 1,000 recordings.

Links: http://www.mediashed.org/TantalumMemorial
129711.biography: The artists Graham Harwood, Richard Wright and Matsuko Yokokoji (UK) have worked together since 2004, firstly as part of Mongrel, an internationally recognized artists’ collective. Working in a fusion of art, digital media and open networks, they aim to reach beyond the hierarchies of power and knowledge to involve those normally excluded from expression and collaboration.

129723.name: The Fragmented Orchestra
129723.authors: Nick Ryan, John Matthias, Jane Grant
129723.description:
“The Fragmented Orchestra” is a huge distributed musical structure modeled on the firing of the human brain’s neurons. It connected 24 public sites across the UK to form a tiny networked cortex, which adapts, evolves and triggers sitespecific sounds via a central space. Each of the sites has a soundbox installed, which streamed human-made and elemental sounds from the site via an artificial neuron to one of 24 speakers in FACT. The sounds are only transmitted when the neuron fires. A firing event caused fragments of sound to be relayed to the gallery and also communicated to the cortex as a whole. The combined sound of the 24 speakers at the gallery were continuously transmitted back to each of the 24 sites.
The sounds of “The Fragmented Orchestra” varied according to location; wind over Black Fell, innercity traffic, chanting from sports stadiums and the chatter of migrating birds arriving for the winter were combined with incidental and performed sounds from members of the public. The public, invited to play the instrument at the 24 sites, were able to hear the effect their playing has on the overall composition of the piece, at each site and at FACT. As members of the public used the instrument they became both player and audience of a vast and evolving musical composition extended across the UK.

Links: www.thefragmentedorchestra.com

Jane Grant (UK) is an artist who works with sound, moving image and drawing. Jane has been working with neurological time patterns and the human voice.

John Matthias (UK) is a musician, composer and physicist. He has released three albums and has worked with many recording artists, including Radiohead (The Bends), Matthew Herbert and Coldcut.

Nick Ryan (UK) is a sound designer and composer who specializes in the development and production of audio for cross-media moving image.

129733.name: Corpora in Si(gh)te
129733.authors: Max Rheiner, Ákos Maróy, Sota Ichikawa, Hajime Narukawa, Satoru Higa, Kaoru Kobota, doubleNegative
129733.description:
“Corpora in Si(gh)te” is an installation based on real-time processing of environmental data. A number of sensors are set up forming a mesh network throughout the target area in order to collect and distribute real-time environmental information such as temperature, brightness, loudness, humidity, wind direction and wind speed.
This sensor network can be seen as the nervous system of the virtual structure. The data collected from these sources is processed by software and translated into autonomous nodes which we call “super eyes”. These “super eyes” are the seeds for the virtual architecture of “Corpora” representing a cellular, distributed network of nodes that react through real-time processing, growing and subsiding like an organism. Each “super eye” collects environmental data from the closest sensor and makes local decisions independently of a central architect. The “super eyes” inadvertently give rise to an architectural structure, both surrounding the exhibition building and neighborhoods. This “information architecture” of “super eyes” has its own spatial perception to make itself transform into various forms by relying on the “super eyes” spatial notation concept. The fluid character of this architecture occurs as a living form. Visitors can observe this process by augmented reality technology through cameras located at the target site.

Links: http://corpora.hu/en/
129733.credits: Supported by YCAM—Yamaguchi Center for Arts and Media Mücsarnok; Kunsthalle Budapest, Hungary; CHB — Collegium Hungaricum Berlin; Transmediale.09
129733.biography: The project "Corpora" is formed by a collective of artists, known together as doubleNegatives Architecture (dNA). The dNA collective was founded in 1998 by Sota Ichikawa. The members are based in Japan, Switzerland, and Hungary, but regroup as a collective for the planning and design of every project. The main members of Corpora are Sota Ichikawa, Max Rheiner,Ákos Maróy and Kaoru Kobata.

129771.name: EarthStar
129771.description:
“EarthStar”is an exploration of electromagnetic and vibrational energy and employs the rigorous methodologies and tools of science, but its overall effect is a poetically charged experience that ultimately emphasizes the sun’s elemental and mythic qualities.
Exploring arcane energies and hidden frequencies, the installation comprises three elements: A formal dynamic space is established between the singular and spectacular footage of the solar chromo-sphere captured by the artists using a hydrogen-alpha telescope. Sitting in opposition to this are two luminous refrigeration units containing virtual aroma compositions of synthesized molecules that represent states of ozone. Building a bridge between these two elements is a resonating and receiving system of VLF antennae tuned to the radio bursts emitted by the sun and fed through an amplifier to provide a real-time, immersive soundtrack.
A super atmosphere is established in the installation, by way of imaginative representations of the sun and the solar winds, and via synthetic aroma molecules that smell ozonic. Ozone has a smell. It is what we smell before a thunderstorm. It’s the smell of electricity due to burning ions. But the excess of ionized air is also the smell of a fresh sea breeze near the ocean. These accords of synthesized molecules created by the artists explore and develop recent research that postulates that smell, like hearing and seeing is defined by being able to discern the frequencies of molecular spin as smell.
The custom-built antennae sculptures act like radio-astronomy antennae. These hand-wound antenna constrained by audio filters resonate to the section of the electromagnetic spectrum known as the VLF (3 KHz to 30 KHz). VLF is the Very Low Frequency range of the spectrum and is dominated by solar noise and the effects of the solar winds on our atmosphere. This frequency range translates directly into audio through basic audio inputs so that we are able literally to listen to the sympathetic activity in the wire object.
129771.biography:
David Haines (UK) and Joyce Hinterding (AU) live and work in the Blue Mountains, NSW Australia, and work both collaboratively and independently. Their collaborative work has produced large-scale immersive video and sound works that explore the tension between the fictive and the phenomenal. These works incorporate Joyce’s investigations into energetic forces and David’s concern with the intersection of hallucination and landscape.

Support by Marco Macon, IASKA (International Art Space, Kellerberrin, WA) and the C3 West project in the early development of this work.

129791.name: The Kinetic Sculpture
129791.description:
“The Kinetic Sculpture” is a metaphorical translation of the process of form-finding in art and design.
714 metal spheres hanging from thin steel wires attached to individually controlled stepper motors and covering the area of six square meters animate a seven-minute-long mechatronic narrative. In the beginning moving chaotically, then evolving to several competing forms that eventually resolve into the finished object, the kinetic sculpture creates an artistic visualization of the process of form-finding in different variations.

Links: www.artcom.de/kinetik
129791.biography: ART+COM (DE) was initially founded in 1988 as an association by designers, scientists, artists, and IT experts. In the beginning, the vision was to explore the new medium of computers and the possible applications. Hence, ART+COM has been a pioneer in this field since the start.Today it continues to be a central source of inspiration for media design, technology, art, and research in Europe.

129852.name: Boris
129852.description:
A boy, Boris, receives the greatest gift of his life, a drum. He loves his drum so much that he never leaves it, playing it constantly for 30 years. While the villagers initially love Boris and his drum, after a while they become annoyed and try to stop him drumming. Nothing works, until they finally chop his arms off. This makes Boris very sad and makes him want to end his life then and there. However, he finds a way to drum again.
This animation is drawn on paper colored with pastels and composited in After Effects. It is done in the organic style I use to tell my stories, letting them flow straight from my mind to yours. I hope you enjoy it.
129852.credits: Director, animator, writer: Daniel Lundquist; sound designer: Mike P. Nelson;
129852.biography: Daniel Lundquist (AT). A year ago I graduated from the Minneapolis College of Art and Design, where I studied animation. I come from a family of eleven so it has always been in my blood to stand out and not blend in with the rest of the world, to be completely original. I don’t know if I will ever achieve this goal or even come close, but as long as I live and breathe I will try. In animation I find the outlet to try and be different, to tell stories in a new and different way. My work is very organic. I try to make it flow straight from my mind through my hand to the paper so that when you watch my animations you feel what I am feeling and understand what I want to say.

129865.name: HA'Aki
129865.description:
“HA’Aki” is a short abstract-impressionist film in which the animation and the music were made simultaneously in an organic process of symbiotic creativity. Film maker Iriz Pääbo tells the highly subjective story of a complete hockey game using a new cinematic vocabulary she calls “animbits”. Päabo readily admits she is not the biggest fan of “Canada’s national game”, so the great, though highly under-appreciated NHL stalwart of the 60s and 70s, Eric Nesterenko, was her hockey muse in this artistic journey. “HA’Aki” is a lyrical and wonderfully unorthodox interpretation of hockey as played in the mind of a lyrical and wonderfully unorthodox animation artist.
Technique 2D and 3D animation.
129865.biography: Iriz Pääbo (CA) has directed, animated, edited and written music for the independent animated films "I've Got a Little Brother", "My Quills Click When I Wal"k, "Bon Vivant", and "Wake Up/Wake Up". Her 1991 breakthrough film, "Leaving the Poisons Behind", aired nationally in Canada and Australia and was screened at festivals in Los Angeles, Leipzig and Uppsala, "tecknicly Inkorect" (1996) was broadcast on Teletoon and screened at the prestigious Annecy and Goteborg festivals. She previously made the award-winning short "Loon Dreaming", for the NFB in 2002. Iriz has participated in a number of group shows, including the Tom Thomson Gallery, Scarborough Arts Centre, Queen’s University and Deleon White Gallery. She had four solo shows between 1997 and 2000, including one at Northrop Frye Hall at the University of Toronto’s Victoria University.

129889.name: French Roast
129889.description:
In a fancy Parisian café of the 1960s, an uptight businessman is about to pay the check when he finds out that he’s lost his wallet. To save time he decides to order more coffee …
“French Roast” is a character-driven short animated film. With no dialog, the story is told through character animation, music and sound. Staging is made of a single frontal master shot with a big mirror in the background to create the equivalent of a reverse shot. The artistic challenge was to translate the very graphic style of the original drawings.
129889.biography: Fabrice Olivier Joubert (FR). Before directing his first CG-animated short film, Fabrice Olivier Joubert built a solid reputation as a traditional and CG animator. From 1997 to 2006, he worked at DreamWorks on "The Prince of Egypt" (1998), "The Road to El Dorado" (2000), "Spirit: Stallion of the Cimarron" (2002), "Sinbad, Legend of the Seven Seas" (2003), "Sharktale" (2004) and "Flushed Away" (2006). In 2005, he animated on the stop-motion feature "Wallace & Gromit: The Curse of the Were-Rabbit", directed by Nick Park (Aardman Studios).

129893.name: Chick
129893.description: “Chick” is a humorous true-life story about malefemale relations. Infatuation and its consequencesare depicted in a ironic way: meeting a guy, dancing, having fun, a sexual act. A man, giddy with the charm of a femme fatale, leaves a room.
129893.credits: Writer and Director: Michal Socha; Producers: Michal Socha. Platige Image: Executive Producer: Marcin Kobylecki; Production Assistant: Marta Staniszewska; Mentor: Prof. Hieronim Neumann (Academy of Fine Arts,Warsaw); Animation: Michal Socha; Music: Meritum - SZCZ; Pawel Szamburski (clarinet), Karol Masluszczak (piano), Tomasz Bandyra (bass); Roman Slefarski (drums), DJ Lenar (gramophone); Sound Director: Jaroslaw Wójcik; Sound Design: Maciej Tęgi; Music Mix: Rafal Smoleń; Theater Mix: Tomasz Dukszta c.a.s.; Digital Postproduction: WFDiF; Malgorzata Rogulska (Laboratory Manager); Promotion, Distribution: Platige Image
129893.biography: Michal Socha (PL), born in 1981. Graphic and animation artist, director. Graduated from the Faculty of Graphic Arts at the Academy of Fine Arts in Warsaw. He has created some animated shorts such us: "The Concert", "Odlot". He specializes in animation and special effects for commercials and TV productions.

129897.name: Audi 'Unboxed'
129897.authors: Russell Brooke, Aaron Duffy, Passion Pictures, 1st Ave Machine
129897.description: The film opens on a large cardboard box in the middle of an empty room. An animated character, who is drawn on the surface of the box, is engaged in the painstaking construction of a mysterious object. At the end of the spot this is revealed to be a perfectly crafted cardboard Audi Q5 car. Finally this transforms into the gleaming real car with the end tag: “We’ve unboxed the box”.
129897.biography:
Russell Brooke (UK) studied animation at the West Surrey College of Art and Design, and shortly upon graduation he started working as a freelance animator for a variety of animation studios around the world. In the 90s he became a director at the Brooke Edwards Animation Studio, and in 2000 he signed with Passion Pictures and works there now as a director, animator and designer. He also acts as a Creative Consultant for the Studio in addition to his role as a director

Aaron Duffy (US) is a director and crochet artist residing in Brooklyn, New York. Aaron graduated from Washington University in St. Louis in 2006 and has since created several commercials, music videos and short films. Aaron is the co-founder of SpecialGuest, a sister studio to 1st Ave Machine. 1st Ave Machine USA Inc. is a New-York-based CGI VFX/animation studio and production company working in the advertising, broadcast, music video and feature film industries.

129898.name: Harmonix 'Rock Band II'
129898.description:
“Harmonix Rock Band II” is a 90-second cinematic using After FX. trailer which introduces the updated game. Set to the classic anthem “Hello There” by Cheap Trick it issues the challenge to gamers, “Are you ready to rock?” The hero band from the “Rock Band I” trailer reprises its role in the film and engages in a car-rooftop stand off with a new rival group in a high-energy battle of the bands.
The band characters, which were designed by director Pete Candeland, are stylized, but are also quite realistic in terms of being threedimensional people who need to move naturalistically, and with a lot of detail in their clothes, hair etc. The props, such as the cars and the American desert backgrounds, also needed to match the same level of detail and authenticity as the detailing in the characters. Added to this, there were two bands instead of the one in the original film, giving eight characters in total, which immediately increased the amount of work that was involved. All these factors meant that a sizeable, specialist crew needed to be gathered together for the project.
It was decided to use motion capture to assist the animation process of the band characters, and we worked with Audio Motion Studios to produce the footage for animators to work to. Director Pete Candeland cast four actors, who played the characters in both bands. Takes of the DV footage that was filmed were selected and BVH files were made that were imported into XSi for animation. Lip synch was also really important for the film, and for this we worked with Image Metrics, who filmed the facial mocap shots.
The characters were modeled using Modo and animated in XSi. In total we had a crew of around 50, including modelers, riggers, animators, VFX artists, compositors, render wranglers and matte painters. The animation was rendered using Mental Ray and composited using After FX.
129898.biography: Pete Candeland (AU/US) grew up in Australia, where he was hired by Disney straight from high school in 1991 after they saw his drawing skills. Since then he has lived in London, Toronto and Los Angeles, where he worked on many projects from commercials to feature films. Candeland joined Passion Pictures as an animation director in 2000. For the BBC's coverage of the Beijing Olympic Games he has recently teamed up with Jamie Hewlett again to direct Journey to the East.

129949.name: This Way Up
129949.description:
Laying the dead to rest has never been so much trouble as in this animated short film by directors Smith & Foulkes at London studio Nexus Productions.
A.T. Shank & Son have a bad day at the parlour when a falling boulder flattens their hearse. Emotional and literal pitfalls lie in wait for the odd couple as they make their way cross country with just a coffin for company. This short animated caper puts the fun back into funeral as their journey and relationship unravel on an epic scale. The eight-minute comedy “This Way Up”, was nominated for an Oscar this year in the “best animated short” category. The film was made in full HD at the Nexus studio in London over a period of five months with their in-house team of animators and designers. It was supported by BBC Film, BBC Comedy and BBC Film Network, Arcadi in France and Mike Judge’s “The Animation Show” in the US.
129949.credits: Director: Smith & Foulkes; Writer: Smith & Foulkes and Christopher O’Reilly; Producer: Charlotte Bavasso and Christopher O’Reilly; Co-producer: Christine Ponzevera; Production Company: Nexus Productions Ltd; Original music: John Greswell and Christopher Taylor for MPM London; International Distribution: Nexus Productions
129949.biography: Smith & Foulkes (UK) graduated from the Royal College of Art animation course in 1997 and teamed up with producers Chris O’Reilly and Charlotte Bavasso at the Nexus Studio. They have gone on to develop a reputation as one of London’s top animation directors and their portfolio spans short films, music videos, commercials and film title sequences. Credits include the film title sequence for "Thunderbirds" and an animated “film within a film” for DreamWorks’ and Paramount’s "Lemony Snicket: A Series of Unfortunate Events". They have also directed for the BBC’s animated comedy show "Monkey Dust". Their commercial work has won them numerous awards and accolades including the Grand Prix Award at Cannes, Lions, a Grandy at the Andys, an ITV Award for Best Commercial and two golds at the D&AD awards. They were the most awarded commercial directors in the US and Europe in 2006.

129974.name: Urs
129974.description: “Urs” is the graduation film of Moritz Mayerhofer at the Institute of Animation at the Filmakademie Baden-Wuerttemberg. For almost three years he drew thousands of mountains, characters and villages. He began the pre-production during an exchange program at les Gobelins, Paris. When he came back to the Filmakademie he joined the class of acclaimed animation director Andreas Hykade (“The Runt”, “Ring of Fire”) to produce his film. He worked day and night to create a deep atmospheric film where he would find the fragile relationship of a man to his mother in the middle of a gigantic set of mountains. His goal was to combine the beauty of 2D matte paintings with 3D character animation and 2D classical effects animation into a painterly unity.
129974.credits: Director, Design, Animation: Moritz Mayerhofer; Producer: Stina McNicholas, Jakob von Moers; Character TD: Jonas Jarvers; Matte Paintings: Moritz Mayerhofer, Julia Ocker, Leszek Plichta, Martin Puttkammer, Felix Mertikat, Johannes Schiehsl; Effect Animation: Jan Locher, Stefan Habel, Hendrik Panz, Benjamin Swiczinsky; Shading: Michael Lederhuber; Lighting: Thomas Moser; Sound Design: Michael J. Diehl; Foley Artist: Marcus Neuberger
129974.biography: Moritz Mayerhofer (DE), born in 1981, successfully applied to study animation at the Filmakademie Baden-Wuerttemberg in 2003. He created a couple of award-winning shorts such as "CAPs", "The Christmas Hitler" and "The Last Tree". In 2005 Moritz was a jury member of Zlin International Film Festival (Czech Republic) and of the Roshd International Film Festival (Iran). He participated in an exchange program at GOBELINS, Paris, to learn more about animation, design and layout.

130154.name: Skhizein
130154.authors: Jean-François Sarazin, Dark Prince, Jeremy Clapin
130154.description:
Struck by a 150-ton meteorite, Henry has to adapt to living offset from his own body by precisely 91 cm.
Following his first (silent) short film “A Backbone Tale” in 2004, which was selected in over 60 festivals worldwide and took 16 prizes, this is director Jérémy Clapin’s second film and for Anglo-French production outfit Dark Prince, whose trademark is about taking animation into new realms, their first foray into the short narrative film arena

130154.biography: Jérémy Clapin (FR), born in 1974, graduated from the Arts Décoratifs school in Paris in 1999. Since then, he has worked in several areas: as a graphic artist, as an illustrator for the press and various publishing houses, and as an independent director working in adverts. In 2004, he directed his first animated short film, "A Backbone Tale" (Une histoire vertébrale), which was featured in over 60 festivals worldwide and won more than 15 prizes. "Skhizein" is his second film; released in March 2008, it has already taken prizes at Cannes, Annecy and Zagreb, and is in international competitions in several forthcoming festivals.

130246.name: The Dark Knight
130246.description:
BUF’s main work on “The Dark Knight” by Chris Nolan was to make Batman’s sonar vision visible. The new technology developed is able to detect the electromagnetic waves emitted by cell phones. By scanning the waves’ behavior in space, the device basically allows him to visualize in three dimensions any environment in which a cell phone is turned on.
Since nothing like this exists in the real world, Pierre Buffin and Dominique Vidal started with the concept of the sonar: a device generating waves to reveal all the volumes around it. However, sonar waves are not visible. A long process of research, supervised by Xavier Bec, head of R&D, lasted eight months. Waves, metaballs, smoke, particles, and more were tried out. Chris Nolan wanted the waves to bounce back off obstacles, but also partly to travel through them. In addition, the device needed to feel harmless and not look like X-ray. The research process continued to determine how fast the waves should be, what fraction should bounce back, how fast it should dissipate and how, so as to find the right combination of wave frequency, speed and rhythm. Finally, the result is like a CG wave to which we have added some noise. The environments in which the wave animation takes place are mainly in the Prewitt building sequence, where Batman uses it to locate hostages, and in the Batcave monitor room, where dozens of monitors visualize different locations. Each environment was built by modeling layers upon layers of geometries, since all volumes are translucent except when hit by a wave. The vision had to cross the rooms all the way through and include the city’s street life in the background. The process was very complex and needed to be repeated for each scene in the monitor room.
Finally, BUF created the film signature’s flaming logo that opens the movie. All the work was created using exclusively proprietary software.
130246.credits: VFX Supervisor (BUF): Dominique Vidal; director: Christopher Nolan; production: Warner Bros
130246.biography: Dominique Vidal (FR). With a masters degree in mathematics and visuai art and technoiogy, Dominique Vidal joined BUF’s team in 1995. He has collaborated on over 20 feature films and 50 commercials, including "Batman and Robin" (Joel Schumacher), "The Matrix Reloaded", "The Matrix Revolutions" and "Speed Racer" (Wachowski Brothers), "Alexander" (Oliver Stone), "Arthur and the Invisibles" (Luc Besson), "Spider-Man 3" (Sam Raimi), "Batman Begins" and "The Dark Knight" (Chris Nolan), and recently "Knowing" (Alex Proyas). As the Supervisor of SFX development, Dominique is involved in graphic and technical research in addition to supervising the post-production.

130304.name: World of Warcraft: Wrath of the Lich King - Intro Cinematic
130304.authors: Jeff Chamberlain, Phillip Hillenbrand, Blizzard Entertainment
130304.description:
The cinematic intro for “World of Warcraft: Wrath of the Lich King” presented an exciting creative and technical challenge, and it marked a number of firsts for us.
It was clear early on in production that we wanted to focus on the character of the Lich King himself, Arthas Menethil. Arthas plays a central role in the story of the expansion, and we knew that not every “World of Warcraft” player would be familiar with the Lich King’s lore from our previous games. As a result, we decided to depart from the “montage” style of cinematic we’d used to introduce World of Warcraft and its first expansion, “The Burning Crusade”, in favor of a more character- and story-driven approach.
Our challenge was to simultaneously provide history for players unfamiliar with the Lich King’s lore, set up what’s happened to the character since his last appearance in “Warcraft III: The Frozen Throne”, and make it clear to players that the Lich King was one of the greatest threats they’d yet encountered in “World of Warcraft”.
This cinematic was also a test bed for many new technologies. It was the first production in which we used Maya for all of our rigging and animation. It was also the first time we used a combination of Maya, Renderman and Nuke for lighting and compositing. We developed a rigging and animation pipeline that took advantage of Maya’s referencing system in order to automatically update character rigs, which greatly sped up the rigging and animation process. Additionally, we were able to use Renderman to create massive armies, hundreds of millions of particles of ice, and realistic snow using far fewer compositing tricks than we had relied on in the past.

130304.biography:
Jeff Chamberlain (US). As a project lead for Blizzard Entertainment, Inc.’s cinematics department, Jeff guides the vision and direction of the award-winning cut scenes featured in the company’s games. He joined Blizzard Entertainment, Inc. in 1998, immediately after graduating from James Madison University with a degree in art, emphasizing computer animation.

Phillip Hillenbrand (US). As a senior producer for Blizzard Entertainment, Inc.’s cinematics department, Phillip is responsible for managing all aspects of a cinematic production from inception to the completion as well as any additional secondary aspects that relate to the project, such as marketing, licensing and trade shows. He currently is working on the real-time cinematics for "StarCraft II".

130308.name: Wall-E
130308.description:
What if mankind had to leave Earth but somebody forgot to turn the last robot off? After hundreds of lonely years of doing what he was built for, namely, cleaning up the planet, WALL-E (short for “Waste Allocation Load Lifter Earth-Class”) discovers a new purpose in life when he meets a robot named EVE. WALL-E and EVE take off on a voyage through our galaxy, setting into motion one of the most exciting and imaginative comedies brought to the screen in the last years. On a fantastic journey across a universe of neverbefore- imagined visions, WALL-E encounters entertaining characters such as a cockroach, or a brave team of malfunctioning robots.
“WALL-E”, a comedy filled with surprises, action, humor and heart!

130308.biography: Andrew Stanton (US), born 1965, joined Pixar Animation Studios in 1990. The first major feature Stanton worked on was "Toy Story" (1995), as a character designer, story artist and writer, as well as providing several voices. On his next animated feature, "A Bug's Life" (1998), Stanton worked as a writer, story artist and co-director. He also wrote and directed the animated feature "Finding Nemo" (2003).

170829.name: Hackmeeting
170829.description:
“Hackmeeting” hosts workshops, conferences, cyber art performances, fosters spontaneous discussion, and much more. Each proposed activity, though, is meant as a facet of a philosophical framework based on sharing, openness, decentralization, free access, human evolution and aimed at a political outcome. Hackmeeting is organized by a community of hackers unique in the world for its desire to funnel the hacker ethics into political activism, far beyond the limits of the technological environment. The “Hackmeeting” community thinks hacking is a tool to alter reality and society as a whole.
The “Hackmeeting” is usually a three-day event and is completely self-organized through an open and non-moderated mailing list (https:// www.autistici.org/mailman/listinfo/hackmeeting) and wiki (http://hackmeeting.org/_wiki/index.php?title=Pagina_principale), as well as a local live meeting in the city that is holding the next one. It often takes place in social centers, community spaces and squats, to stress the close relationship between hacking and the underground political scene. (http://aia.mahost.org/pro_spaces.html)
The first two days are dedicated to workshops, conferences and debates. The third is usually dedicated to a big plenum, where all the participants analyze new ideas and possibilities pointed out during the meeting, sum up all the event and reflect and examine projects for the future. For the first time ever, this year’s “Hackmeeting” was preceded by a warm up, to reach as many people as possible. The warm up was a series of events in various universities in Milan (Accademia di belle arti di Brera, Fisica, Bovisa, Bicocca, Scienze politiche, and Cascina Torchiera), between June 9 and 18. These were open conferences presented by researchers, experts, activists on ethics and hackers’ culture issues such as hacking and net art history, open-source, fear-embedded and surveillance-bulimic societies, information security and social control issues, open design and 3D animation, peer-to-peer economy, ecohacking (hacker approach to ecology).
The “Hackmeeting” itself took place in Sos Fornace, Rho, (sosfornace.org) from June 19 to 21: three days of workshops, lan space, sharing, meetings, discussions on free software, code, net neutrality, peer-to-peer and also digital countercultures, economies without capital, free speech against repression. Dedicated to the people who have adopted a critical and proactive approach towards the advancement of new technologies— which are more and more tied to social control, the business of war and the commercialization of every vital space.
170829.biography: Hackmeeting is a twelve-year-old story. It was born in 1998 and has been held every year since then, all over Italy, from north to south, in Florence, Milan, Rome, Bologna, Turin, Pisa, Genoa, Naples, Palermo, Catania, Parma. It has brought together nerds, cyber activists, geeks, techies, but also anyone who cared to subscribe to a general definition of hacking as changing one’s own life to suit one’s own desire, overcoming limits and borders, self-managing tools and spaces. The Hackmeeting has always focused on open hardware and free software, on digital countercultures, economies without capital, free speech against repression, and tried to point out the evolution and the impact of computers and electronic communication on the information system and on all of our lives.

legacy_14972.name: Perpetual Storytelling Apparatus
legacy_14972.description: The “Perpetual Storytelling Apparatus” is a method and device revealing the relations between inventions by crawling through millions of patents and their references. Patents are manifested thoughts or goals of the inventor, thus reflecting the mindset society had at a certain point in time. Much like scientific papers, patent documents contain references to so-called “prior art”—thus pointing to the principles the invention is based on. There are about 25 million references for the over 7.5 million patents issued. Because patents contain references, it is possible to find a path from one patent to another. This principle corresponds to the “six degrees of separation theory”. Applied to patents, the approximate level of separation is about seven nodes. The machine’s mechanism reproduces the patents and their relations in a never-ending stream of semantically connected drawings. Surprising connections between seemingly unrelatedobjects and ideas emerge

legacy_15442.name: : am Dienstag um neun sind die Erdbeeren reif
legacy_15442.description: “: am Dienstag um neun sind die Erdbeeren reif” (“: on Tuesday at nine, the strawberries are ripe”) is an enterable music theater piece told by five answering machines. The piece plays in a fictional dictatorship; when or where is not more closely specified. A resistance group called sponpartisan dares to carry out subversive artistic actions and so hovers between legality and the underground. They communicate via analogue telephone wires, which are almost obsolete and whose surveillance has been suspended as a result. They use answering machines to arrange meetings and tell each other their plans. Acoustically, this piece focuses with great consistency on the special aesthetic quality of these devices. The sounds and the entire music were exclusively generated using the sounds found recorded on answering machines. The piece is 25 minutes long and runs in a loop, the end and the beginning converging smoothly. Visitors can enter the space whenever they like. A central aspect of the project is the special spatial and acoustic situation. The five devices form an ensemble that plays chamber music. Yet unlike at a concert, the audience does not sit on chairs at a proper distance but is able to move between the players, and can therefore greatly influence the sound experience by their positions. The protagonists are old discarded apparatuses and most of us have many memories associated with them.

legacy_15559.name: Jamming Gear
legacy_15559.description: “Jamming Gear” consists of a module in which timing is controlled using a gear as the physical interface and a unique software system. In European music such as classical music, the control was based on time; a bar in the timing was fixed. A composition method that controls the timing by a variably fixed mark has begun to appear in contemporary music since it occurred in recording technology. This work is the performance device the realized the variable timing control with the characteristic of the gear.

legacy_15654.name: Truce: Strategies for Post-Apocalyptic Computation
legacy_15654.description: In their seminal paper “Flying in Tune: Sexual recognition in mosquitoes”, Gabriella Gibson and Ian Russell discovered an inspiring phenomenon: male mosquitoes change their buzzing frequency to match that of a female mosquito. This synchronization brings their wing beats to within a millisecond or less of one another. The authors suggest that this phenomenon facilitates the mosquitoes’ ability to copulate mid-flight. We take advantage of this phenomenon to engage the mosquitoes in song, inspired by the North Indian classical vocal tradition of Dhrupad. The computer produces a stimulus sound to which the mosquitoes synchronize. Subsequently, the computer sings a third voice that responds to the musical inflections of the mosquitoes’ buzz. These three voices come in and out of harmony depending on the mosquitoes propensity to maintain its sync with the stimulus signal. Each mosquito is equipped with a loud-speaker for providing the stimulus signal, a sensitive microphone for picking up the mosquitoes’ buzz, a camera for giving us a closer look at the insect, a kinetic component that allows the mosquitoes to rest every few minutes and a light bulb that shows the mosquito’s activity. We invite our visitors to interact with the mosquitoes: offering a finger tip for the mosquito to land: slowly approach the mosquito from below and stop about a quarter of an inch away from the mosquito. The mosquito will recognize the landing spot and extend his/her legs to reach you. Exhaling on the mosquito: the carbon dioxide in our breath excites and entices the mosquitoes.

legacy_15674.name: Speeds of Time - Versions 1 and 2
legacy_15674.description: “Speeds of Time” is a musical deconstruction of the most famous acoustic icon and symbol of time, Big Ben. Live sensors and microphones are mounted on the clockwork mechanism and near the bells of Big Ben to generate a spatial-acoustic composition, which is placed in a historic colonnade of the New Palace Yard, directly below and within earshot of the bells. The presence of the sound sculpture in this setting interacts with the natural sound of the bells, creating a multidimensional acoustic zone. While this work was installed in Westminster, a 12-hour multi-track recording of the sound sculpture was made that makes it possible to fully recreate the real time sense of this artwork, which can be realized as an eight-channel sound installation. This recording is fully accurate to real time and, if started at precisely five seconds before 10 o’clock, it will faithfully keep time.

legacy_15931.name: HiperBarrio
legacy_15931.description: Imagine a world in which every community library from the southern tip of Chile to the northern reaches of Siberia were laboratories of local culture rather than just repositories of books, magazines, and newspapers. Imagine if every community were in charge of shaping its own narrative, of writing and contextualizing its own history.So much of what we know about the world today has been written by strangers as they briefly pass through on their explorations. This was certainly true for San Javier La Loma, a small working-class community on the outskirts, of Medellín, Colombia. Ever since the internet became the greatest source of information about the world around us, San Javier La Loma’s reputation has been defined by foreign journalists and human rights advocates who traveled to the region to report on the harrowing violence erupting between guerrilla groups, paramilitaries and drug lords. Even after peace returned to the community its violent reputation remained. Local librarian Gabriel Jaime Vanegas was eager to recover San Javier La Loma’s rich and overlooked history. In 2007 Álvaro Ramirez, a media professor in Norway and a native of Medellín, approached Vanegas with a proposal to teach his young library users how to keep video blogs as a way to rescue their community’s cultural history. Over the following two years “HiperBarrio” has trained dozens of young citizen journalists how to use new media tools to produce feature stories about local personalities, events and stories. They have produced videos and blog posts about street art, poetry, politics, youth culture, music and environmental issues. They have also brought together their divided community both online and in person by frequently organizing events that combine live music, dancing, and digital art exhibitions featuring content from the project’s website. As a result of their involvement, the young citizen journalists have been invited to join the local community council to participate in policy discussions. Some members have authored an online collaborative novel while others have led a campaign to build a house for “Dirty Suso”, the subject of one of their documentary videos.“HiperBarrio” has become a model for other cities and countries hoping to transform their libraries into centers of local cultural production. Gabriel Vanegas was invited to speak at the annual meeting of the Network of Chilean Libraries to share his experience of transforming a humble library from a space of mere consumption to creative cultural production. Members of “HiperBarrio” have been invited to national and international conferences to present their work. In the future they plan on transforming all of Medellín’s community libraries into a network of cultural incubators. (Text: David Sasaki)

legacy_16658.name: Dickson Experimental - How in the Year 2000 the Oldest Sound Film in History Came into BeingWie im Jahr 2000 der älteste Tonfilm der Geschichte entstand
legacy_16658.description: AbstractWhen is a sound film a sound film? This paper traces the history of [“Dickson Experimental Sound Film”], which was synchronized in the year 2000 by cutter and sound designer Walter Murch. Using his digital editing system, he brought together the sound from a wax cylinder and moving images from a film, both of which had been recorded in Edison’s laboratory in about 1895. This film ranks as the “oldest synchronous film in existence”. Yet since in 1895 Edison’s Kinetophonograph had no device for synchronization as we know it today, we should ask if [“Dickson Experimental…”] has not in fact only existed since Murch synchronized it.Proceeding from this question, the attempt to comprehend just how entwined the circumstances of the development and reconstruction of [“Dickson Experimental…”] are, also raises certain questions about the possibility of “audiovisual historiography” and the complications involved. In this paper this (re-)construction is organized around two aspects of one concept of audiovisuality and its historicity, both of which seem important to me. The first of these aspects is the relation between the “audible” and the “visible” in different dimensions—the technical, media-related, perceptual, historical, and so on—i.e., in a very broad sense, so that it becomes possible to speak of the multiplicity of this relation. The second aspect is the respective temporalities of these relations that meet or collide with each other and hence evolve. Moreover, I would like to pursue the idea that certain incoherencies in these histories, such as addressed in the initial question, are unavoidable, because it is exactly at such points that a history of audio vision can become specific and critical. These complications were exceptionally dense already in the project formulated by Edison, a project that couples time-based technical media (the phonograph and the kinetograph) operationally in order to produce a kind of full presence of what is past. And yet these relations reshape themselves— propagate, reproduce themselves, form chains of consequences—into different arrangements in their own unique and revealing way. In the perceptual and “material” technological context of Edison and Dickson’s experiments in the Black Maria laboratory, the project to “complete the phonograph” consists of two separate media and this separation later articulates itself in separate archives for films and for phonograph cylinders. The histories of the development of sound film can relate to their objects in different ways, yet—as “talkie”—sound film also describes itself and its history. But exactly such a “self-description” of [“Dickson Experimental…”] is undermined because other possible imagesound relations—between the movement of the violin’s bow and the resulting sounds, and between the music and the dance—are being tested. Thus, an experiment was conducted in the Black Maria laboratory, the assessment of whose significance—between technology and perception— is put off until Walter Murch, repeats this experiment, in conjunction with his digital editing system, at another point in history. Hence, I would like to put forward taking the “experimental”of sound film and its history seriously.Excerpt[“Dickson Experimental…”] consists of a single shot with three elements that take up almost equal parts of the picture in front of a black backdrop: a large funnel protrudes from the left into the picture; in the middle there is a middle-aged man wearing a suit and hat, playing the violin; and on the right, two younger men who awkwardly, but touchingly, hold each others’ arms and dance in three-quarter time. […] Actually, the funnel we see in the picture contributed on two levels to the development of [“Dickson Experimental…”]. First, “technically”: if the funnel had not been in the picture, it would have meant that the phonograph was too far away from the sound source to have been able to record much that could have later been used as a soundtrack. Second, “iconographically”: if the funnel had not been not in the picture, the idea that the sound must have also been recorded during the shoot, and that this recording might have survived somewhere, would not have forced itself upon anyone with such inevitability. And it was this that first led to the title [“Dickson Experimental Sound Film”] and then to its reconstruction. These two levels do not—a priori—go seamlessly from one to the other, rather the possibility of moving back and forth between them is subject to certain preconditions. In the 1930s, the Museum of Modern Art declared film a subject of art history and established a film department. Among other items, this department acquired a forty-foot-long nitrate print (which was self-combustible and in danger of decomposing) from the Edison Historic Site (EHS), in other words, exactly the film that later would become part of [“Dickson Experimental…”] and was transferred to safety film in 1942. But because this was “purely” a film archive, the film was stored and screened as a “silent” film, even though reference was occasionally made to the existence of an accompanying phonograph cylinderiv— as if to demonstrate very literally the dictum of Deleuze / Foucault, that is, that the audiovisual archive is disjunctive. Though just how literally should we take this? In reference to Michel Foucault’s archaeology, Gilles Deleuze described the “disjunction” of the “audiovisual archive” as the historically variable fissure between the “sayability” of discourses and the “visibility” of “nondiscursive practices” that makes things emerge in “machines”—for instance, the “clinic”. This fissure is also a shared boundary at which the visible and what is sayable relate without ever coinciding. This disjunction is a “battle”, “‘discourse cutting into the form of things’ and vice-versa”. Hence the term “archive” here does not designate a material facility, but the respective historical regularities of emergence. As an example, Deleuze refers to contemporary sound films that demonstrate this non-relation. Should not sound film also be described as such a “machine”? Yet then it would be necessary to show where sound film becomes more than technology, in a narrow sense, and how at concrete “small” points, for example, “apparatuses […] had aesthetic consequences that had epistemic consequences that had apparatus-related consequences—and many other combinations and courses. How, in the case of [“Dickson Experimental…”], it comes about that a phonographic cylinder and film recording are separated by “intergovernmental agency red tape”, and where they meet again. Though to do so it would be important to differentiate between, first, the way discourses can negotiate film as their discursive subject; and, second, how sound film—which is initially on the side of visibility— relates seeing to hearing (soundtracks threaten to mix noise, music/and or language) in specific ways; and then third, at which points visibility and sayability “border” on each other.

legacy_16660.name: Eye hEar: Music, Art, Film & the Culture of Synthesia
legacy_16660.authors: Simon Shaw-Miller | Birkbeck College, University of London
legacy_16660.description: This book, “Eye hEar”, is about communication between art and music. It takes the form of episodes, some conceptual others based around works or artists and composers. It is necessarily selective and is more importantly conceived as part of an ongoing exploration of art and music relationships. I use synaesthesia as a conceptual conceit to think between and across sound and sight, art and music: to think of art and music outside the frame of sensory exclusivity.The first part of the book explores the emergence of a particular sensibility, absolute music (chapter 2) and the historical coincidence of the birth of synaesthesia (chapter 1). It goes on to consider the work-concept and importance of notation in sighting musical thought (chapter 3). Synaesthesia is offered as a conceptual paradigm for interdisciplinary analysis, in its multi-sensory and cross-modal nature. Absolute music is the opposite: an attempt to take the world away from music, the development of a fetishization of the ear. Absolute music is also abstract music, but the book argues that precisely because of this abstraction the visual is critical to us as producers and consumers in locating and communicating with music. The tension between the physical activity of making music and the abstraction of musical sound is resolved in sight; it is not an accident that we often say we are going to “see” a concert. The book argues that musical meaning is embodied in performers and consumers, in objects and history, and music is an art of objects, performances, texts and contexts; sights and sounds. Extract from Chapter 1“Colour hearing” entered the English medical consciousness fully in 1881, when the “London Medical Record” published an article, later reprinted in a number of American and European medical journals, where the term was used in preference to any Greek language derivatives (i.e., chromesthésie, hyperchromatopsie ). Audition colorée soon became popular in France, until in 1892 Jules Millet replaced it with a broader term, a Greek language derivative: synesthésie. In scientific terms, after this initial flowering of interest, there was a sharp decline in published work on the clinical condition. This is largely due to the paradigm of behaviourism becoming dominant, which rendered unobservable hypothetical constructs and notions of “mental states” unfashionable. Behaviourists restricted themselves to the observable. Lawrence Marks points out that between 1881 and 1931 there were 74 publications on the topic of synaesthesia. This is in contrast to the period between 1932 and his own study (1974/5), when a mere 16 were published. In artistic terms, the interest in synaesthesia derives from a number of sources. In part they were, ironically, a reaction to the very science that was turning its attention to the study of synaesthesia: Darwinism, positivist philosophy and the triumph of industrialism within emerging capitalist ideology were countered by some artists with an eclectic mix of neo-Platonic, Pythagorean ideas and occult ideas, but with a principal focus on subjectivity and interiority, both psychological and spatial. Having said that, it is also true that many artists saw no incongruity between their aims and those of science. Discussion of experimentation with cross-sensory experience was partially a reaction to over-specialization and notions of objective certainty, but synaesthesia could also be variously and loosely applied.Perhaps the best-known manifestation of what has been called synaesthesia is within the Symbolist movement. Primarily presented as a literary movement by Jean Moréas in the manifesto “Le Symbolisme” published in “Le Figaro” on 18 September 1886, it soon became international in scope. Symbolism represented an exploration of subjective experience, a strategy for reclaiming the irrational. However, for many artists associated with the movement, the form of idealism they embraced cannot really be described as neo- Platonist. For most of the movement’s thinkers, the notion of an art of ideas was personal and subjective, or if it did have a social dimension, then it was drawn to myth. Idea in this context refers more to a sensual rather than an intellectual manifestation.The poets who formed the original group of Symbolists all regarded themselves as followers of Charles Baudelaire. Indeed, the name Symbolism comes from Baudelaire’s poem “Correspondances”, part of the cycle “Les Fleurs du Mal” written in 1857. The first two stanzas: [in translation]  Nature is a temple and her living pillarsSometimes let slip confusing words;Man passes through this forest of symbolsWhile all around they watch him, knowinglyLike lingering echoes from distant placesReverberating in a profound unityVast as night and as lightPerfume, colors and sounds correspondA virtual manifesto proclaiming that in the absence of clear meaning the poet, attentive to his own experience, must make sense of the world. There is a world beyond rational consciousness, where the senses conjoin or correspond; an imaginative site of artistic creation. The second part of “Eye hEar” moves to a consideration of multi-sensory and multi-media issues. The bridge chapter (4) considers spaces as both related to the concert hall and museum in their attempts to provide ideal circumstance for the consumption of music and art. As ideal sites they help throw into relief the ideology that supports them. The white cube of the modernist art museum is a conception that aspires to a form of autonomy, to separate artworks from the world, to draw fixed boundaries and segregate them spatially. Music operates as an exemplum in this case precisely because it has so often been positioned as the art form par excellence of the disembodied—sound alone. Music is objectless, existing only in the air for a moment. What puts it there, its material production, is regarded as somehow “extra-musical”. In the visual arts, the white cube seeks to capture a space and hold art in it, outside time. It is a capsule that aims to preserve the artwork in a universal site beyond the vicissitudes of the world. The philosopher Thomas Nagel has described this idea in his definition of objectivity as “the view from nowhere”; the view from a point that ignores, or forgets the subjective filters through which we feel, see and hear the world. It is ironically a view founded on the trope of sight. Objectivity needs “perspective” to acquire a view, a view in which objects and subjects become transparent. The eye alone fixes the picture on the white wall. Music’s autonomy, similarly addressed to the ear alone, is what gives it the status of exemplum, but also conflicts with its etymological twin the museum—both words share a root in the idea of the muses, for sound is not visible, it cannot be shown, or can it? It is the contention of this book that music has deeds and that they are visible. The white cube is an idea appropriate not only to the art museum, but also the concert hall. Chapter 4 concludes by way of an allusive ploy. I provide a reading of Stanley Kubrick’s film “2001: A Space Odyssey” that links a number of conceptual strands, around space, object, the ‘Gesamtkunstwerk‘, sound and vision; it is intended as a fantasia.The approach of this book, therefore, has a different ontology to one that considers music as just a sounding art. I propose a conception of music that sees it. Many aspects of musical practice rely as much on sight as on sound; notation; conducting; communication among groups of musicians; the presentation and packaging of music, both live and recorded, etc. But more fundamentally than this, music is visual because it is part of our social and cultural fabric. It is not “heard from nowhere”, it is embodied in the processes of production and reception; it is always experienced somewhere. Music’s power comes from its relative fluidity as a form of cultural signification, but it always carries with it the touch of sight located in a space produced by bodies.Chapter 5 considers the ‘Gesamtkunstwerk‘ that is Schoenberg’s opus 18 music drama “Die glückliche Hand” (“The Lucky Hand”). It links to chapter 4 in Schoenberg’s aspiration to have it made into a film. The circumstances around its production and the concomitant aesthetic developments in both Schoenberg’s music, theory and painting, help clarify concerns about music’s synaesthetic perception.Chapter 6 returns to the critique of absolute music and its autonomy discussed in chapter 2. The boundaries between one art form and another, between one sense and another, and even between artworks and the everyday world, are eroded in the aesthetics of an artist and a composer not often paired: Andy Warhol and John Cage. In this way synaesthesia can be evoked as a model for thinking across divisions. Their work raises the issue of the frame as a conceptual device for dividing one space from another: art from the everyday, music from the extra-musical, art from objects. Schoenberg and Cage are also significant because, as a one-time teacher and student, they stand, chronologically and ideologically, at either end of the period of high modernism. This period represents a formalism that focuses on media specificity and exclusivity to produce a self-contained and framed art. Significantly, this modernist notion of purist autonomy is “derived from the example of music”, to quote one of modernism’s most conspicuous critics, Clement Greenberg, and is held aloft on the edifice of absolute music.

legacy_16666.name: The Order of Sounds - The Interplay of the Arts from the Bauhaus to Black Mountain CollegeDie Ordnung der Klänge - Das Wechselspiel der Künste vom Bauhaus zum Black Mountain College
legacy_16666.authors: Andi Schoon | Hochschule der Künste Bern
legacy_16666.description: AbstractThe Bauhaus is considered a reservoir of early twentieth century artistic trends whose common aim was to establish and cultivate correspondences between the arts. This approach was motivated, among other things, by the desire of fine artists to find a new set of rules after the move toward abstraction had made a qualitative comparison with the outside world impossible. Hope now focused on finding this new set of rules in the (abstract) relations of music. Legitimized by synesthesia, rule-oriented classifications of colors and sounds began making the rounds — but because they still adhered to the subjective, they often sparked controversy. The inclusion of a temporal, dynamic and, thus, musical plane in what had been the static spatial arts soon seemed to be more universally applicable (and through the theory of relativity, scientifically supported). At the Bauhaus, the strategies ranged from the cubist-futurist simulation of movement in paintings to the precursors of abstract film, which appeared emphatically on the scene as “visual music” (‘Augenmusik’). At the Bauhaus theater, more fleeting forms—for instance, “colored light plays” (‘Farbenlichtspiele’)—were evolved. Moreover, many projects have been documented that attempted to play the stage like a real moving abstract painting.
