Ratkje; sculpture: Geir Hjetland; sound engineering: Bjørn Kolbrek; production: Torkil Sandsund; technical advisor: Robin Stöckert / Soundscape studios; artistic inputs: Harald Fetveit; samples: Frode Haltli. Commissioned by: Vevringutstillinga 2010. Supported by: Norwegian Culture Council, KORO, Sogn og Fjordane Art museum.
131116.biography:
Maja S. K. Ratkje (NO), composer and performer received an Award of Distinction in 2003 for the album “Voice”. http://www.ratkje.com.

Geir Hjetland (NO), artist, his large metal works are a result of being close to both the metal industry and the natural world of the west coast. http://www.geirhjetland.com.

Bjørn Kolbrek (NO) is studying for a master’s degree in acoustics, his main interest is horn loudspeaker systems.

Torkil Sandsund (NO) is a theater director and art producer.

Wenche Wefring (NO) lives in Vevring and works for Vevringutstillinga that commissioned “Desibel”.

131143.name: Heart Chamber Orchestra
131143.description:
The “Heart Chamber Orchestra”—HCO—is an audiovisual performance. The orchestra consists of 12 classical musicians and the artist duo TERMiNALBEACH.
Each musician is equipped with a heartbeat sensor. The heartbeats of the musicians control a computer composition and visualization environment. The musical score is generated in real time by the heartbeats of the musicians. They read and play the score from a computer screen in front of them. HCO forms a structure where music literally “comes from the heart”.
The sensor network consists of 12 individual sensors, each fitted onto the body of a musician. A computer receives the heartbeat data. Software analyses the data and uses various algorithms to generate the real-time musical score for the musicians, the electronic sounds and the computer-graphic visualization.
While the musicians are playing, their heartbeats influence and change the composition and vice versa. The musicians and the electronic composition are linked via their hearts in a circular feedback structure. The emerging music evolves entirely during the performance.
The resulting composition is the expression of this process and of an organism forming itself from the circular interplay of the individual musicians and the machine.
HCO takes the idea of a traditional symphony as a framework. Each of the movements and their forms will illuminate the ongoing process from different sides.
Computer graphics generated from the HCO data establish a different sensual and narrative layer. The interplay of audio and video allows for a synaesthetic experience for the audience. The heartbeats of the musicians and their relation to each other become audible and visible.
HCO is not a composition in the traditional sense. It draws its inspiration from music, art and science.
131143.credits: A project by TERMiNALBEACH initiated and produced by TEKS—Trondheim Electronic Arts Centre in cooperation with the Trondheim Sinfonietta.
131143.biography:
TERMiNALBEACH formed by Erich Berger and Peter Votava aka PURE.

Erich Berger (AT/FI), an artist and cultural worker is interested in information processes and feedback structures, which he investigates with installations, situations, performances and various interfaces. His work is shown internationally in festivals, exhibitions and galleries. http://www.randomseed.org

PURE (AT/DE), composer, musician and developer, has released over 30 CDs and vinyls of solo and collaborative works in different styles under various pseudonyms on labels such as Mego (AT) and Staalplaat (NL). His latest album, Ification, was released at the end of
2008 on the Portuguese label Crónica. http://www.pure.test.at

131147.name: rheo: 5 horizons
131147.description:
“Rheo: 5 horizons” is an audiovisual installation composed of five flat-panel displays and five multi-channel speakers. Each vertical image pairs with each mono channel sound, and each video is synchronized to each audio. They are juxtaposed in line like a five-member ensemble and they behave like five independent audiovisual apparatuses. The spatial cognition of the sound can be enhanced by being synthesized with the movement of image. That is, the behavior of the image indicates the sound source position, the sonic direction and drive. It provides the space to rediscover the sonic movement, position and the relation between ego and sound. These resonances have an impact on sensory perception and develop a similar synaesthetic experience. The sound is given extra width and depth by the integration of auditory and visual sense and it forms a spatial audiovisual construction that gives a new understanding of space.
The term “rheo” in the title comes from the Greek, meaning flow, current or stream. And this work translates temporal and spatial transition to audiovisual motion as dynamic fluid. It embodies the notion of fluid time by utilizing audiovisual composition in space. The integration of imagery and sound lays out a spatially temporal movement, direction, speed, shapes, colors, weights and textures on a parallel time line. It shapes the dynamic of moving sounds and images into a diagram. The multiple layered sounds and images create the time sculpture in the cycle of an eight-minute loop.
131147.credits: Concept, direction, composition, programming by Ryoichi Kurokawa; Produced by Cimatics; With the support of Canon Europe; Format: installation / 5 HD plasma displays, five speakers; Year: 2010; Duration: 08:00 loop. http://www.cimatics.com; http://cpn.canon-europe.com
131147.biography: Ryoichi Kurokawa (JP), born in 1978. The world-renowned Japanese audiovisual artist Kurokawa’s works take on multiple forms such as installation works, recordings and concert pieces. In his language, a new international benchmark in the world of digital art, field recordings and computer-generated structures coexist in harmony and open the gateway to an imaginary world where complexity and simplicity alternate and combine in a strange symbiosis. In recent years, his works have been shown at international festivals and museums including the Tate Modern, Ars Electronica, Transmediale, Macaba, Shanghai eArts, and Sonar.

131149.name: Glücklich auf dem Weg nach unten/Happy Going South
131149.description: “Glücklich auf dem Weg nach unten / Happy Going South” is a solo performance with amplified objects. Threaded rods of different lengths (3x2 meters and 6x1 meters) and material (stainless steel, brass) are amplified through Schertler contact microphones attached to small double flowerpots (also a kind of analog filter) and played with washers in different sizes and material. The toy “Klopfspecht” (tapping woodpecker) has been separated from its original and now plays on amplified stainless steel bars, which like the threaded rods have varying frequencies. Big flowerpots are also amplified with a contact microphone and played with thin steel knives.
131149.credits: “Glucklich auf dem Weg nach unten/Happy Going South”, by Hanna Hartman was premiered at Raum für Kultur, Dresdener Bank, Frankfurt am Main curated by Oliver Augst. The DVD was filmed and edited by Teresa Iten 2009/2010 and produced in cooperation with the Swedish Music Information Center. Recorded at Kule Berlin.
131149.biography: Hanna Hartman (SE) is a sound artist and composer living in Berlin. She studied literature and theater history at the universities of Uppsala and Stockholm, radio and interactive art at the Dramatiska Institutet, and electro-acoustic music at the EMS in Stockholm. Since the early 1990s she has composed works for radio, created sound installations and given numerous performances all over Europe. Her many awards and grants include the Prix Europa (1998), the Karl-Sczuka-Preis (2005), the Phonurgia Nova Prize (2006), and a Villa Aurora grant (2010). During 2007 and 2008 she was composer-in-residence for Swedish Radio.

131314.name: Adapting for Distortion
131314.description:
Hiroaki Umeda has often highlighted the fact that his abstractly devised and highly anti-narrative works speak of the condition of contemporary man: it is therefore emblematic, even disturbing in a way, how in “Adapting for Distortion” the body of the performer seems to slowly fade away and go out of focus in those luminous spirals until it becomes just a vibration, a quiver of the flesh. A shadow.
“Adapting for Distortion” is inspired by kinetic art and uses the latest computing developments. Distortion of time, change of movement and immobility are at the heart of this performance, using optical effects in order to “widen the power of dance and to question the role of visual perception".
131314.credits: Company: S20 (JP); Choreographer: Hiroaki Umeda; Dancer: Hiroaki Umeda; Sound: S20; Image: Bertrand Baudry, S20; Production: Le Studio/ La Manège – Scène Nationale Maubeuge, Romaeuopa, S20
131314.biography: Hiroaki Umeda (JP) is a choreographer and dancer but is now recognized more as a visual artist and a mover. He also makes sound, visual image, lighting design for his own dance pieces, which have been highly acclaimed internationally and have been invited by important theaters and dance festivals as well as multimedia festivals all over the world. Together with choreography pieces, he is now working on sound and video installation pieces as an extension of this solo project.

131327.name: INJECT
131327.description:
A human body is injected in a cistern. Over the course of 45 minutes, the pressure the liquid exerts multiple neurosensorial transformations on him. From his epidermal fiber to his nervous system, he reacts to influxes of viscosity in this liquid chamber. His cortex, lacking oxygen, gradually loses all notions of the real. Like a human guinea pig, a matter-body whose psychological states are the object of kinetik tableaux, of singular temporal spaces.

Herman Kolgen initiated the “INJECT” project in 2008. The genesis of the principal visual material for this project was a shoot, in an immense cistern filled with water, which lasted six consecutive days. Yso, the performer, had to be immersed for over eight hours a day in the glass tank, oscillating between weightlessness and lack of oxygen. With the aid of various digital video recording and photographic systems, Kolgen assembled many series of temporal sequences, images that he then assembled into a flexible and modular body. It is a matter of a narrative progression, in perpetual circles of influence and movement, where the real is dislocated.

“INJECT” is a modular performance in HD format and multichannel audio.
131327.credits: Fundings: Arcadi, Canadian Council for the Arts.
131327.biography: Herman Kolgen (CA) is a multidisciplinary artist who lives and works in Montreal. A true audiocinetic sculptor, he draws his primary material from the intimate organic relationship between sound and image. Kolgen works to create objects that assume the form of installations, video and film works, performances and sound cinetic sculptures. Constantly exploring, he works at the junctures of different media, as well as elaborating a new technical language and singular aesthetic.

131334.name: BUG
131334.description: The “BUG” project is a permanent site-specific sound installation located in Berlin at Brunnenstrasse 9. Done in collaboration with the architect Arno Brandlhuber of B&K architects, this work is unique in that it’s the first time a new complete building has been knowingly wired up to sense sound and vibration and present it live to an anonymous public. Located in the former eastern sector of the city the building is designed, built and owned by the architect. The five story mixed-use structure contains gallery spaces on the ground floor along with private living and studio space above. Conceived as a type of architectonic microphone, this project utilizes eight seismological sensors permanently embedded in the concrete at various points throughout the building. Micro-vibrations traveling within the matrix of materials are converted to an electric signal that are then amplified and mixed down to a live two-channel stereo output. This sound is available 24 hours a day via a headphone jack located on the facade at the street level constantly rendering the structure’s acoustic fingerprint. The proliferation of portable headphones readily carried by individuals for use with mobile phones, mp3 players and iPods allow the spectator to “jack in” to the building and thus the “BUG” functions as a delivery device and amplifier of sounds and actions that surround everyday lives.
131334.credits: Supported by: Carsten Stabenow, Anne Kockelkorn, Tuned City, Berlin; Arno Brandlhuber, B&K Architekten + ERA, Emde, Schneider, Berlin; Haupstadtkulturfonds, Berlin
131334.biography: Mark Bain (US) born in 1966. He lives in Amsterdam. He has shown internationally, notably, at the Venice Theater Biennale, Boijmans Museum, Rotterdam the Platform Gallery, Istanbul, the Macba,Barcelona, the List Art Center, Cambridge and at the Schirn Kunsthalle, Frankfurt. He has worked in the collections of the Centre Georges Pompidou in Paris, the Porin Taide Museum in Finland and the MIT Museum in Cambridge, USA

131353.name: Hostage
131353.description:
“A work will only have deep resonance if the kind of darkness I can generate is something that is resident in me already.” Anish Kapoor

We live in a technological society, in a new Renaissance period, and there is no reason for the arts to stay away from technology. Nanotechnology is widely considered to be the basis of the next technological revolution. It is within this fairly new scientific field that inspiration may lie for the arts, ready to be unfold and be researched (in the same way as the theory of relativity inspired artists as Picasso and Braque to create cubism).
Nano art is the expression of the new technological revolution and reflects the transition from science to art using technology. Nano art is generally considered as a new art discipline related to micro-/nano-sculptures created by artists/scientists through chemical/physical processes and/or natural micro-/nano-structures viewed through powerful research tools such as the scanning electron microscope and the atomic-force microscope.
Working with nanotechnology as an artist is a statement, because by definition, the infinite can neither be revealed nor consumed. Nano art offers a non-vision.
The importance of my artistic proposition is to bring nano art to a visible (macroscopic) domain and contextualize it within the rich history of painting (e.g. Baroque painter Caravaggio and his famous chiaroscuro effect, Kazimir Malevich’s black squares, Ad Reinhardt, Mark Rothko, etc.).

Developing the darkest painting (material) in the world

My proposal is to develop the darkest (and largest) nano [1] -engineered painting in the world. This novel material will be the reference for black in the same way as the atomic clock is for time. The super-dark material, a thin coating comprised of low-density arrays of loosely vertically aligned carbon nanotubes, absorbs more than 99.9 percent of light while minimizing reflection.
In order to pursue this sublime ideal and go beyond the liminal (e.g. the current threshold of black), I will research and use anti-sublime strategies, using scientific tools and methodologies, and introduce them into my artistic praxis. The current idea is to make the scale bigger, in order to create a truly immersive experience for the spectator, hence questioning how the art work relates to space.
Secondly, I want to explore the meta qualities of the artwork (e.g. the way in which way the artwork can function as some kind of photovoltaic system, harvesting light and rendering it into electricity). For this I will need to interface the artwork with heat and light sensors. In essence the sensors will pick up data, which could for instance trigger a light source. This set up would create a perfect feedback loop between the artwork and the light source. My final aim is to construct a (sensory) experience hovering between vision and non-vision, artistic, scientific and metaphysical worlds.
The title "Hostage" refers to the fact that no light can escape from the painting and that it captures all light at all wavelengths.

Notes

[1] Nano derives from the Latin word for dwarf. One nanometer is one billionth or 10-9 of a meter. One micron = 1000 nanometers. One nanometer is about the diameter of three to six atoms (depending on the element) or 1/100,000th of the width of a single human hair.
A rough definition of nanotechnology could be: “the design, characterization, production and application of (novel) materials, (novel) devices and systems (that have unique properties) by controlling shape and size of the nanoscale”.
131353.credits: The project is made in close collaboration with Rice University, Houston, Texas, USA. This specific collaboration echoes, for example, the collaboration of the French artist Yves Klein and chemists to create his famous “International Klein Blue” (IKB). A first small prototype (70mm x 70mm) premiered in January 2010 at the MediaRuimte in Brussels. Concept: Frederik De Wilde. Fabrication of nano material: Nanomaterials Laboratory at Rice University, Houston, USA, Prof. P. M. Ajayan, Dr. Lijie Ci and Daniel Hashim. Special thanks: Ars Electronica, SMARTbe, the Flemish Ministry of Culture and the University Hasselt.
131353.biography: Frederik De Wilde (BE), born 1975, studied fine arts (MA), audiovisual arts (MA) and followed a preliminary education in architecture, studied one year of philosophy and concluded his studies with a post-graduate degree in new media, arts & design at Transmedia (post-graduate) where he learned software programming. Frederik works on the interface between art, science and technology, with strong interests in ecology, physics and social innovation. His work has been exhibited worldwide at festivals and has received several awards. Currently Frederik is collaborating with LAb[au], Q-02, The University Hasselt (BE), Carnegie Mellon University (US), Rice University (US), Karlsruhe University (DE), University Leiden (NE) and Rochester University (US).

131361.name: Intelligent Solar-Powered 3G-WiFi Broadband Access
131361.description:
In typical solar-panel installations for communications and broadband projects, the solar panel(s) and battery(ies) are oversized to compensate for the weather when the sun is weak, when it is cloudy, raining, or for night time periods of operation to prevent downtime. The standard charge control module only regulates the electrical flow from the solar panel to the battery to prevent overcharging. Any communication equipment is electrically connected to the battery side of the charge control circuit and the typical engineering design assumes the communication equipment will operate at maximum power usage. There is no association or interaction with the communications equipment to control its power usage, so the solar panel and battery system is oversized to compensate for this.
While in the average situations this is not an issue, but where cost, form factor and portability are critical engineering and social factors these are the most important factors. The size and cost of the solar panel(s) and battery(ies) can prevent deployment of systems due to cost or size, especially in developing regions. Using an intelligent solar-power control module and software for communications equipment will reduce the size (and cost) of the batteries and solar panels. Using smaller batteries will also reduce the environment impact when they expire and need to be recycled.
It is the purpose of this device is to provide a method and means for controlling the power usage of a communications router based on the electrical output of a solar panel(s) and battery(ies) voltage\charge level. This is accomplished through an Ethernet interface and Internet protocol (IP) format using an intelligent solar-power control module and specialized control software installed and running on the communications router processing sub-system.
The two pieces of technology outlined here are the intelligent solar-power control module and the software for power management and the monitor. These allow for smaller solar panel(s) and battery sub-system to be utilized for communications routers to reduce cost, form factor and portability. It is a simpler system for use in developing regions, specifically for schools.

Links: www.green-wifi.org/prix
131361.biography: Bruce Baikie (US) currently heads Green WiFi, a solar-powered WiFi & green data center social enterprise and works full time for Oracle. His background includes a BS in mechanical engineering from Michigan Technological University and advanced studies in international business from the University of Wisconsin. He is also active with Engineers without Borders and supporting OLPC (One Laptop Per Child).

131372.name: Studiolab
131372.description:
Engineering Solar-Powered Species

The Towards Biosolar Cells research program at Leiden University in the Netherlands addresses questions of green energy and the creation of sustainable biomass. The TBSC program combines natural and technological components to create solar collectors that supply fuel rather than electricity. Bioartists are collaborating in the development of these “artificial leaves”. In order to integrate bioartistic research, we have involved artists at all levels of the scientific practice. Research begins with “Elysia chlorotica”, a wild species that is half plant, half snail. This sea slug eats chloroplasts from algae and becomes solar powered so it does not have to eat for long periods of time. Recently it was discovered that this snail has genetic information to repair the chloroplasts and keep them going; if the genes that allow the snail to maintain the functional integrity of the chloroplasts can be laterally transferred, it is possible the genes can be utilized for other organisms, ultimately for humans. This generates the possibility to produce solar-powered species for food and biofuel directly from the sun, reducing our ecological footprint.
The scientific aim is to examine the possibility of equipping higher organisms with genes that enable them to keep chloroplasts alive, with the goal of increasing and improving the conversion of sunlight into photosynthetic energy supply for animal organisms. There is an aesthetic dimension to all scientific practices, from preparations of stock solutions to the choosing and cloning of gene inserts and the reading of results. The artistic discourse is therefore taking place in practices working at the interaction between humans and organisms as models for presentation. What are the political implications of these approaches? How do these practices deal with questions of manipulation, objectification and instrumentalisation of non-humans? What kind of research is done in the bioartist’s laboratory? How do we measure its worth?

Links: http://www.waag.org/project/studiolab
131372.credits: BioArt artist Adam Zaretsky in collaboration with Prof. Huub de Groot (bio-solar cells) and Prof. Rob Zwijnenberg (Faculty of Humanities, Leiden).
131372.biography: Adam Zaretsky (NL) is a bio-artist working in biology and wet lab art practice: ecology, biotechnology, non-human relations, live art and gastronomy. This involves biological lab immersion as an artistic process. He focuses on the legal, ethical and social implications of biotechnological materials and methods. He is currently a PhD student at Rensselaer Polytechnic (NY) and heads Vastal (the Vivoarts School for Transgenic Aesthetics Ltd.) at the WAAG in Amsterdam (NL) while researching in Leiden, where he is associated with the de Groot group. www.vimeo.com/vastal

131450.name: Chaos Computer Club
131450.description:
The “Chaos Computer Club”, founded in 1981, is world’s oldest and most renowned hacking community. Based in Germany, the “Chaos Computer Club” is a non-governmental organization that focuses both on the integration of the hacking community and educating the public on complicated issues. Carefully analyzing the nature of technology and weighing chances against risks in the use of it has been a key factor in the work of the club.
The CCC has proved to be an influential force in German society on a variety of topics, including but not limited to privacy, digital freedom, risks and opportunities for technology and politics for the information society. Strongly adhering to the principles of hacker ethics, the CCC supports open structures and transparency in politics and society while maintaining a strong stand on the privacy of the individual.
The club is actively using digital media in the form of mailing lists, wikis, websites and podcasts to provide information and discussion of topics to the public.
The CCC, and especially the Chaos Communication Congress event, serve as a forum for the political-technical community encouraging open discourse, unlimited disclosure. The CCC disapproves of secret communities and governments working in secret. The CCC also encourages and supports the development of open systems, open source software and has itself realized a variety of projects at this level.
The influence on German and European society and politics has been strong and has helped achieve some groundbreaking decisions by the German Constitutional Court (Bundesverfassungsgericht) and similar institutions in other European countries reversing a variety of laws endangering privacy and democracy. This includes but is not limited to
a) a ban on election ballot computers in the Netherlands and Germany, keeping the voting process private and free from computer fraud
b) the repeal of the laws on “online searches” in Germany
c) the repeal of the German data-retention law

Apart from its political work, the CCC has been an outstanding contributor to hacker culture.
a) The Chaos Communication Congress and Chaos Communication Camp have pioneered a new form of conference that has influenced events around the world.
b) The CCC-based Blinkenlights project has been a role model for modern interactive media art in public space.
c) The worldwide Hackerspaces movement has been strongly influenced and motivated by the CCC structure in Germany, Austria and Switzerland.
In 1984 the Club became famous for its “BTX Hack”, a discovery of security flaws in the state-run Videotex network. A surprised public, basically knowing nothing about computers and networks, suddenly discovered that technologically savvy individuals were able to transfer huge amounts of money from a bank to the club exploiting these flaws. Returning the money and notifying the press about this incident before anybody noticed made the club immediately famous for its “Robin Hood” approach. This kind of “public hack” became the signature feature of the CCC.

Links: http://www.ccc.de/
131450.biography: The Chaos Computer Club (DE) was founded in 1981 with “1984” in mind. The club started as a loose community of computer experts and people with various other expertise and interests. In 1984, the CCC also founded its annual “Chaos Communication Congress”, which today is world’s biggest meeting for alternative technical research, with more than 5,000 attendees from all over the world. In 1999 the spin-off event, the “Chaos Communication Camp”, redefined the idea of the congress, bringing hackers out in the open air over several days, demonstrating the vast variety of cultural achievements that the worldwide hacker scene has created over a period of many decades. Today the CCC has more than a thousand members worldwide and is influential in many international groups and events. The concept of regional CCC groups CCC has sparked the concept of “hackerspaces”throughout the world, with more than 400 such spaces being founded since 2000. The CCC is generally seen as the core influence on this powerful cultural movement.

131452.name: ceibalJAM!
131452.description:
“ceibalJAM” is a volunteers’ organization born in Montevideo in 2008 one year after the Uruguayan government launched Plan Ceibal (http://www.ceibal.org.uy/) to provide laptop computers to all school children and teachers in the country.
The organization is based in the international community of developers and educators, with members from different countries and special links with SugarLabs, the organization that developed most of the base software being used in Uruguayan schools.
After Plan Ceibal started we noticed the need for local interactive contents to be developed and for a broader knowledge of the technologies introduced, which mostly came from the US-based organization OLPC (One Laptop Per Child, (http://laptop.org). Moreover, we saw that if some basic computing skills were not brought closer to common people, teachers and children, the computers’ potential would be underused.
At the same time, there was a lot of discussion around the kind of software that had to be used in the computers, whether it had to be open source or proprietary. As there were big lobbies promoting proprietary software usage, we wanted to show in practice that it was possible to make a more open and participatory development environment, sharing software and technological knowledge with organizations and volunteers from all around the world.
That’s how “ceibalJAM” started, with two main goals in mind: 1) Learn, master and disseminate information technologies introduced by Plan Ceibal. 2) Develop educational software applications using the free software model.
In these years we have built a strong community, mainly linked by a mailing list with more than 300 subscribers and a portal with more than 100 active users.
Our major working events are the “ceibalJAM” meetings, which are two-day activities in which volunteers take the first hours to teach their works-in-progress and projects, then take a time to discuss how to go ahead, and finally take most of the meeting time for development. So far we have held four of these meetings in Montevideo and two in other cities in the country. Two more “ceibalJAM” meetings are planned for 2010.

Links: http://ceibaljam.org
131452.biography: ceibalJAM had its first outing in May 2008 with a first meeting at the Universidad de la República. Since late 2008 ceibalJAMhas established its own place on the web: http://ceibaljam.org. There we can store information about ongoing projects, as well as keeping the community in touch and informed about its activities. In November 2009 a civil, non-profit association was established.

131459.name: CulturaDigital.Br
131459.description:
CulturaDigital.Br is an initiative of the Brazilian Ministry of Culture in partnership with the National Education and Research Network.
It is an experimental platform for social and collaborative media for public use, fully developed with free software with the goal of providing an environment for public policies related to digital culture in Brazil.
In order to promote a better comprehension of the various scenarios that form the mosaic of digital culture in Brazil and to make it easier for the public to participate in issues concerned with monitoring and assisting in the construction of public policies and regulatory frameworks that will shape the digital sector, the Ministry of Culture, the National Education and Research Network (Rede Nacional de Ensino e Pesquisa— RNP) and people from civil society launched the Brazilian Digital Culture Forum.
The experiment began with the release of the social network CulturaDigital.Br and the invitation of experts and networks of cultural activists to register and set up a profile of their digital references (their blog, Twitter, Delicious, Youtube etc.) on the forum.
The environment was built to bring people and their social streams together, linked by the tag #culturadigitalbr, organizing and documenting their participation in the debate.
In the second half of 2009 the forum hosted several meetings around the country and also on the online platform to discuss policies for digital culture related to the five main themes proposed by the CulturaDigital.Br team: memory, communication, art, infrastructure and economy.
Digital culture is a new and emergent term. It has been used in different forms by different sectors and incorporates different perspectives about the impact of digital technology and networking in society. The organizers of the CulturaDigital. Br network see its role as convening a collective analysis of these broader perspectives and encouraging the participation of all stakeholders in an innovative process of collaborative construction of public policies for the digital sector in Brazil.
Notably, the process of the Brazilian Digital Culture Forum is happening at a time when our country is dealing with major debates on regulatory frameworks and public policies that directly affect the landscape of digital culture.
As one of the most important processes, the public debate over a civil framework of the Brazilian Internet (Marco Civil da Internet Brasileira, http://culturadigital.br/marcocivil/) has been completely developed within the CulturaDigital.Br platform.

Links: http://www.culturadigital.br
131459.credits:
“CulturaDigital.Br“ was created by the Ministry of Culture of Brazil, with RNP, FLi Multimidia and Brazilian Digital Culture Lab. The coordination team is formed by José Murilo Jr. (Ministry of Culture), Rodrigo Savazoni (FLi Multimidia), Alvaro Malaguti (RNP), Antonio Carlos Nunes dos Santos (RNP), Claudio Prado (Brazilian Digital Culture Lab) and José Luiz Herencia (Ministry of Culture). The platform team is formed by José Murilo Jr. And Rodrigo Savazoni (Coordinators) FLi Multimidia team: Gabriela Agustini, Caru Schwingel, Lia Rangel, Fabiano Rangel and André Deak.
Ministry of Culture content and technical team: Guilherme Aguiar, Alcione Carolina, Antonio Albuquerque, Daniel Prado, Yasodara Córdova, Lincoln Sousa, Marcos Lopes e Rafael Lucas. CulturaDigital.Br is also formed by Cicero Inacio da Silva, Diogo Moyses (from Intervozes), Oona Castro (from Instituto Overmundo) and Rogério Santana Lourenço.
131459.biography: CulturaDigital.Br was created in 2007 by the Ministry of Culture of Brazil, with RNP, FLi Multimidia and Brazilian Digital Culture Lab (www.culturadigital.org.br). At the moment the platform has 3,815 registered members across all 26 Brazilian states and the federal district of the central government. Registered users are representatives of government at various levels, public institutions, activists, scholars and others interested in discussing new business models, art and technology, copyright law, access to broadband, Internet legislation, digital communication and funding for culture among other things. Currently, these members post 257 blogs on these issues and maintain 171 active discussion groups.

131461.name: the ubiquitous #unibrennt cloud
131461.description:
On Thursday, October 22, 2009, hundreds of students spontaneously occupied the Audimax, University of Vienna’s biggest auditorium. Immediately large sections of the population, including teachers and many existing organizations, expressed their solidarity. The movement was directed against decades of failed educational policies, the structural reform of universities in the course of the Bologna Process, and chronic underfunding of the educational system. Remarkable was that it was not central organizational structures (e.g., official student associations) that were at work here, but network structures created ad hoc and communicating via Twitter & Co. (hashtag: #unibrennt).
With the emergence of “unibrennt” (‘Die Uni brennt!’ / “The university is on fire!”), something appeared on the scene that was to profoundly affect many people’s lives. “unibrennt” is also certain to influence the form and success of future protest movements. It has already set an example, one that shows NGOs and others how to achieve “digital communities” by interlinking activities in different ways in the streets, conference halls and online; and by providing live streams as well as enabling participation via integrated platforms and wikis.
The “ubiquitous unibrennt cloud” has made all this happen without funding, full-time employees or specialists. Against the backdrop of a common goal, and based on premises of self-organization and the need for structural and political clout, a large number of people have played roles of equal importance. Which explains how it has been possible within such a short period of time to set up media centers, live streams, servers and homepages using private equipment; or how community kitchens have been organized; and first aid stations and cleaning crews, fitted out. Moreover, it explains how these and many other functions and nodes could be kept running 24 hours a day, seven days a week, week after week – and at that by students, many of whom have to work alongside their studies, and lecturers and instructors, who must also teach and work.
A movement such as “unibrennt” is not just a unique event but statistically a highly improbable one. For repeatedly in the course of the movement, there have been situations that have made its continuance unlikely. Many things need to come together and work for such a “ubiquitous cloud” to grow and survive. It is at these moments that the movement’s network has to function and overcome precarious situations. The “unibrennt” network consists of people and groups, occupied lecture halls and private spaces, mobile phones and laptops, division of labor and teamwork, Facebook fan pages and Skype conferences, wikis and international e-mail lists; it has spread everywhere, from the server room of the University of Vienna to self-hosted blogs, from street actions in Kiel and a community kitchen in Munich, to a networking meeting in Graz and a poster campaign in Basel. For many, a connection consists in belonging to the movement. It’s about communicating via the WWW and deciding matters in the “cloud”. While existing organizations attempt, in time- and resource-consuming processes, to achieve a top-down implementation of wikis, blogs, feeds and video conferences through training, pressure and incentives – the movement has collectively learned these techniques at an incredible rate.
Communication tools and identities are created and maintained collaboratively 24 hours a day. Passwords are changed weekly. Documents are managed through Google docs and wikis. SMS lists are put together for emergency evacuations. Media monitoring has been outsourced within the cloud via a string of links to online media reports and a Flickr album of newspaper scans. Press releases, lists of demands and open letters are sent by e-mail to the media and available on platform websites, wikis and links to everyone interested. In collaboration with the “live stream” team, a team of photographers and videomakers document the plenary sessions, sit-ins, demos, flash mobs and more.
Project teams ensure the transparency of the movement’s objectives and of contact data in wiki. Everything that takes place on these teams and in plenary sessions is documented live and presented to the public via video projector. Minutes, resolutions and petitions are sent out and stored on a wiki where they can be viewed and edited. Plenary sessions are available via live streaming and stored online in a video archive. Interaction via chats, tweets or video conferencing is the order of the day. Debates spread to social networks, where they continue. Topics, dates and links are posted incessantly; and resources, requested and organized.
Of course, all these materials are not just stored in online archives, but are also accessible to the public, and may be used and modified free of charge.
--- “unibrennt” began at 2 p.m. on October 22, 2009. Over the course of the next four days “unibrennt” grew explosively. On October 26, 2009, news of what was happening reached hundreds of thousands when the entire media world ran the same lead story: “Unibrennt!” Tens of thousands were on site or involved online. The following weeks were marked by rapid growth and differentiation, both internally and externally. Three weeks later, there was talk of a wildfire for the first time. In the meantime, the movement has spilled over to the rest of the German-speaking world and beyond.

Links: http://unibrennt.at

131482.name: Puncar Action!
131482.description:
“Project Puncar” is the first digital-divide program fully utilizing web 2.0 services in Asia. Maintained by Association of Digital Culture Taiwan (ADCT), “Puncar” has been using its Internet facilities to bring digital volunteers to remote villages to Taiwan since May 2008. It systematically travels around Taiwan to teach information technology and applications, such as blogs, Twitter, Google Maps etc. Students include the young and the old.
“Puncar” directly addresses “the last mile” issue, sending personnel, connections and resources to needy remote areas. It is hoped to increase public awareness of the digital divide and of related issues. It also aims to bridge the digital divide not only by channeling urban resources into the countryside, but also by exporting existing economic values to the villages.
In less than two years, members of the project have traveled to 150 places and covered more than 50,000 km of this island. It has also grown to manage a fleet of four vans, four full-time employees and 30 volunteers across different regions. ADCT believes the nature of the Internet can help to democratize and make transparent the collective intelligence that has fueled human development in the past. We also believe that resources can be aggregated and distributed by using modern web technologies, and we believe that only by visiting all possible stakeholders in local communities and NGOs in Taiwan can we lay the basis for future possibilities.

Links: http://puncar.tw
131482.biography: Founded by a group of bloggers and enthusiasts involved in digital culture community in 2005, Association of Digital Culture Taiwan (ADCT) aims to promote web 2.0, citizen media, blog and other Internet-based concepts in Taiwan. ADCT also works to bridge the digital divide by providing courses and workshops in remote villages and elementary schools and encouraging Internet users to participate in cultural issues. The Puncar Project was founded by the Tim Shyu, TH Schee and Cheng Li Hsu.

131485.name: Sourcemap
131485.description:
Whether buying the ingredients for a meal, planning a meeting or designing a product, the choices we make every day have vast social and environmental impacts. Until now, advertisements have provided most of the information about which products are green or ethical. A superficial approach, which fails to account for the life-cycle of products, endangers sustainability by betraying the trust of consumers and downplaying the efforts of industry. “Sourcemap.org” is a tool for understanding the story behind products in order to support sustainable decisions. Many third-party services rate products, but “Sourcemap” is the first resource that makes environmental assessment tools available to the general public.
A web calculator allows anyone to measure the carbon footprint of products during manufacturing, shipping, use and end-of-life. A novel mapping interface displays the trajectories taken by each element of a product and helps to determine which products are better suited to certain locations. Modern supply chains are too complex to be monitored by any single entity, but a crowd-sourced approach allows us to piece together a collective understanding of resource flows.
“Sourcemap” is socially functional so that the contributions of each user – whether a consumer, a designer or a producer – can be shared on a variety of digital and physical media. Producers can use supply chains published on “Sourcemap” to market transparent and sustainable business practices. The maps can be shared on any site (such as a Youtube movie), printed onto advertisements or packaging or linked through two-dimensional barcodes (such as QR codes) that consumers can look up using a mobile phone in a retail store. With every entry on “Sourcemap” the collective database grows, providing more choices to users seeking to make sustainable decisions. A “Carbon Catalogue” containing footprints of hundreds of materials and processes is continually being improved and expanded by user contributions and by a team of life-cycle assessment specialists. A database of producers, including the geographic locations of mines, farms and manufacturing plants, is growing with every supply chain contributed. By working closely with small businesses, government agencies, NGOs and large industries, the “Sourcemap” team is adding sustainable practices to the site and building additional calculators and visualization of various social and environmental metrics for sustainability.

Links: http://www.sourcemap.org/
131485.biography: Originated at the MIT Media Lab, “Sourcemap” is made possible by a world-wide community of volunteers dedicated to transparency and sustainability. The site was released publicly on September 1, 2009. In the first six months, the site registered over 1,200 users, who generated over 700 maps. Today “Sourcemap” is being expanded in partnership with design schools, regional governments and medium-sized and large businesses, in an effort to build a geographically distributed resource for finding socially and environmentally sustainable products and for disseminating industrial best practice.

131490.name: BOSCO-Uganda (Battery Operated Systems for Community Outreach)
131490.description:
“Bosco - Uganda” (Battery Operated Systems for Community Outreach) connects war-torn and isolated camps that were formerly for internally displaced persons (IDPs) (now village trading centers) to a network of communication stations. We connect these rural locations in northern Uganda to solar-powered PCs, connected to long-range WiFi Internet with access to VoIP telephony and a digital camera.
The idea behind “Bosco” is to draw people together in a collaborative, community effort. We call this ICCT Training (Information, Communication, and Collaboration Technology). “Bosco” has scaled up and doubled its presence in the region over the last year. We are now located at 22 sites in northern Uganda. We have put our communication systems in rural schools, health clinics, CBO/NGO offices and outposts, local government offices, and community centers. We provide direct Web 2.0 training to volunteer-trainer user groups in these areas. In turn, these users follow our training of trainers Web 2.0 curriculum to pass on valuable ICT skills to their fellow community members. This is leading to the development of productive livelihood skills: people gain literacy, draft development proposals and engage in other collaborative community activities within their communities.
In sum, the “Bosco” technical solution is able to help communities in five main ways: 1) Education: equipping schools with appropriate technology and community centers with a tool that allows people to become their own self-advocates in a time of great need; 2) Communication and collaboration: VoIP phones and Internet allow service providers (local CBOs/NGOs) to get in touch with their beneficiaries. Our Wikispaces site and Intranet forum also allow local users to express themselves and design local solutions to local problems, all in the public eye; 3) Development: our network connects major social service providers in the area, including the Catholic Church, Caritas International, War Child Holland and local governments; 4) Cultural enrichment: culture in northern Uganda has been scourged by 20 years of war and isolation. People are now using the web and our Wikispaces site to pass on cultural practices; 5) Information access: there were no newspapers in the IDP camps and cell phones were rare.

Links: www.bosco-uganda.org www.bosco-uganda.wikispaces.net
131490.biography: "Bosco" founders first traveled to Uganda in 2004 and connected with local leaders in the Archdiocese of Gulu in northern Uganda. The first pilot phase of “Bosco” in seven IDP camps near Gulu, Uganda, began in April 2007. Local leadership for the project was developed and local technical assistance to maintain the project was established. In 2008 “Bosco” hired its first full-time staff to run the project and implement its training and expansion. Today we have seven full-time staff locally and have expanded our network to 22 site locations in rural community centers, schools, local government offices and CBO/NGO outposts among others.

131531.name: web2.0 suicidemachine
131531.description:
Liberate your newbie friends with a web2.0 suicide! This machine lets you delete all your energy-sucking social-networking profiles, kill your fake virtual friends and completely do away with your web2.0 alter ego. The machine is just a metaphor for the website hosted by the moddr_ server – the belly of the beast where the web2.0 suicide scripts are maintained. Our service currently runs with Facebook, MySpace, Twitter and LinkedIn! Commit NOW!
The suicide machine is, of course, a radical solution for the by now popular term “unfriending,” which became the Oxford English Dictionary word of the year 2009. There are for sure good aspects in staying connecting with friends and family living abroad using Facebook & Co., but (most) people are not fully aware of the privacy trade-offs. Those services will hold your collected information on their servers forever and use the acquired data for targeted marketing analysis. Seamless connectivity and rich social experience offered by web2.0 companies are the very antithesis of human freedom. Users are entrapped in a high resolution panoptic prison without walls, accessible from anywhere in the world.
We do have a healthy amount of paranoia to think that everyone should have the right to quit their 2.0-ified life with the help of automated machines. So we hope that by removing your contact details and friend connections your data is being cached out from their backup servers. This can happen after days, weeks, months or even years.

Links: www.suicidemachine.org
131531.biography: The web 2.0 suicide machine started with a club event we have been organizing where the idea was to collectively delete your social network profiles. Later on, we developed it further into a completely automated web service. The team, based in the Netherlands, consists of Danja Vasiliev (server maintenance) and Walter Langelaar (production manager). We are experimentalists and interventionists on everyday technologies. Our mission is to display a critical perspective on contemporary media through our artistic practice.

131532.name: TEDtoChina
131532.description:
“TEDtoChina” is a significant visionary project in the Chinese free culture movement. Its practice is a testimony of several concepts and ideas, including Sharism, Creative Commons, Webridge, Open Brand, Social Professional Service, and Cloud Volunteers Management.
TED (technology, entertainment and design) is a conference, gathering the world’s most fascinating thinkers and doers to disseminate their ideas. The “TEDtoChina” project was founded on October 25, 2008, as an independent TED tribute project that uses the TED logo with permission from TED.
Operating as a free culture project and an education project, “TEDtoChina” aims to distribute TED’s inspiring and enlightening ideas to China. We hope to foster citizen spirit that can be a force for good in local communities. Be part of the change is a resonant idea at TED—and we want to bring this idea to people through our coverage.
The “TEDtoChina” Chinese site covers TED talks, TED Conferences, TED Prize, TEDx, TED Fellows and the TED Open Translation Project. By March 2, 2009, the “TEDtoChina” Chinese site had published over 540 posts and received 121,040 visits and 337,290 page views from 549 cities in China and 106 countries around the world. In addition, it has inspired Chinese TED fans to form a local community to discuss TED-related topics and local social innovations.
As a daily publishing website, the “TEDtoChina” Chinese site has grown into an online hub of the TED phenomena in the Greater China area by supporting and reporting TEDx events, servicing TED Chinese translators and spreading TED Prize updated reports.
Our team is also active in organizing and supporting small TED-inspired offline group events. For example, we have held such events in Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, and Xiamen in October 2009. The Shanghai “TEDtoChina” chapter also hosts biweekly book-club events related to TED presentations and speakers. We are working on the plan to organize offline events in over 20 cities in 2010.
We are in the process of building up version 2.0 of the “TEDtoChina” Chinese site by using the open-sources code from “1kg.org”, a social networking site, and building up the English version of “TEDtoChina” for the purpose of communicating TEDx China events to the global TED community.

Links: http://www.TEDtoChina.com
131532.biography: We started TEDtoChina back in October 2008 based on an idea from Tony Yet and Oliver Ding of broadcasting the TED message to the 1.3-billion-plus Chinese-speaking folks in the world. During the first stage (from October 2008 to August 2009), we invited friends to join the project. As of March 17, 2009, we have had seven site editors. After several months, we recognized the invitation model was ineffective with regard to the scale of the project. During the second stage (from August 2009 to November 2009), we publicly recruited volunteers. Over 25 writer volunteers have joined our project since then. We reorganized the publishing team and built five writing groups, including Monday@TEDtoChina, Tuesday@TEDtoChina, Wednesday@TEDto- China, Thursday@TEDtoChina, and Friday@TEDtoChina. Each group is led by a coordinator. Now in our third stage (from December 2009 to present), we are building a formal team structure.

131553.name: Fix My Street
131553.description:
“Fix My Street” helps people view and discuss local problems they have found and report them to their local council simply by locating the problem on a map or taking advantage of GPS in smartphones.
After entering a postcode or location, users are presented with a map of the area. They can view problems already reported in the area or report ones of their own simply by clicking on the map at the location of the problem.
Problems are reported to the relevant council by e-mail. The council can then resolve the problem in the way they normally would. Alternatively, users may discuss the problem with others on the website and then get together to lobby the council to fix it, or fix it directly themselves.
We sought to use the benefits that Internet technologies could bring to local communities and build a simple service that allows people across the UK to report common local problems such as graffiti, broken street lights, leaking pipes etc. by sticking a pin in the map. What makes it different is that it will provide a public place where users can see what has been reported by other users, make comments on what’s going on, and subscribe to alerts when new developments occur. With £10,000 from the Department of Constitutional Affairs (now the Ministry of Justice), maps from Ordnance Survey and time from our core developers, we mixed up some open-source technologies (Yahoo’s JavaScript libraries, Perl and PostgreSQL), wrote new functionality to cut up the map tiles from the OS originals and put together a website allowing people to report local problems to their council by clicking on a map.

Links: http://www.fixmystreet.com
131553.credits: FixMyStreet is a site to help people report, view, or discuss local problems they’ve found to their local council simply by locating them on a map. It launched in early 2007, and since then has grown to host over 95,000 reports, with over 1,000 reports now being made per week.
131553.biography: Fix My Street was launched in Britain in early February 2007 and has subsequently been adapted to create foreign versions in places as far apart as Brazil, New Zealand and South Korea. This site was built by mySociety, in conjunction with the Young Foundation. mySociety is the project of a registered charity, which has grown out of the community of volunteers who built sites such as TheyWorkForYou.com.

131574.name: Map Kibera
131574.description:
Until recently, Kibera, a massive slum in Nairobi, Kenya, was a blank spot on any public map. The Nairobi City Council considers it a forest, and it was not marked on Google and “OpenStreetMap” online maps, despite an estimated one million people living in this informal area smaller than New York’s Central Park. Although many non-governmental organizations, government offices and academic institutions have been involved in data collection and even mapping in Kibera, none of the results were publicly shared or available at a local level. “Map Kibera” was created to address this gap, based on the premise that without basic knowledge of geography and available resources, it is impossible for residents and other stakeholders in any community to have an informed discussion on how to improve the lives of citizens.
So in November 2009 “Map Kibera” trained 13 young people, one from each village in Kibera, in the tools and techniques of “OpenStreetMap”. Over three weeks, assisted by local GIS professionals, they collected data with GPS units and edited their map using open-source software. Since we were newcomers to Kibera, this was made possible through strong local partnerships with Kenyan organizations Carolina for Kibera, Kcoda (Kibera Community Development Agenda) and Sodnet (Social Development Network). We also worked widely with the technical and international development communities in Nairobi, building relationships for the project and involving participants from wider society.
Data without a story has little life. At the same time, we engaged community media groups in Kibera (the newspaper *Kibera Journal*, radio station Pamoja FM, and online video group Kibera Worldwide), showing how they could tell more effective stories using digital media and map information. Using the Ushahidi platform, we began development of a community media aggregator, which publishes reports with geographic context on *http://kibera.ushahidi.com/. Realizing that community journalists needed extra support in order to broadcast their stories, we trained Kibera Worldwide’s Flip video program in digital reporting and editing, and they accompanied mappers in the field.
The result is one of the densest maps ever created in the commons, poised for use in many applications, and an empowered nascent community of data users and storytellers in Kibera. Current projects emerging in Kibera based on this pilot include: a community journalism partnership among media groups within Kibera for improved reporting and online presence; mapping of the locations of CDF projects; merging map data with other research on Kibera from other organizations to create a shared knowledge base; a joint SMS reporting platform for local news and urgent needs.

Links: http://mapkibera.org/
131574.credits: Abdul Faraj, Anusa Pisanec, Arafat Mohammed, Douglas Namale - Mapper, Erica Hagen, Evans Kipngletich, George Otisno Ouma, Gideon Odiambo - Mapper, Gideon Victor Kapila Mwakina - Mapper, Hassan Yusuf - Mapper, Jeffrey Okoro, John Kipchumba, Joshua Goldstein, Kennedy Kibet Rotich, Kennedy Odhiambo Ogola - Mapper, Kevin Otieno - Mapper, Leonard Okwako - Mapper, Luchiri, Lucy Fondo - Mapper, Marimbo Fednance, Maureen Omino - Mapper, Midred Joyce Amwayi - Mapper, Mikel Maron, Millicent Achieng Odoyo - Mapper, Philip Thigo, Primoz Kovacic, Regynnah Awino - Mapper, Robert Muinde, Zack Muindi - Mapper
131574.biography: Map Kibera emerged as a crazy idea from a Nairobi Bar Camp in April 2009. Mikel Maron and Jubal Harpster developed a project concept, and found funding from JumpStart International. Much preparation took place before arrival, particularly facilitated by colleagues at Ushahidi. Erica Hagen and Mikel Maron arrived in Nairobi October 2009 to lead the project. Partnerships were quickly established with Sodnet, Carolina for Kibera, and Kcoda. A team of local youth was recruited, trained, and created the map with incredible speed. We are now working in partnership with Unicef.

131594.name: The Tor Project
131594.description:
The “Tor Project” is a non-profit enterprise dedicated to the research and development of tools, technologies, education, and advocacy of online privacy and anonymity. Our products are released as free software, free documentation and a volunteer-run “Tor” network. As a result, we are the largest anonymity network on the Internet today. We estimate that roughly 2,000 volunteers currently run relays and around half a million people use *Tor* daily. There have been 30 million downloads of “Tor” over the past two years.
The objectives of the “Tor Project” are to develop and establish a community-run network that provides reliable anonymity and privacy to anyone with the “Tor” software. We want to be the leaders in the relevant fields of research as well as the domain experts in anonymity and privacy online. We need a large community of people working as peers in order to achieve these goals. A decentralized model removes the need to trust any one entity over another and provides for long-term sustainability of the community.

Links: https://www.torproject.org/
131594.biography: Tor was originally designed, implemented and deployed as a third-generation onion-routing project of the Naval Research Laboratory. It was originally developed with the U.S. Navy in mind for the primary purpose of protecting government communications. Today it is used every day for a wide variety of purposes by the military, journalists, law enforcement officers, activists and many others. The “Tor Project” is composed of a growing group of people committed to providing online anonymity and privacy. The list of active and past contributors to “Tor” can be found at https://www.torproject.org/people.

131600.name: MakerBot Operators
131600.description:
Up until last year, 3D printing could only be done by the wealthy or those with access to elite institutions. The “MakerBot” 3D printer is cheap and open source and comes as a kit. Once you’ve put it together, you’re a “MakerBot” operator. “MakerBot” operators work together to bring 3D printers to the desktops of the world and to create a community around digital design and community innovation. With a “MakerBot”, anyone can create an object from a digital design in less time than it takes to go to the store. The “MakerBot” operator community has participated in the machine's development and the community members support each other by sharing designs and helping each other to create beautiful and practical 3D printed objects on Thingiverse.com.
The project is fully open source. The machine’s design files, electronics and software are all openly documented under GPLv3 and the community encourages open-source licenses for digital design files.
The greatest thing is that the “MakerBot” operator community is united in developing the infrastructure to make it easy so more and more people will be able to create things on their 3D printers instead of going to the store. Members of the “MakerBot” community are also exploring ways of using 3D printers to help with disaster relief.
A recent example that showcases how great the community is was Cathal Garvey, a “MakerBot” operator in Ireland with a mouse problem. He asked the community to publish open-source designs for mousetraps that would catch but not kill the mouse. By the next morning there were eight new mousetrap designs on Thingiverse! (http://www.thingiverse.com/tag:mousetrap)
The community has a Google group, a Flickr group, a Twitter presence, a Facebook group and an IRC channel.

Links: http://makerbot.com http://thingiverse.com
131600.biography: The “MakerBot“ operators community grew up around the open-source “MakerBot“ Industries hardware, which is a cheap and affordable 3D printing machine. The digital designing “MakerBot“ operators use Thingiverse.com to share and collaborate and bring digital designs into the world of the physical. The production team is lean, but there are over 1,000 members in the worldwide “MakerBot“ operator network.

131602.name: CBA - Cultual Broadcasting Archive
131602.description:
As the audio database principally for Austrian free radio stations, the “Cultural Broadcasting Archive CBA” is a central distribution tool for non-commercial media production. The open-access communication and exchange platform enables the mutual sharing of radio programs as well as access to and publication of content from sources outside the respective coverage areas of local broadcasting stations. More than 9,000 rebroadcasts from radio stations all over Europe have been documented since 2004 alone. The radio network community consists of more than 500 individuals, groups and editorial staff and regularly publishes content on http://cba.fro.at.
The long-term, joint archiving of media productions from 14 radio stations located in different regions of Austria has resulted in the emergence of a continually growing pool of alternative media coverage items, which are freely available not only for private use but also for research purposes. CBA reports on the social, political and cultural events of individual regions and, over the course of the last ten years, has become an important contemporary document of considerable local significance.
There are now over 13,000 audio reports on a broad range of subjects available for streaming, downloading or as podcasts: from ethnic minority programs to programs on women’s, media and migration policies, from critiques of globalization to programs about art, literature, independent cultural work or philosophy. The platform enables content, events and discourse that go largely unnoticed by the media to reach a wider, translocal public and supports simple networking and communication between producers and listeners through means of feedback.
The platform is continually being further developed and tailored to meet the practical needs of free-radio operators, in particular with a view to maximizing openness. This has led not only to a critical debate about the tension between the demand for public accessibility and legislation regarding the exploitation of intellectual property, but also to creative projects: the visual representation of the database (http://cba.fro.at/timeline) makes the archive more intuitively accessible, while the interactive audiovisual installation “Out Of Demand” (http://outofdemand.fro.at) makes it come alive in a sensual way.

Links: http://cba.fro.at/index.php
131602.biography: CBA—Cultural Broadcasting Archive began in 1999 on the initiative of Linz Radio FRO (Free Radio of Upper Austria). 2000-2001: The Austrian Association of Free Radio finances the project and further develops the platform to a significant extent, in accordance with the needs of the users. 2002: The archive is made available more quickly to non-German speaking radio producers through translations and workshops. In 2010 CBA is re-launched again and is promoted as an open source project. Participants: Manuela Mittermayr (1999-2000), August Black (2001), Roland Jankowski (2001), Ingo Leindecker (since 2000), Doris Prlic (2006-2009), Mario Kishalmi (2006), Thomas Diesenreiter (since 2009).

131603.name: Kloop
131603.description:
The Kloop Media Foundation’s primary goal is to develop journalism and new media in the Kyrgyz Republic. It does this by developing websites that work as a space for free expression and training journalists and bloggers. The main project is the “Kloop.kg” youth web portal. This fulfills two distinct functions: a news service with material by young journalists and a blogging platform for everyone.
The “Kloop.kg” web portal was established in June 2007 with support from the Dutch-based Hivos Foundation. During the first two years of activity its news service has become an important source of high-quality news for and about the Kyrgyz Republic. Material for the news service is produced by high-school and university students trained in the foundation’s media school. Annually more than 60 students participate in the training, and some of them have already been hired by other media. The blog-hosting platform at “Kloop.kg” now is the biggest in the Kyrgyz Republic (with more than 1,600 blogs as of March 2010).
The Kloop New Media School provides journalistic training for high-school and university students. Its main emphasis is on the development of practical skills. From the very beginning all students must start producing material that fits criteria of Western journalism (the BBC is used as a reference and role model). After review by the editor (of course, in the beginning there is always more editing) the material is published by the “Kloop.kg” news service. This motivates students, gives them important skills of working with the editor and under time-pressure, adds articles to the portfolio of work and provides access to feedback from their audience.
The average age of journalists contributing to the news service at “Kloop.kg” and studying at the New Media School is around 15 to 18. They deal with a broad range of events related to the Kyrgyz Republic: from politics to sports, from culture to economics. Despite their youth, “Kloop.kg” journalists often cover major events in the country much faster and much more accurate than other media.
During the April 7 revolt in Kyrgyzstan, despite possible threat of serious pressure from the authorities, “Kloop.kg” published information about the first protests in the town of Talas, when almost all other the media were silent.

Links: www.kloop.kg
131603.biography: The Kloop.kg (KG) web portal was established in June 2007 with support from the Dutch-based Hivos Foundation. During its first two years of activity its news service has become an important source of high-quality news for and about the Kyrgyz Republic.

131624.name: MediaDropBox
131624.description:
MediaDropBox“ ist ein Programm, mit dem man ganz einfach Multimediadateien für ein USB-Gerät umwandeln und Multimediadateien, die sich auf einem USB-Gerät befinden, abspielen kann. „MediaDropBox“ macht das Verwalten von Multimediadateien auf portablen USB-Geräten, wie etwa MP3-Player, Handys oder auch USB-Sticks, noch einfacher, weil die Bedienung des Programms sehr innovativ und einfach ist. „MediaDropBox“ unterstützt das Konvertieren und die Wiedergabe von Multimediadateien. Alle wichtigen Funktionen für das Verwalten von Multimediadateien sind in einem Programm auf einem portablen USB-Gerät vorhanden. Das Konvertieren von Multimediadateien ist besonders einfach, weil man nur die zu konvertierende Datei vom Dateimanager auf das Fenster von „MediaDropBox“ ziehen muss. Auch mehrere Dateien können konvertiert werden. Die Zusatzinformationen einer Audiodatei werden beim Konvertieren auch auf die neue Audiodatei übertragen. „MediaDropBox“ soll die Probleme mit unterschiedlichen Dateiformaten lösen. Bei der Installation von „MediaDropBox“ kann man verschiedene Konfigurationen für verschiedene USB-Geräte auswählen und muss die Kodiereinstellungen nicht selbst vornehmen.
Das Programm wurde auf dem Betriebssystem Ubuntu erstellt. Als Entwicklungsumgebung wurde NetBeans IDE (Integrated Development Environment) verwendet, und das Programm ist in der Programmiersprache Java programmiert. Für das Konvertieren der Dateien wird FFmpeg verwendet und für die Wiedergabe der Dateien MPlayer. „MediaDropBox“ besitzt eine grafische Benutzeroberfläche, mit der MPlayer und FFmpeg gesteuert werden können, um auch weniger fortgeschrittenen Benutzern die Möglichkeit zu geben, die Funktionen von MPlayer und FFmpeg nutzen zu können.

Quellcode und Programm kann man auf http://MediaDropBox.sourceforge.net/ herunterladen.
131624.biography: Romana Dorfer, geb. 1991, besucht seit 2006 die HTBL Kapfenberg Fachrichtung Elektrotechnik (Regelungstechnik). Ihre Interessen sind Radfahren, Fernsehen, Einkaufen, Schminken und Programmieren. Sie möchte später einmal Produktentwicklerin oder Produktdesignerin für Elektrogeräte werden.

131630.name: More Than Just a Box / Trashed
131630.description:
„More Than Just a Box“ handelt von einer Kiste, die auf einem Parkplatz steht, sich von selbst zu einer Art Gebäude entfaltet und sich wieder schließt. Das Ziel dieses Projektes war, reale Videoaufnahmen mit computergenerierten Bildern zu vereinen.
Damit das Endergebnis möglichst realistisch aussieht, wurde, freihändig und sehr wackelig, mit einer langsamen Bewegung nach links gefilmt. Auf dem Parkplatz wurden mehrere Papierstücke platziert, die einer Matchmoving- oder 3D-Tracking-Software als Anhaltspunkte dienten. Diese Software kann die Kamerabewegung des Videos im dreidimensionalen Raum fast exakt nachstellen.
Nachdem die Box modelliert und animiert war, wurde sie sozusagen durch diese virtuelle Kamera aufgenommen und in das reale Video eingefügt. Dadurch wirkt es, als wäre die Box wirklich auf dem Parkplatz gestanden und gefilmt worden.

„Trashed“ ist ein experimenteller Stop-Motion-Clip, der vor allem durch die verrückten Sounds und die nicht zusammenhängende Handlung lebt. Das Projekt war ursprünglich nur als kleines Stop-Motion-Testvideo gedacht, fand aber dann bei immer mehr Leuten Gefallen.
131630.biography: Florian Grünberger, geb. 1993, besucht das BORG Grieskirchen, ist interessiert an Film, Visual Effects und an elektronischer Musik.

131635.name: eEx NetLab, eEx Network Symphony
131635.description:
Das „eEx NetLab“ ist eine Software, die in C# geschrieben wurde und mit der man komplexe Netzwerkfunktionen und -simulationen einfach via Point & Click zusammenstellen kann. Die Oberfläche ermöglicht es dem Benutzer, verschiedene Komponenten wie Router, Netzwerkkarten, Geschwindigkeitsmesser und vieles mehr mit der Maus aus dem sich links befindenden Werkzeugkasten auf die Arbeitsfläche in der Mitte zu ziehen und diese dort miteinander zu verbinden oder zu konfigurieren. Komplexe Funktionen lassen sich auf einfachste Weise zusammenstellen und verstehen, da sämtlicher, durch das Programm laufender Netzwerktraffic visualisiert wird und auch aufgezeichnet werden kann. Die Programmbibliothek, die hinter der Anwendung steht, exportiert über 2.000 dokumentierte Funktionen, Objekte, Eigenschaften und Konstanten, die in eigenen Projekten verwendet werden können.

Darauf aufbauend wurde auch das Programm „eEx Network Symphony“ realisiert, das aus Datenströmen aus dem Netzwerk Töne generiert und so eine Symphonie des Netzwerkes bildet.
131635.biography: Emanuel Jöbstl, geb. 1991, besucht die HTBLuVA Villach (Abteilung Informationstechnologie mit Schwerpunkt Netzwerktechnik), Interessen sind Musik, Programmierung und Fotografie, er möchte später einmal an der Entwicklung neuer Technologien beteiligt sein.

131667.name: Vom Himmel gefallen
131667.description:
Mein Film „Vom Himmel gefallen“ handelt von zwei Aliens, die auf einer in der Luft schwebenden Platte leben. Eines Tages entdeckt das Alien Mike einen Koffer, aus dem ein Geräusch kommt. Vorsichtig nähern sich Mike und seine Frau Kate dem Koffer. Als sie ihn öffnen, sehen sie ein Minischlagzeug, das immer größer wird. Mike freut sich zwar sehr, denn er wollte schon immer ein Schlagzeug haben, allerdings hat ihm bis jetzt noch niemand das Schlagzeugspielen beigebracht. Ganz plötzlich fällt ein Alien vom Himmel, das genau so wie Mike und Kate aussieht. Dieses behauptet, dass es Mike das Schlagzeugspielen beibringen kann. Zuerst zeigt das fremde Alien den beiden seine Schlagzeugkünste. Anschließend nimmt das Alien seinen „magischen“ USB-Stick und steckt ihn Mike in den Arm, um damit die Schlagzeugdateien zu übertragen. Sodann kann Mike wie ein Profi Schlagzeugspielen.
Ich habe alle Stimmen der Charaktere des Filmes selbst gesprochen und dann in einem Audiobearbeitungsprogramm nachbearbeitet.
Für den Film selbst habe ich ein aufwändiges 3D-Programm verwendet und dann alle Szenen zusammengeschnitten. Für die Schlagzeugszenen habe ich bei einem Freund selbst Schlagzeug gespielt und das aufgenommen.
Die Titelmelodie zu meinem Film habe ich mir selbst ausgedacht, auf einem Keyboard gespielt und aufgenommen.
131667.biography: Michael Schmidl, geb.1998, besucht die 2. Klasse des BRG XIV, Linzer Straße in Wien. Er interessiert sich für Filme, 3D-Grafik und Sport (Fußballspielen: Verein Austria XIII, Snowboarden, …) und möchte später Filmemacher werden.

131669.name: HomeMadiLex Workshop Sounds
131669.authors: Matthias Bergsmann, HBLA für künstlerische Gestaltung Linz
131669.description:
Meine Arbeit ist ein subjektiver Rückblick auf die ersten vier Jahre an meiner Schule; eine Sequenz für jedes Jahr. Als Basis (Rhythmus etc.) dienten mir Musiktitel der Interpreten Eminem, Patrice, Gorillaz und Shantel. Diese wurden bewusst ausgewählt und stehen symbolisch für die Lieblingsmusik des jeweiligen Jahres. Das Original habe ich völlig entfernt und durch Geräusche ersetzt, da ich keine Rechte für diese Musik besitze.
Die Geräusche, aus denen sich die Sequenzen zusammensetzen, habe ich aus sechs Unterrichtswerkstätten mitgeschnitten (HomeMadiLex = Holz Metall Malerei Druck Bild Textil) und anschließend kombiniert. Die Zuordnung der Geräusche zum jeweiligen Jahr basiert auf der persönlichen Erfahrung, wie wichtig die Werkstätte im jeweiligen Jahr für mich war.
Ich filmte die Geräuschquelle und wandelte die Videos anschließend am Computer in Audio-Dateien um. Das Cover kreierte ich aus entnommenen Screenshots besagter Videos, die ich danach noch weiter bearbeitete.
131669.biography: Matthias Bergsmann, geb. 1991, besucht den Maturajahrgang 2009/10 der HBLA für künstlerische Gestaltung, Linz. Zu seinen Interessen zählen Musik, Filme, Videospiele, Kunst, Comics, Grafik/Design. Matthias möchte später künstlerisch (eventuell auch kommerziell) im Multimedia-Bereich (vor allem Audio) tätig sein, ein künstlerisches Studium in diesem Bereich ist sehr wahrscheinlich.

131705.name: 3d-dancing-diving-devils
131705.authors: Tolga Cosar, Matthias Zeni, dr.-Aloys-Weissenbach-HS, Elena Kihr, Johannes Christler, Philip Mader
131705.description:
Die Idee, einen Roboter zu bauen, der die Cartesianischen Taucher(Teufel) automatisch steuert, hatte Johannes Christler. Cartesianische Taucher wurden in der 2. Klasse im NKP-Unterricht (Naturkundliche Praxis) gebastelt und waren für alle Schüler schon bekannt. Für die Umsetzung seines Vorhabens hat Johannes seinen Lehrer/Coach sofort gewonnen, und ebenso schnell waren seine vier Klassenfreunde überzeugt, bei diesem Projekt mitzumachen.
Die ersten Versuche wurden mit einer 0,5-Liter-Flasche durchgeführt. Dabei wurde gleich klar, dass die Steuervorrichtung mit einer viel größeren Flasche umgesetzt werden muss. Den Luftdruck in der Flasche mit der Legopumpe zu erzeugen, war dann das geringste Problem. Viel schwieriger hingegen stellte sich die technische Umsetzung der Steuerung dar. Die Möglichkeit, mit einem Gasdruck- oder Magnetsensor die Steuerung zu verwirklichen, scheiterte am Preis für die Sensoren. Mit den Sensoren der Schule wurden dann Versuche durchgeführt, und mit einem Lichtsensor konnte das Problem schließlich gelöst werden.
Beim Umstieg von der kleinen Flasche auf die große 55-Liter-Schnapsblase kam eine neue Schwierigkeit dazu.
