Nach Erzeugung eines Luftdrucks von ca. 0,5 bar in der Flasche flog uns der Stöpsel um die Ohren. Doch mit der gleichen Verschlussmethode wie bei Sektflaschen wurde auch diese Hürde geschafft. Die videotechnische Dokumentation hat Johannes übernommen. Es war seinem Team und ihm ein Anliegen, nicht nur für die u19-Jury ein Video zu drehen, sondern auch Schüler zum Nachbauen zu animieren und das Video in Form einer Bauanleitung zu veröffentlichen. http://www.roboter.tsn.at
131705.biography: Tolga Cosar, Elena Kihr, Philip Mader, Matthias Zeni, Johannes Christler besuchen gemeinsam die 3. Klasse der Dr.-Aloys-Weissenbach-Hauptschule in Telfs/Tirol mit dem Schwerpunkt BioTeC (Biologie, Technik = Physik + Chemie + Werken und Computer).

131706.name: Is this Healthy? - Vom Barcode zu Gesundheitsrelevanten Daten am Handy
131706.description: Die „Ausgangssituation, die in diesem Projekt gelöst wurde, ist folgende: Ein Käufer in einem Geschäft hatte bisher nur schwer die Möglichkeit, sich über gesundheitliche Folgen und Risken von Inhaltsstoffen, wie z.B. E-Nummern in Produkten, zu informieren. Mit der Google-Android-Applikation „Is this healthy” ist es nun möglich, den Barcode eines Lebensmittels mit der Handykamera zu scannen und danach Informationen zu den einzelnen Inhaltsstoffen in Form eines Ratings (Smilies) und den möglichen Gesundheitsschäden (wie Krankheiten) zu erhalten. Dies ist für Personen mit Allergien und auch Personen mit Gesundheitsbewusstsein sehr hilfreich, da sich hinter harmlos erscheinenden Namen wie E133 oder Aspartam Gesundheitsrisiken wie Hyperaktivität, Asthma oder sogar Krebs verstecken können.
131706.biography: Johannes Schrefl, geb. 1992, maturierte 2010 am Europagymnasium Auhof. Seine Interessen liegen in der Kommunikationstechnik, und zu seinen Hobbys gehören Laufen, Radfahren, Snowboaden, Wind- und Wavesurfen.

131713.name: Move It
131713.authors: Julia Molnar, Bianca Biedrawa, Yuliya Potapova, Landstraßer Gymnasium
131713.description:
Der Film entstand im Rahmen eines Schulprojekts zum Thema „Animationsfilm und dessen Möglichkeiten“. Die Anforderung war, in einem kurzen einminütigen Film eine Botschaft zu verpacken. Diese Animation zeigt die Mischung eines realen Films mit 3D-Figuren, die zeigen, dass man in der Schule auch Spaß haben kann.
Der Schauplatz dieses Projektes ist unser Gymnasium, wo gezeigt wird, dass diese Figuren genauso in die Schule kommen wie wir, aber das Klassenzimmer nicht erreichen. Die Animation vereint auf kunstvolle Weise Musik mit modernen Elementen von HipHop und dem Wunsch, einfach auch in der Schule Spaß zu haben, und das allen zu zeigen.
Hinter der Musikauswahl stand natürlich der tiefere Gedanke, durch den Titel „Move it“ einen gewissen Grad an Beschwingtheit und Leichtigkeit in den Schulalltag einzubringen. Wir haben mit Absicht auf jegliche Handlung verzichtet und wollten nur gute Laune und Freude vermitteln.
131713.biography:
Julia Molnar, geb. 1994, besucht das GRg 3 Kundmanngasse/Landstraßer Gymnasium. Ihre Hobbys sind Tanzen, Lesen und Laufen. Julia möchte Journalistin werden.

Yuliya Potapova, geb.1993, besucht das GRg 3 Kundmanngasse/Landstraßer Gymnasium. Sie interessiert sich für Zeichnen, Lesen, Mangas und Radfahren und möchte Architektin werden.

Bianca Biedrawa, geb. 1993, besucht das GRg 3 Kundmanngasse/Landstraßer Gymnasium. Ihre Interessen sind Lesen, Tanzen, Reisen, Gitarre, Film und Schwimmen, und sie möchte Architektin werden.

131741.name: Brain Computer Interface
131741.authors: Armin Schnürer, Alexander Berth, HTL Leonding, g.tec (Guger Technologies)
131741.description:
Ist das menschliche Gehirn ein Computer? Zufälligerweise stießen wir vor einiger Zeit im Internet auf einen Artikel mit dieser Schlagzeile. Er handelte von einem Mann, der am Locked-in-Syndrom, hervorgerufen durch amyotrophe Lateralsklerose, litt.
Locked-in-Syndrom bedeutet, dass jemand körperlich beinahe vollständig gelähmt ist, gleichzeitig aber sein Verstand intakt und aktiv ist. Man sagt, lebendig begraben zu sein, kommt diesem Zustand am nächsten – keinerlei Kommunikation oder Bewegung sind möglich.
Die moderne Wissenschaft eröffnet Möglichkeiten, solchen Personen zu helfen. Sogenannte Brain Computer Interfaces ermöglichen Locked-in-Patienten, wieder mit der Umwelt zu kommunizieren. Ein Brain Computer Interface – kurz BCI – stellt ein direktes Kommunikationsmedium dar, das einen Menschen in die Lage versetzt, einen Computer ohne manuelle Interaktion zu steuern.
In Kooperation mit g.tec (Guger Technologies) hatten wir das Privileg, unsere persönlichen Erfahrungen mit dieser faszinierenden, zukunftsweisenden Technologie zu machen.
Unsere Diplomarbeit befasst sich mit dem menschlichen Gehirn und seinen Möglichkeiten, einen Computer mittels Gedanken zu steuern. Unser Ziel war es, ein BCI der Firma g.tec in die virtuelle Welt Second Life zu integrieren, um dort eine Figur zu steuern – ausschließlich mit der Kraft der Gedanken.
Die generelle Funktionsweise sieht wie folgt aus:

• Die mittels EEG gemessenen Daten werden zum PC übertragen.
• Die Daten werden verarbeitet und ausgewertet.
• Das Resultat wird an die jeweilige Applikation (in unserem Fall Second Life) weitergeleitet, welche die spezifischen Aktionen ausführt.
Der Benutzer sieht das Resultat und bekommt so sein nötiges Feedback, das für den Lernprozess enorm wichtig ist. Ohne dieses Feedback ist ein BCI beinahe unmöglich zu realisieren.
131741.biography:
Armin Schnürer, geb. 1990 in Kirchdorf an der Krems, besuchte erst die Unterstufe des BRG Kirchdorf und dann die HTL Leonding für EDV und Organisation (fünfjährig mit Matura). Seine Hobbys sind Kraftsport, Musik und Laufen.

Alexander Berth, geb. 1990, besuchte erst die Unterstufe des BRG Kirchdorf und anschließend die HTL Leonding für EDV und Organisation (fünfjährig mit Matura). Zu seinen Hobbys zählen Musik, Gitarre spielen, Reisen und Sport.

131779.name: Over the Top: Episode 1
131779.description:
„Over the Top“ ist eine Cartoonserie über zwei Freunde, die versuchen, sich in einer mysteriösen und geheimnisvollen Welt zurechtzufinden. Zusammen mit einer Einheimischen werden sie viele Abenteuer erleben und Gefahren bestehen. Wie es dazu kam, dass die beiden sich in dieser Welt befinden, wird in der ersten Episode beschrieben.
In ihr treffen Bob und Matt an einem ganz normalen Schultag im Schulhof auf ein Mädchen, dessen Verhalten auffallend und ungewöhnlich ist. Für Bob ist es Liebe auf den ersten Blick, und er begibt sich auf die Suche nach ihr, nachdem er sie aus den Augen verloren hat. Matt hingegen kann nicht nachvollziehen, wieso Bob so viel an dem Mädchen liegt. Zuerst hilft er seinem Freund, es wiederzufinden, doch sehr bald schon reißt ihm sein kurzer Geduldsfaden, und er beginnt, Bobs Motive zu hinterfragen.
131779.biography: Tarek Khalifa, geb.1991, besucht seit 2002 das Amerlinggymnasium in Wien, interessiert sich für Cartoons, Filme und Musikvideos und möchte später Cartoonist werden.

131800.name: Asyl
131800.description:
Als Erstes möchte ich eine kleine Information über meine Erfahrungen mit der Materie Film bekannt geben. In der Unterstufe der AHS besuchte ich den Freigegenstand Leseclub. Einige der gelesenen Bücher haben wir verfilmt, wie zum Beispiel Michael Endes „Die unendliche Geschichte“ oder „Schwarze Kürbisse“ von Malika Ferdjoukh. In kleineren Gruppen bearbeiteten wir eines oder mehrere Kapitel. Seitdem unser Klassenvorstand und Leiterin des Leseclubs, Prof. Sybille Wimmer, das Arbeiten mit Medien auch in unserer Klasse praktizierte, nahmen wir jährlich an verschiedenen Wettbewerben teil. Mit Manuel Tilgner produzierte ich in den letzten Jahren drei Filme. Allesamt waren Animationsfilme mit Plastilin- oder Holzfiguren.
Kurz zum Inhalt des Films: Der Protagonist flieht aus seiner von einem Bürgerkrieg geprägten Heimat in ein wohlhabendes Land. Dort erhofft er sich ein friedliches und glückliches Leben. Doch auf den Straßen zeigen Menschen auf ihn oder ignorieren den Fremden, indem sie ihm den Rücken zukehren. Dann versucht er sein Glück beim örtlichen Asylamt. Ohne Erfolg, sein Antrag wird abgelehnt.
Mir bereitet die Zusammenarbeit mit Manuel große Freude, denn wir sind ein eingespieltes Team. Wir haben meist ähnliche Ideen oder ergänzen die des anderen. Ein Punkt, der unsere Arbeiten von den anderen in unserer Klasse unterscheidet, ist Kreativität. Wir versuchen, immer neue Methoden zu finden, um jedes unserer Projekte zu verbessern. Diesmal haben wir über alle Bilder einen Filter gelegt, wodurch sie wie gezeichnet aussehen.
131800.biography:
Thomas Gatt, geb. 1995, besucht seit 2005 das BG/BRG Sillgasse in Innsbruck. Seine Hobbys sind Snowboarden, Schifahren, klettern, Bergsteigen (Mitglied beim Alpenverein), Musik hören, lesen, Computer spielen, Animationsfilm, Fotografie.

Manuel Tilgner, geb. 1994, besucht derzeit die 5. Klasse des BG/BRG Sillgasse in Innsbruck.

131807.name: Terraforming
131807.description: Eine Horde Roboter und irrwitziger Maschinen wird auf extraterrestrische Landschaften losgelassen. Getrieben durch den Befehl, diese Welt dem Menschen gefügig zu machen und auszubeuten. Zwischen Habgier und toxischer Strahlung brummt die Basis-KI, während sie Sauerstofftanks entleeren lässt. Solarfelder schimmern im kalten Morgenrot, und die aufblasbare Wohnkapsel wird für die Ankunft der menschlichen Pioniere versiegelt. Über dem verstreuten Lager aus Gewächshaus, Fabrik und Extraktor ist der metallen blitzende Orbiter stationiert – zehntausend Meter im Zenit, nur darauf wartend, neueste Atmosphärenproben zu empfangen. Gefroren und zerbrochen verwirft sich hier der schwarze Boden. Zum ersten Mal seit Ankunft steigt diffuser Dampf über die Ebene. Sodann heißt es vom Orbiter: Das Ziel der Mission ist die Verwandlung dieser toten Wüste in florierende Gärten – „Terraforming“.
131807.biography: Nikolaus Sulzenauer, geb. 1992 in Wien, besucht das Realgymnasium in Stockerau. Seine Interessen liegen im Spannungsfeld zwischen Kunst und Wissenschaft – primär Astronomie, Digital Art.

131811.name: Automatisierter Drehfußballtisch
131811.authors: Michael Moitzi, Stefan Polic, HTL BULME
131811.description:
Ein Drehfußballtisch wurde so automatisiert, dass eine gesamte Drehfußballmannschaft selbstständig agiert.
Motivation dieser Arbeit war, dass des Öfteren nur drei Leute zum Spielen anwesend sind. Um trotzdem ein Spielen zu ermöglichen, wurden zunächst Tormann und Verteidigung automatisiert. Um zu testen, wie weit man einen Computer mit unserem Wissen programmieren kann, wurde anschließend das gesamte Team automatisiert.
So werden nun Tormann, Verteidigung, Mittelfeld und der Sturm über mehrere Computer angesteuert.
Dazu suchen wir über Kameras den Ball auf der Spielfläche. Sobald die Bildverarbeitung einen Spielball erkannt hat, gibt diese die X- und Y-Koordinaten der Position zurück, auf welcher sich der Ball im Moment befindet.
Mithilfe dieser Koordinaten wird laufend die Position für die Spielerstangen des automatisierten Teams ermittelt. Wenn sich der Ball in Reichweite einer Spielerstange befindet, wird ein Schussbefehl an eine speicherprogrammierbare Steuerung (SPS) gesendet.
Diese SPS kommuniziert wiederum mit acht Servoverstärkern, welche die gewünschte Bewegung an die jeweiligen Motoren weiterleiten.
Die komplette Bildverarbeitung und Positionsberechnung der Spielerstangen wird im Programm LabVIEW realisiert. Bei der Bildverarbeitung wird pro Kamera ein PC verwendet, der Daten über eine UDP-Verbindung mit dem zentralen PC austauscht.
Weiters sollen die Bewegungen des gegnerischen menschlichen Teams mittels diverser Sensoren erkannt werden. Dafür wurden bisher unter anderem Magnetband-Längenmesssysteme verwendet. Weiters wurde eine herkömmliche Laser-Maus so umfunktioniert, dass wir mit dieser ebenfalls die Position der gegnerischen Spielerstange erkennen können. Vorteil der Laser-Maus ist, dass die Schuss- und Linearbewegung erfasst werden können.
131811.biography:
Michael Moitzi, geb.1991, maturiert momentan an der HTL BULME Graz-Gösting. Seine Interessen sind Basketball, Technik und gute Filme. Weiters macht er sich auch einmal einen gemütlichen Abend mit seinen Freunden.

Stefan Polic, geb. 1991, maturiert momentan an der HTL BULME Graz-Gösting. Seine Interessen sind Tennis, Fußball und Schwimmen. Weiters verbringt er auch gerne einmal einen Abend mit seinen Freunden.

131826.name: Chindogu
131826.description:
Anlass für die Entstehung dieser Arbeit war meine Bewerbung für die FH Salzburg, bei der das Thema „Chindogu“ auf kreative Weise umgesetzt werden sollte. „Chindogu“ ist ein japanischer Begriff für eine witzige Erfindung, die scheinbar nützlich ist, aber im Grunde mehr Probleme bereitet als löst.
Nachdem ich die Grundidee hatte, begann ich den Raum in 3D zu modellieren. So war es nachher leichter für mich, mir alles Weitere auszudenken.
Ausgangsmaterial für die 2D-Inhalte (Charakter und Zutaten) sind Videos, in denen mein jüngerer Bruder, Bernhard Riedl, die Bewegungen ausführt. Die Einzelbilder aus den Videos zeichnete ich nach. Insgesamt entstanden so über 1.300 Frames.
Mir ist bewusst, dass es einfachere Möglichkeiten gibt, um einen Zeichentrickeffekt zu erzeugen. Ich wollte jedoch nicht auf die besondere Wirkung verzichten, die durch diese Methode entsteht.
Die Musik sollte die gemütliche Atmosphäre unterstreichen, zugleich aber auch lebhaft wirken. Ich entschied mich für zwei Lieder von „Slagsmålsklubben.

Die Botschaft ist: Die Aussicht auf einen leckeren, mit viel Einsatz gebackenen Kuchen lässt mit ein bisschen Optimismus alle Probleme vergessen!
131826.biography: Johannes Masanz, geb. 1990, maturierte am BRG 15 in Wien und ist zurzeit Zivildiener. Seine Interessen: Animation, Musik, Sport. Er hat vor, Animation zu studieren.

131829.name: Der weiße Hai
131829.description:
Nach einem Besuch im Zoom Kindermuseum, wo die Kinder jeweils einen bestehenden Krimi weiterentwickeln, dazu Bilder malen, erzählen und animieren konnten, wurde die Idee geboren, einen weiteren Animationsfilm vom weißen Hai zu machen.
Diese Tiere sind sehr spannend, gefährlich und faszinierend, und außerdem gab es eine Dokumentation im Fernsehen, dass der weiße Hai vom Aussterben bedroht ist, da er gejagt wird, weil er eine Gefahr ist.
In einer Persiflage auf YouTube habe ich gesehen, wie ein Mensch einem Hai entstiegen ist, und das habe ich in meiner Animation verarbeitet. Ein Mensch wird vom Hai verschluckt, er kommt aber wieder heil aus ihm heraus, wie im Märchen. Dann gibt es noch die kleinen neckischen Fische, die den Mut haben und sich trauen, den großen Hai anzuknabbern. Sobald der Hai das Maul aufreißt, kann man auch einen Reifen sehen. Denn die großen Haie verschlucken alles, was ihnen vor die Nase kommt, auch Autoreifen, diverse Gegenstände, einfach alles – auch das war sehr faszinierend.
Die Arbeit wurde großenteils mit dem Computer gezeichnet, mit verschiedenen Pinselspitzen und Fülleimer. Die Animation wurde mit dem Programm Flash gemacht, und die Geräusche habe ich selber dazugemischt. Bei der Umsetzung hat mir meine Mama geholfen. Da es recht lustig war, möchte ich weiter einen Film machen – oder vielleicht auch ein Monstertruckspiel?
131829.biography: Matthias Riedler, geb. 2002, besucht die 2. Klasse Volksschule in Wien. Die Interessen sind sehr vielseitig, aber Lieblingsbeschäftigungen sind Computerspiele und GameBoy, Lego kaufen und zusammenbauen, aus allen möglichen Sachen etwas basteln. Auch die Schulferien sind sehr beliebt, da kann man endlich ausschlafen. Berufsziel ist Konstrukteur – da kann man planen und bauen, aber wer weiß, nach dem super Erfolg des Animationsfilms …

132206.name: capacity for (urban eden, human error)
132206.description:
This system uses a custom-built computer-controlled four-axis positioning table to “print” bio-architectural constructions out of moss and seeds. Suspended in a clear gel growth medium, the moss begins to grow and the seeds sprout. The algorithmically generated patterns drawn by the system are based on the Eden growth model and leverage mathematical representations of both urban growth and cellular growth, thereby connecting the concept of city with the concept of the organism. This project is also working to realize the idea of dynamic and fluid computer space altering the expression and formation of a living and growing biological material via its collaboration with an engineering mechanism.
The software of the piece began as a Processing application created by Mitchell Whitelaw that was modified to export code that communicated with Mach3. Mach3 is the CNC control software for the machine.
The structure was custom-made using aluminum extrusion rod, plastic and glass. For the mechanics, a rack and pinion system was implemented and a four-axis motor driver kit complete with stepper motors was mounted to the frame. The extruding mechanism, designed by Ryan Wolfe, uses a linear stepper motor, a custom circuit and an Arduino to communicate with Mach3.

Poetics of the Code
The Eden growth model is a surface fractal that has been used to describe bacterial growth. As stated by Philip Ball in “The Self-Made Tapestry”: “Watching a bacterial colony grow is like watching a city expand into urban sprawl, except that it happens in days rather than decades. The inhabitants of the colony multiply and what drives this multiplication and growth is a supply of food.” This association has also been made by applied mathematicians and urban designers. In his essay “Connecting the Fractal City” Nikos A. Salingaros writes: “Living cities have intrinsically fractal properties, in common with all living systems.”

Links: www.allisonx.com
132206.biography: Allison Kudla (US) is an artist-in-residence and educator for the Center for Experimental Media Arts at Srishti School of Art, Design and Technology Bangalore, India. She holds a bachelor of fine arts from the School of the Art Institute of Chicago, 2002, and is a doctoral candidate at the University of Washington’s Center for Digital Arts and Experimental Media (DXARTS). In her most recent projects, she has been exploring the combination of traditional pattern-making and plant tissue culturing to make hybrid living installations.

132262.name: Dirk, the homeless robot
132262.authors: Mirjam Langemeijer, Electric Circus, Fred Abels
132262.description:
Dirk is a life-size humanoid robot/automat who looks like a vagabond and walks behind a shopping trolley. His legs are driven by a (partly visible) mechanism located in the shopping trolley. The legs move in a natural way and with enough strength to make the robot walk as well as a human (and move the trolley).

The performance is purely a street show as this is the natural habitat of a vagabond. Dirk strolls through the streets pushing his rattling shopping trolley. Sometimes he pauses his journey to play a little tune on his organ and hold out his hand to collect some coins from the crowd around him. People have instinctive repulsion from homeless people but in this case there also is a strange attraction. This dilemma creates tension excitement and heated discussions among the audience. It is both confronting and amusing for the audience when they realize they have mistaken a robot for a human being. It’s an experience no one in the audience had ever encountered before (until now).

The inventor Fred Abels’ main goal is to create a robot that on first encounter would be indistinguishable from a human being. With the help of puppeteer Mirjam Langemeijer he has achieved and surpassed this goal. Dirk took his first steps in 2004. Finishing the Dirk project has taken several years. Fred and Mirjam are still developing Dirk to have more interesting interaction with the audience. Now in progress: during the performances Dirk is operated by a (hidden) remote control. The artists are now working on programmed functions and sensors to give Dirk a more autonomous life. Maybe one day he will stand on his own two feet, as a free robot vagabond, wandering through the streets.

Links: www.electric-circus.eu
132262.biography:
Fred Abels (NL) is an artist and inventor specializing in kinetic art. He has worked for the Kröller Müller Museum in the Netherlands, as a restorer for kinetic sculptures and as an assistant to the artists Dennis Oppenheim and Jim Whiting. His projects have been shown in galleries, exhibitions, dance parties and festivals worldwide. With his companion Mirjam Langemeijer he creates unusual street theatre with robots, playing all over the world.

Mirjam Langemeijer (NL) is a puppeteer and a maker of visual theatre. She has immersed herself in visual storytelling with her enchanting puppets and unusual objects. Mirjam has experimented extensively with the art of puppet theatre, in particular with street shows. Since 2004 she has been working with the artist/inventor Fred Abels. Together they pioneer new approaches to puppetry using several techniques such as animatronics.

132289.name: Measuring Angst
132289.description:
Birth and death are only a rewind button away. This is a world where meaning is found in a videotape. That videotape can be both rewound and fast-forwarded, endlessly replaying the best events again and again. Will the physical world eventually be subject to the same rules?
This sculpture is made possible by a system of armatures similar to those one might find within the prehistoric animal exhibits in a natural history museum. They differ in that they are mechanically driven and allow for varying positions of the broken pieces of marble. A system of electronic drives, stepper motors, ballscrews, linear shafts and computer software similar to what one might find in a high-tech assembly plant provides the movement.
Both the irony and beauty of this sculpture ultimately lie in the question, “Has this sculpture successfully cheated death, entropy and time?” We have become accustomed to the ability to pause the video, finding a frame just before the moment of death or just as we please. In a similar fashion, I wish to make a sculpture that cheats death and time.
Within the world of mathematics it is just as easy to go backwards as it is forward. It is only within human experience that going backwards poses such a problem. We and our perceived physical surroundings are locked into a series of moments where the future is possible and varied but the past is locked and cannot be revisited. Humanity has been slowly eroding the power of time to hide the past. This happened first with language, then with the written word, and now, after progressing through mathematics, to the media, modern technologies and sciences.
We now have tools that allow us to go back and re-understand, reinterpret and re-imagine what has happened. These tools have always been flawed by subjective perspectives and the limits of mechanical reproduction. Nonetheless, we tend to accept these tools and we live in a world where the past is more alive than ever. We have lost our hold on the specific moments in which we live and spend much of our time watching media. Living events are now viewed as if they have already transpired. Will we continue to live increasingly within manifested media worlds? This sculpture takes these ideas to an extreme where the physical object has been separated from media’s power to rewind and is finally subject to the raw linear power of mathematics and science.

Links: http://oppositionart.com
132289.biography: Jonathan Schipper (US) grew up in rural California. He holds a BFA from the San Francisco Art Institute (1996) and an MFA from the Rinehart School of Sculpture (Baltimore, MD. 1998). He attended Skowhegan School of Painting and Sculpture (2001). He now lives and works in Brooklyn NY.

132308.name: Bare Conductive
132308.authors: Bare Conductive, Matt Johnson, Isabel Lizardi, Bibi Nelson, Becky Pilditch
132308.description:
“Bare” is a skin-safe conductive ink invented by four designers’ intent on creating a new space between wearable technologies and electronic implants by applying electronic circuitry directly to the skin.
A thorough study of the history of body art and ornamentation led to the creation of an ink that humanizes wearable technologies and provides a sensuous method of applying electronics to the body through customized circuitry.
Temporary, non-toxic and water-soluble, “Bare” is composed of conductive particles suspended in materials that are commonly found in food and cosmetic products. This combination is the result of extensive research into a wide array of inert and non-toxic ingredients allowing for the safe application directly on the skin.
The design-led development process behind “Bare” generated over 120 different material samples before reaching the final formula. “Bare” has the consistency of paint and can be applied with a brush, stamp or spray.
The ink is currently best suited to low power, information-lean applications such as switching and simple data transfer. The ink has the potential to replace and augment existing technologies where wires are cumbersome or undesirable.
“Bare Conductive” seamlessly connects traditional forms of body ornamentation with contemporary wearable electronics, humanizing wearable technologies, and providing an elegant alternative for the application of electronics to the body via customized circuitry. “Bare” is currently being developed for use in medical devices, stand alone products, rapid prototyping and larger-scale applications in the built environment.

Links: www.bareconductive.com
132308.biography:
Matt Johnson (UK) has recently finished both his MA and MSc. Work has included the development of a skin-safe conductive ink and proprioception research.

Isabel Lizardi (US/UK) studied fine arts and Japanese studies at the University of Pennsylvania, and then moved to Kyoto, Japan where she studied traditional crafts for two years. In 2007 she moved to London to pursue a master’s degree in industrial design engineering at the Royal College of Art. She co-founded Bare Conductive Ltd.

Bibi Nelson (UK) did a master’s degree in innovation design engineering at the Royal College of Art, and before that she worked for Jason Bruges Studio, a Shoreditch-based design studio specializing in interactive lighting and installation.

Becky Pilditch (UK) is currently based at the Royal College of Art and Imperial College. She first became interested in prosthetics a few years ago during her mechanical engineering degree, when she realized that super + artificial limb = exciting opportunity.

132332.name: Men In Grey
132332.description:
“Men In Grey” emerge as a manifestation of network anxiety, a fearful apparition in a time of government wiretaps, Facebook spies, Google caches, Internet filters and mandatory ISP logging.
Operating at the intersection of hacking and invasive situationist action, any open wireless network becomes our stage for a reverse-engineering of network dependence and the implicit trust we place in the metal and minds that make it all work.
In the grey suit of an unidentifiable bureaucrat, carrying briefcases filled with hardware and software, the “Men In Grey” dissect wireless network traffic and then reflect it back upon its users to unsettling, yet often comical, effect. We do this using several advanced, automated hacking techniques, organized into six tactical groups:

The Glance
Any image downloaded by a user of the network will appear on the screen on the side of a briefcase.

The Utterance
Facebook, AIM, ICQ, Yahoo, IRC, MSN Messenger chat will also appear on the briefcase alongside loud recital through a speaker on the case using a text-to-speech synthesizer.

The Mirror
Full web-pages browsed by a user on the network will appear on the case.

The Forgotten
Earlier browsing sessions are “replayed” to the user on their computer, with each successive click.

The Lost Identity
Web pages are manipulated, URLs redirected, chat text altered, images seen on one laptop replace those in webpages of another.

The Trace
Detailed network topology, system fingerprints, routing tables and host-names displayed on the side of a briefcase.

Importantly, the “Men In Grey” never view the output of the briefcases and nor do they store any data. All logs are destroyed by crushing the storage device—a small SD card—under foot at the point of departure. This act doubles as our calling card.

Links: http://meningrey.net
132332.biography:
Julian Oliver (NZ/DE), is a New-Zealand-born artist, inventor, computer programmer and teacher based in Berlin. He has presented papers and projects at many museums, international electronic art events and conferences worldwide. His work has received several awards, ranging across technical excellence, artistic invention and interaction design.

Danja Vasiliev (RU/DE) is a Russian-born computer artist currently living between Berlin and Rotterdam. Working with diverse methods, technologies and materials, Danja
ridicules the contemporary affection for digital life and questions the global tendency for cyborgination. Works by the artist are often described as technological interventions, whether they are hardware, software or conceptual pieces.

132335.name: for those who see
132335.description:
The digital bit is everywhere, pixels can be found by the billion. However, as an isolated signal, it is worthless. Only in unison do digital signals have the potential to create meaning and beauty. For this reason, as part of my diploma studies I have attempted to find a “pixel” that, while being capable of producing a picture as a result of coalescing with other pixels, is also discernible as a single entity and elicits a certain aesthetic fascination.
Our sensory experience depends on electromagnetic waves. Although four of the human senses are not affected by light, the perception of light is in fact considered the most important of the senses in healthy people. What is interesting is that the same physical waves that allow us to see can be used in another frequency for the invisible transfer of digital data. Data and vision, perception and invisibility, together they form an interesting coexistence. The installation “for those who see” demonstrates this interplay by showing how a phenomenon which is actually invisible becomes a visibly perceptible “pixel”.
Sound pressure, created by means of a loud speaker located in a rectangular box, churns the air around a circular opening so that a vortex ring is created. The energy produced by the sound provides the vortex ring with momentum—invisible, just like the sound itself. This aesthetic phenomenon is only made visible by means of mist. If knocked, the vortex ring moves linearly in the air for a moment before it gradually loses mist and vorticity and disperses.
The basic structure of the installation is made out of a matrix of 7 by 7 boxes. Released singly into the air, the individual rings are perceived during their brief trajectory as forming patterns, surfaces, symbols and entities.
Although our visual perception is highly attuned to recognizing concrete information, this installation offers the opportunity to experience a moment of visual freedom: depending on his focus, the viewer is invited to contemplate at times the overall picture, at other times a small part of it, and to witness aesthetically how fascinating it can be to see something previously invisible to the naked eye.

Links: www.bitsbeauty.de/for-those-who-see/
132335.credits: Mentoring: Jana Patz, Burkhard Schmitz, Walter Scheiffele. Thanks to: Benjamin Frenzel, my bitsbeauty team.
132335.biography: Daniel Schulze (DE), his work encompasses the fields of interaction design and physical computing and has been shown at Ars Electronica, Linz, the Jewish Museum, Berlin, and the Museum for Communication, Berlin. In 2009 Daniel Schulze founded his own company, bitsbeauty, and since then has described his work as digital design—a hybrid of art, design and technology. His work has included a piece for the touring exhibition “Die Sprache des Geldes” at the Museum for Communication, Berlin.

132425.name: The Toaster Project
132425.description:
“The Toaster Project” chronicles my attempt to make an electric toaster from scratch—literally from the ground up. Starting with digging up the raw materials from abandoned mines around the UK, then attempting to process them myself at home, and finally forming them into a product that can be bought for just £3.94.
My toaster cost £1187.54 and took me nine months to make. I managed to obtain and process just five materials—iron, copper, mica, nickel and plastic—compared to the 100 or so used in the shop-bought version. The laboriousness of producing even the most basic material from the ground up exposes the fallacy in a return to some romantic ideal of a pre-industrialized time.
It’s an electric appliance that disavows the infrastructure on which it relies. A convenient item that rejects the convenience of consumerism. A mass-produced domestic product, “manufactured” on a domestic scale. Its contradictions, however, serve to highlight the amazing efficiencies of modern capitalism, but also to question our current trajectory. Massive industrial activity in the pursuit of additional modicums of comfort at lower prices - small trifles, such as an evenly crispy piece of toast, to which we quickly become accustomed.
I like toast though, as well as many of the other trappings of 21st-century life. But at a moment in time when the effects of industry are no longer trivial in relation to the wider environment, the throwaway toasters of today seem unreasonable. The provenance and the fate of the things we buy is too important to ignore.

Links: www.thetoasterproject.org
132425.credits: Thomas Thwaites (UK), with help from Simon Greton (video, UK), A Young Kim (book design, Korea), Daniel Alexander (photography, UK), Jan Cilliers (mining advice, UK), Irene Gunston (smelting help, UK).
132425.biography: Thomas Thwaites (UK) Technology, science, economics and culture … trends, fictions and beliefs. Thomas Thwaites is a designer whose work examines how these interact to shape our present and our possible futures. He graduated from the Design Interactions masters program at the Royal College of Art in 2009. As an undergraduate he studied economics and biology at University College London, and this training informs his design work. He imagines scenarios, designs products and undertakes projects that aim to identify and communicate ambiguities in technological and social change.

132427.name: Merrick
132427.description:
“From an unknown location, I break into Ikeas’s computer server. In this nerve center, the CAD files for every Ikea product are stored and downloaded worldwide. By infecting the CAD files with the ‘Elephantiasis virus’ I have just designed, I can hack the entire range of products. The virus causes random deformities, like lumps, cracks and humps, which only show up when the customer prints his product at home with his 3D printer.”

The “Merrick” originated during a fantasy about the development described above. The “Merrick” is a digital file infected with the human “Elephantiasis virus” and then converted into a tangible product by using a 3D printer. Every lamp that is printed will therefore be different. Three-dimensional printing at home might sound like science fiction. But it is far from unthinkable. Consumer 3D printing is still in its infancy, but is expected to spark off a new revolution.
132427.credits:
Technology: selective laser sintering; Material: polyamide; Color: white; Light source: 7W / 220-240V / 50/60 Hz / 55m; Editions: limited; Dimensions: height 32 cm, diameter 20 cm; Weight 1.3 kg

Platform 21, Amsterdam, (NL); Henk Bunning TNO Eindhoven,(NL); Leo Veger and Maarten Willemstein (photos); Supported by: Platform 21 Amsterdam, (NL); Funding: SenterNovem; Sponsors: TNO Rapid Manufacturing, Eindhoven, (NL)
132427.biography: Daan van Berg (NL), born 1976, attempts to play with appearances and the expectations these instigate. This results in objects, furniture or products. Furthermore, he works as a freelancer on projects in the field of interior design, architecture, visual arts and product design.

132432.name: Maelström
132432.description:
“Maelström”—an installation inspired by Edgar Allen Poe’s short story.

The story
A man and his brothers are surprised by the wind. Their ship is dragged into a powerful and destructive whirlpool and slowly pulled into the depths. Overwhelmed by intensity and exhaustion, the man’s horror turns into curiosity. He recognizes that the safety of the ship needs to be abandoned as only things of a specific shape and mass resist the destructive downpull. He attaches himself to a water cask and goes overboard, handing himself over to the vortex. His observations keep him alive, but his hair turns white and his limbs are weakened all in the space of just one day.

The installation
Psychoanalysis, X-rays and cinema have begun to directing our views to the inside of things and ourselves. Inner phenomena are difficult to perceive because we are either in their very center or outside. Natural phenomena may be too big or frightening for us to see completely. “Maelstrom” tries to combine these two perspectives to look at how the inner and outer worlds may interrelate when images, stories and information are flowing through our heads at accelerating speed. When things start to become blurred and foggy.
The installation melts down concept and technique, digital and analog to a working organism. It attempts a synthesis of cinema and sculpture and is based on generative, material processes. “Maelstrom” is an autonomous mirror of reality in which perception and dream, the visible and invisible, the imaginary and the material are to come together to form a whole.

Image, sound and animation
A machinery in the background of “Maelstrom” controls a powerful magnet that influences the complex behavior of magnetite particles suspended in a solution of water and glycerin. Custom-made software is responsible for guiding the endless drawing process. The sound mainly consists of the noises produced by the machinery. The combination of image and sound, of light and movement produce an experience that can hardly be documented. The particles’ fine material structures and groups can only be judged when seen for real. The magnetic nature of the particles makes them move as groups or surfaces. Every change influences the whole image. The surface is constantly in movement and caught in distant reactions. Cause and effect seem to lose connection.

Links: www.romankirschner.net/maelstrom
132432.credits: Funded by Communauté française de Belgique—Arts Numérique and the Ministry of Education, Art and Culture. Created in residency at Lab[au] office for architecture and urbanism.
132432.biography: Roman Kirschner, born 1975. His work is at the intersection of fine art and media art. He is best known for his acclaimed artwork “Roots”. He studied philosophy and art history in Vienna and audiovisual arts in Cologne. His work has been exhibited worldwide and received international prices, including ZKM’s 2003 International Media Art Award.

132442.name: Virtual Mirror - Rain
132442.description:
“Virtual Mirror—Rain” is a spatial intervention which senses the rain falling outside and literally mirrors it inside the building in its original form—water. There are 16 rain sensors outside, each connected to one corresponding drop maker inside. Every time a raindrop falls on a rain sensor outside, the same raindrop is synthesized and reflected back to the sky from the floor inside. The installation makes the rain “fall up” inside.
In addition to the exterior rain sensors, there is one rain sensor in the middle of the installation indoors. By dripping water drops on it, the visitors are able to interact with the installation and to activate all 16 drops to fall up simultaneously from the floor into the sky.

“Virtual Mirror—Rain” is a part of an ongoing series of installations entitled *Virtual Holes* and “Virtual Mirrors”. The series investigates the relationship between weather phenomena and the built architecture in urban environment, where our dependence on, and thus awareness of the external weather conditions is minimized.
In the preceding project, “Virtual Holes”, rain, wind and sunlight are sensed, coded and then literally synthesized inside in their original forms—water, wind and light, embodying the immediate weather conditions inside.
In the case of “Virtual Mirrors”, the phenomena are reflected—an active gesture directed towards the phenomena themselves. On the one hand, the interventions undo architecture, but on the other hand, they also enable the architecture to “sense” the outside weather conditions.
By directly influencing the interior, everyday weather phenomena acquire metaphorical connotations, while the built interior, being directly dependent on the external weather phenomena, becomes unpredictable. This newly established relationship between the inside and the outside blurs the border between the two. The installation enables us to see the daily transitory weather phenomena as something significant, not only within the installation, but also outside.
132442.biography: Tao G. Vrhovec Sambolec (SL/NL), born 1972, is an artist and musician. His works include audiovisual and mixed-media installations, interventions in public spaces and composed and improvised electroacoustic music. In his installations he investigates relations between evanescent phenomena such as sound and weather phenomena and architectural and social spaces. His works have been shown and performed internationally.

132446.name: Super Kingdom : Monarchy
132446.authors: Dugal McKinnon, London Fieldworks, Jo Joelson, bruce gilchrist
132446.description:
In 2008 London Fieldworks created “Super Kingdom”, an installation of animal “show homes” modeled on the authoritarian architecture of dictators’ palaces set within the ancient woodland of King’s Wood, Kent, England. In 2009 the artists re-purposed their forest-based installation as a film set for a digital moving image work: “Monarchy”.
“Super Kingdom” can be viewed as a social engineering experiment for animals—a new community in the making referencing despots’ palaces, gated community developments such as Alphaville in Brazil and the fortified exclusivity afforded to the wealthy and super-rich—all designed to keep urban reality at bay.
The title, “Super Kingdom”, is a reference to both the utopian imaginary and biological taxonomic hierarchy. The project reflects both human and animal hierarchy as territorial relationship to landscape; it is informed by changing habitat, the displacement of animals as a consequence of urban development and conservationist strategy, and global concerns about fluid populations and porous borders.
The project was initially inspired by reports of anomalous animal behavior in the natural world as a response to shifting environmental cues, and the controversial conservationist practices of re-wilding and assisted migration where animals are strategically re-located—redolent of human social engineering projects. The project also drew on the artists’ experiences of edge cities or self sufficient off-worlds and the collision of habitats and inequality that exist around them and resulted in the series of “Super Kingdom” structures referencing the off-worlds, the architecture of fear (as Tunde Agbola describes fortified lifestyles in Lagos), and the architecture of dictators’ palaces.
The score for “Monarchy”, by their long-term collaborator Dugal McKinnon, contributes to the sense of dislocation through shifts in what sonically seems to fit or not fit with what is seen. Mixing naturalistic sounds of flora, fauna and weather—recorded in New Zealand woodlands—with industrial noise results in a terrifying soundtrack for the English countryside, which serves to challenge our presumptions of the safety and longevity of the woodland environment.

Links: http://www.londonfieldworks.com/projects/super-kingdom/index.php
132446.credits: Commissioned by: Stour Valley Arts; Supported by: Arts Council South east, Arts Humanities Research Council, Henry Moore Foundation, London South Bank University
132446.biography: London Fieldworks was co-founded by artists Bruce Gilchrist and Jo Joelson in 2000. Their practice moves between landscape, the East-London-based studio and the gallery, reflecting an interdisciplinary enquiry into how natural phenomena and human experience are interpreted and manifest in science and art. Imaginatively sited projects typically engage with technology and the methods of science within a wider cultural context to explore data and narrative. Their projects are concerned with the mediation of experience and the exploration of ecology as a complex inter-working of social, natural and technological worlds. London Fieldworks recently returned from a British Council artists’ residency in the Brazilian Atlantic rainforest. www.londonfieldworks.com

132487.name: Ocular Revision
132487.description:
Biology, which defines the cell as the basic unit of life, is a discipline broadly impacted by an ocular frenzy of the modern age. Prior to the microscope, the life sciences were limited to anatomical investigations. Optical devices of this period include telescopes, microscopes, endoscopes, oscilloscopes and a multitude of related visual tools. The visual information produced by these devices was based around the lens, which like the eye that it aided was fundamentally circular.

Conversely, the DNA image belongs to a different regime of late 20th century screen-based information, Cartesian coordinates, x,y locations and the database. And while the 19th century marks the age of biology, the late 20th century marks the “post-biological” age, because DNA is increasingly understood as a code rather than a material substance. The post-biological turn marks a point of cybernetic fantasy in which the infinite complexity of the wet organism is finally humbled by the easily quantifiable genetic code that supposedly exercises total control over the flesh.

“Ocular Revision” is an artwork using an alternate mechanism for the analysis and display of the DNA image. Typically, DNA is visualized in a rectangular chamber containing a porous gelatin within an electrical field. When DNA is inserted into one side of this gelatin the electrical current pulls it across the gel at a rate corresponding to its molecular length and thus differentiates DNA by size.

“Ocular Revision” uses a custom-made, experimental circular-gel electrophoresis rig to visualize DNA bands. The radial design and inside-out polarization allows the apparatus to create DNA images reminiscent not of a “bar chart” or a “progress bar” on a computer screen, but rather a slow emergence, a signal, an attraction or repulsion.

“Ocular Revision” seeks to nudge DNA imaging back toward the realm of biology. The goal is to force DNA to be read as substance rather than mere code and thus hopefully break a deadlock in genetics caused by its overly simplistic operationalization. The images produced by the custom rig resemble geographic maps of the twin hemispheres. These “genetic maps” could be interpreted as simplistic form-based puns in which the circle is a visual metaphor for a heavenly body like the earth. But at a deeper level they call attention to ingrained metaphors such as “genetic mapping”, which are problematic because “mapping” implies (distanced) simplification, abstraction and exploitation.
132487.credits: Supported by: Renew Media (Formerly Rockefeller Foundation) Fellowship; University at Buffalo, Buffalo, NY. USA
132487.biography: Paul Vanouse (US) has been working in emerging technological media forms since 1990. Interdisciplinarity and impassioned amateurism guide his art practice. His electronic cinema, biological experiments, and interactive installations have been exhibited in 20 countries and widely across the US. Vanouse’s work has been supported by Creative Capital Foundation, Renew Media Foundation, New York State Council on the Arts, New York Foundation for the Arts, Sun Microsystems, Pennsylvania Council on the Arts, Heinz Foundation, Mellon Charitable Trust, and National Science Foundation. He is an associate professor of visual studies at the University at Buffalo, where he co-directs the Emerging Media MFA.

132489.name: FEAR 09/19
132489.description:
Did you ever get a compliment about your smell when you were not wearing a perfume?

Many individuals are highly sensitive to the smell of a component of body odor and sweat called androstenone. These people do not like the smell; they compare it to urine or perspiration. They decide whether or not they like a person based on smell.

I chose to work with men because their sweat contains a lot of androstenone. Nineteen men (bodies) from 19 different parts of the world have only one thing in common: they all suffer from a severe phobia – THE FEAR OF OTHER BODIES. Each man was given a special electronic device to carry all the time. During a fear attack he was to place it under his armpit to suck in his sweat. The collecting pad from the device was sent to me overnight. I analyzed and simulated the original sweat using headspace technology in my lab, Re_searchLab, Berlin.
The sweat molecules were then reproduced chemically. The manufactured smell molecules were microencapsulated in tiny bubble units.

The FEAR of smell
The smell of FEAR

The sweat smell bubbles have been integrated into a transparent, smell-neutral binder used to “paint” the walls. Only touching (the wall/the body) can break the bubbles and release the smells. The smells have all been placed next to each other without any clear borders, like bodies next to each other. They are only separated by the numbers found in the top left corner of each “portrait.”
132489.credits: Supported by: IFF (International Flavors&Fragrances Inc.) New York, Mr. Geza Schoen, Berlin, MIT, Cambridge
132489.biography: Sissel Tolaas (NO/IS), artist/researcher and professional “inbetweener”. After diving on oil rigs in Norway, I climbed out of the sea to study mathematics, chemistry, linguistics and visual arts in five different countries. Living in Berlin since the smell of communism. Working on smell, language and communication since 1990, connecting them to science, art, business, academia and children. Established the RE_searchLab Berlin, supported by the IFF (International Flavors & Fragrances Inc.) in 2004.

132491.name: EAR ON ARM
132491.description:
The “EXTRA EAR” was first imaged in 1997 on the side of the head. But this location was not an anatomically safe site and no surgical assistance was found to make it physically possible. In 2003, an alternate approach was taken, growing small replicas of my ear using living cells. The “EXTRA EAR: ¼ SCALE” was done in collaboration with Tissue Culture &Art and Symbiotica. But it was not possible to tissue engineer a life-size ear with a biodegradable scaffold. In 2006 funding was found to surgically construct and cell-grow an ear on the inner forearm where the skin is thin and smooth. This was both an ergonomically and anatomically plausible position, providing easy access to the ear and minimising its inadvertent scraping or damage.
The first surgical procedure involved inserting a kidney-shaped expander and port into the arm. Several times a week sterile saline solution was self-injected. The intention was to create a pocket of excess skin to assist with the ear construction. The first serious problem occurred when the expansion process was done too rapidly. A necrosis resulted, which had to be excised during the second surgery. It necessitated rotating the position of the ear around the arm, ironically matching the original 3D model and animation.
To give the ear its structure, a Medpor scaffold was inserted and the skin suctioned over it to provide the initial shape. The Medpor implant is a porous, biocompatible polyethylene material with pore sizes ranging from 100-250 micrometers. Because Medpor has a pore structure that is interconnected and omnidirectional, it encourages fibrovascular ingrowth, becoming integrated with the arm at the inserted site and not allowing any shifting of the scaffold. During the second procedure a miniature microphone was positioned inside the ear. At the end of the surgery, the inserted microphone was tested successfully. Even with the partial plaster cast, the wrapped arm and the surgeon speaking with his face mask on, the voice was clearly heard and wirelessly transmitted. The microphone had to be extracted several weeks later when a serious infection developed. In fact the artist almost lost an arm for an ear.
At present, the ear is only a relief of an ear. To fully realize the 3D structure, further surgeries are needed to lift the helix, to construct a conch and to grow a soft ear lobe using extracted adult stem cells. The ear lobe will most likely be constructed by creating a cutaneous pouch, which will be filled with adipoderived stem cells and mature adipocytes. It is still somewhat experimental with no guarantee that the stem cells will grow evenly and smoothly— possibly resulting in a cauliflower ear!
With the microphone re-implanted and connected to a wireless transmitter, the ear will become Internet- enabled in any wifi hotspot. A person in Linz will be able to listen in to what the ear is hearing in Melbourne or New York. A bodily structure has been replicated, relocated and now will be rewired for alternate capabilities. It will become a publicly accessible mobile and acoustic organ for people in other places. The body becomes an extended operational system—extruding its awareness and experience. The biological body is not well organ-ized. The body needs to be Internet-enabled in more intimate ways. The “EAR ON ARM” project suggests an alternate anatomical architecture, the engineering of an extra organ for the body: an available, accessible and mobile organ for people in other places. Locate and listen in to another body elsewhere …

Links: http://www.stelarc.va.com.au/projects/earonarm/index.html
132491.credits:
Acknowledgements
Surgical Team: Dr. Malcom Lesavoy, MD; Dr. Sean Bidic, MD; Dr. William Futrell, MD; Stem Cell Consultant: Dr. Ramon Llull, MD. Project Coordination: Jeremy Taylor, October Films. Funded by Discovery US. Ear On Arm 3D model and animation: SIAL, RMIT, Melbourne. Photographic Documentation by Nina Sellars, funded by the Australia Council for the Arts.
132491.biography:
Stelarc (AUS) explores alternate anatomical architectures. He has performed with a THIRD HAND, STOMACH SCULPTURE and EXOSKELETON, a 6-legged robot. FRACTAL FLESH remotely actuates the body with electrical stimulation. PROSTHETIC HEAD is an embodied conversational agent that speaks to the person who interrogates it. EAR ON ARM is a surgical and cell-grown construct that will be Internetenabled, for people in other places. Recent publications include “Stelarc: The Monograph”, edited by Marqand Smith, foreword
by William Gibson (MIT Press 2005). He is chair in performance art, Brunel University West London, and senior research fellow at MARCS Auditory Labs, University of Western Sydney. Stelarc is represented by the Scott Livesey Galleries, Melbourne. http://www.stelarc.va.com.au, Second Life link: http://tr.im/jFGN

132496.name: Der Kleine und das Biest (The Little Boy and The Beast)
132496.authors: Uwe Heidschötter, Studio Soi, Johannes Weiland
132496.description:
Since Haro’s Dad left home his mother has completely changed. She can’t play with him properly any more, broods over old photos, doesn’t laugh any more and her bad mood spreads everywhere. She has turned into a real beast. Haro has to deal with a lot of things on his own. Sometimes it’s great, but other times it’s truly exhausting.
“The Little Boy and the Beast”, produced by StudioSoi and directed by Uwe Heidschötter and Johannes Weiland, is realized with a combination of CG characters and 2D, hand-drawn environments resulting in a lush, warm and illustrative feel contrasting the film’s stark subject matter. The animated short was created for the German children’s TV show “Siebenstein” broadcast by ZDF/KI.KA.
132496.credits: Regie: Johannes Weiland / Uwe Heidschötter; Production: Carsten Bunte; Screenplay: Marcus Sauermann; Design: Uwe Heidschötter; Animation: Philip Rudolph / Johannes Schiehsl / Hugo Hernandez; Rendering /Compositing: Bin-Han To; Sound: Christian Heck / Music: Andy Groll; Supported by: ZDF Enterprises
132496.biography:
Johannes Weiland (DE), born in 1977, began his studies at Ludwigsburg’s
Filmakademie Baden-Wuerttemberg in 1998, where he is currently teaching
animation classes. Since his graduation 2003 he has worked as a director/animator
at Studio Soi Ludwigsburg/Germany and Studioaka, London. He has directed a number of award-winning films

Uwe Heidschötter (DE). In 1995 he began his education in design at Schule für Gestaltung, Cologne. He graduated from the Lycée Téchnique des Arts et Métiers, Luxembourg, where he studied classical animation. For several years he worked as a CGI character animator for Ambient Entertainment in Hanover. Currently he works as a freelance character designer and illustrator in Berlin. His artwork can be seen in his self-published book “Augenblick”, Ashley Woods “Swallow” books three and five and on his blog: heidschoetter.blogspot.com.

132506.name: The Man in the Blue Gordini [L'Homme á la Gordini]
132506.description:
End of the 70’s, an imaginary suburb, the custom is to wear neither underwear nor trousers, only orange tops. With the help of a masked rebel driving a blue R8 Gordini, Mister R and his wife plot a radical clothing revolution and the assault of monochromic orange totalitarianism.

The absurd and the idiotic, with a libertarian impetus aiming at the overthrow of social codes and values, here are the main characteristics of this story. A kind of slap in the face of conventions and propriety. To provoke against the grain, a bit as if one were to wander through a nudist village in shorts, not out of a sense of decency, but simply from a desire to be different.
But the subject of this story is not to criticize either the nudists or the emancipation of the
seventies, however. The most important thing for the main characters, is to break themselves free from any form of standardization, whether liberal, ideological, moral, or linked to tastes or fashion...
132506.credits: Director: Jean-Christophe Lie; script and graphic author: Jean-Christophe Lie; producers: Prima Linea Productions; Valérie Schermann and Christophe Jankovic; original soundtrack: DJ Moule; animation: Jean-Christophe Lie and Julien Dexant; backgrounds: Céline Puthier; compositing: Jean-Michel Bonnet; logos and posters: Pierre Di Sciullo; editing: Céline Kélepikis; sound design: Sébastien Marquilly; mix: Fabien Devillers
132506.biography:
Jean-Christophe Lie (FR), born 1970. His professional career began in the Walt Disney Studios in
Montreuil, as assistant animator. Later he supervised the animation of the Triplettes characters in ”Les
Triplettes de Belleville“, a film by Sylvain Chomet. Jean-Christophe then joined the team of Michel Ocelot
and Bénédicte Galup to create reference animations with the whole of the team of ”Kirikou and The Wild
Beasts“. In the Prima Linea Productions studio he gained his first experience as assistant director for Blutch
in the feature film ”Fear(s) of the Dark“. In 2008/2009 with the same production company he directed his first short film: ”The Man
in the Blue Gordini“, which won several awards, among others the Special Jury Award at CICDAF of Changzhou (CN).

132524.name: Precise Peter
132524.description:
Ever since the birth of his son, precise Peter has been looking forward to this day. The little tike is going to be introduced to the ins and outs of the family ritual at last! The fish has been prepared, the garden is ready and the sun is shining just as planned. The celebratory dinner can begin! “Precise Peter” is an amusing reflection about a barbecue which, to all intents and purposes, could have taken place in my own family. The son’s delight at being allowed to participate for the first time in the world of grown-ups exceeds even his father’s pleasure at seeing the family ritual unfold according to his well-honed plans.
In keeping with the father’s character, the world in the film is geometric. Every frame, every sequence and every object corresponds to an angle of 90 degrees. The color spectrum is typical of that of a holiday photo, illuminated for posterity by Photoshop. The precision of the 3D computer animation (Autodesk Maya) proved itself to be well suited to the manipulation of the film’s world. However, an animatic of finely detailed drawings was also needed as a starting point for an accurate execution of the idea.
132524.credits:
Screenplay, Director, Animator: Martin Schmidt; Sound Design, Music: Roman Beilharz, http://www.uvasonar.com; Produced at Kassel University College of Art, Germany
Funded by the Hessian Film Board (Hessische Filmförderung), Germany
132524.biography: Martin Schmidt (DE), born 1983. He studied visual communication from 2002 to 2010 at Kassel College of Art where he has been working since 2010 as an art assistant. He was a member of the jury of artistic producers at the Youth Media Festival Berlin in 2007.

132546.name: Nuit Blanche
132546.description:
A dramatic and visual short film, “Nuit Blanche” explores an experience many of us have had before—a fleeting yet powerful bond with a perfect stranger. Set in a dark cobblestone street in the 1950s, a man catches the gaze of a woman in a cafe across the street. This split-second moment becomes suspended in time, as the two gravitate towards each other in a hyper-real fantasy where nothing can hold them back.
An unforgettable moment with a stranger happens to everyone, especially in a large metropolitan city. It lasts for a split second and then things get awkward so we turn away. I wanted to take that moment of attraction and stretch it in a hyper-real fantasy where things unfold like slow- motion photography. I wanted to create something beautiful within the cliché. It is a daydream recorded on film that turned out exactly how we imagined it.
The actors in “Nuit Blanche” were shot in a greenscreen studio in Toronto. All the street environments and sets were created digitally in post-production with matte paintings of still photographs taken in Paris and Toronto. Pre-production took a few months of part-time work as we created an animated pre-viz and did numerous visual effects tests.
The challenging part was that we had to create almost everything. There was a huge volume of assets to make, from wet streets to 3D leaves and cars. But the hardest was trying to figure out what the main effects should look like. After breaking real glass at over 2000 frames per second on set, we realized that it would never look the way we wanted. We had to create and animate the glass in 3D. The visual effects took about eight months of work with Marc-Andre Gray as the main visual effects artist. It was a grueling process but it was a pleasure to do because we were very passionate about the project.
For 3D we used Maya and Mental Ray, 3ds Max and Vray. For compositing we used After Effects. The matte paintings were done in Photoshop and mapped in 3D. Editing was very simple as we only had about 24 shots. We used Adobe Premiere as it integrates very well with After Effects. Our computer was a first generation dual-core Athlon running windows XP. It is now considered an antique but we still use it!
132546.credits:
Directed by: Arev Manoukian; Produced by: Stephanie Swedlove & Arev Manoukian; VFX by: Marc-Andre Gray; Music by: Samuel Bisson; Starring: Michael Coughlan & Megan Lindley; Cinematographer: Arev Manoukian; Casting: Jeff Marshall; Assistant Director: Andrew Cividino; Production Designer: Arev Manoukian & Marc-Andre Gray; Art Director / Costumes: Dan Levy; Camera Operator: Jay Pavao; Camera Assistant: Max Armstrong; Gaffer: Alan Poon; Editor: Arev Manoukian; Compositor / Animator: Marc-Andre Gray; Effects Supervisors: Marc-Andre Gray & Arev
Manoukian; Additional Compositing: Arev Manoukian; Matte Painter: Pat Lau; Colorist: Andre Chlebak. Nuit Blanche is a Stellar Scene Pictures film produced in Canada.
132546.biography: Arev Manoukian (CA). Raised in a family of artists and engineers in Montreal, Arev Manoukian plays with art and technology to tell stories in ways that challenge his imagination. He recently turned one of his day dreams into a short film, the stunning hyper-real fantasy „Nuit Blanche“. After studying film in Toronto, Arev soon began directing music videos for local bands which went to air on Much Music. Recently he has directed interactive jobs for clients such as Mazda, Axe, Wrigley Gum, 20th Century Fox and the NFL. Arev directed Nokia’s interactive commercial „The Passenger“, a Cannes Cyber Lions and One Show finalist.

132591.name: Avatar
132591.description:
“Avatar” follows the journey of Jake Sully, a paralyzed former marine recruited to help a strip-mining operation on an extra-terrestrial moon. The harsh yet beautiful terrain of Pandora is home to an indigenous race known as the Na’vi. Jake’s mission is to infiltrate the Na’vi in the hope of enlisting their help. To succeed he must make use of a new technology that enables him to inhabit the body of a genetically bred Na’vi. This “avatar” allows Jake to escape his wheelchair and walk again.
To make the film possible, Weta Digital faced two major challenges. First, the world of Pandora had to be brought to life, complete with alien creatures, vegetation and landscapes. Second, a cast of unique digital characters had to be created, characters that could convey the emotional weight of the story and express the subtleties of each actor’s performance.
“Avatar” is not a typical effects movie, where visual effects are used principally to enhance and support the live action. There are entire scenes of the movie that have no live action; everything you see uses photo-realistic CG to create the world of Pandora.
Pandora is a dense, lush jungle filled with exotic vegetation and wildlife. Weta put this jungle environment together with thousands of digital assets and hundreds of characters and creatures moving through it. We used custom-developed software to paint the finest details of virtually every leaf in the jungle. To tell the story effectively requires the audience to relate to each Na’vi character on the same emotional level they would for a live actor.
Weta Digital devised a system of capturing each actor’s performance and translating it to their Na’vi counterpart with the highest level of detail. Getting faces right was a particular challenge. Making that happen required us to reinvent the world of motion-capture animation. This included new techniques using a virtual stage and camera where the actor’s performance translates to the digital character’s performance in real-time. Animators added ear and neck animation to complement the facial performance and we key-framed finger, hand, and tail animation.
The eyes being “the window to the soul” are the cornerstone of any believable CG character.There’s also a complex set of textures definingveins and skin blemishes. One of the most visually elaborate shaders we have allows each character’s eyes to react to light in an incredibly realistic fashion.
132591.credits:
Joe Letteri – Senior Visual Effects Supervisor; Eileen Moran – Visual Effects Producer; Eric Saindon – Visual Effects Supervisor; Dan Lemmon – Visual Effects
Supervisor; Guy Williams – Visual Effects Supervisor
132591.biography: Weta Digital (NZ) is a world-leading visual-effects company based in Wellington, which provides a full suite of digital production services for feature films and high-end commercials, from concept design to cutting-edge 3D animation. Weta was formed in 1993 by a group of young New Zealand film makers, including Peter Jackson, Richard Taylor and Jamie Selkirk. It later split into two specialized halves – Weta Digital (digital effects) and Weta Workshop (physical effects). Weta provided visual effects for Peter Jackson’s blockbuster movies “The Lord of the Rings trilogy”, “King Kong” and many other Hollywood productions among them “I, Robot”, “X-Men: The Last Stand”, “The Day the Earth Stood Still”, and “The Lovely Bones”. Most recently Weta Digital has completed work on James Cameron’s “Avatar ”.

132596.name: Alma
132596.description:
Alma, a little girl, skips through the snow-covered streets of a small town. Her attention is caught by a strange doll in an antique toy shop window. Fascinated, Alma decides to enter …
„Alma“ is an independent CG short film. It is Rodrigo Blaas’s first short film as a director. Originally from Spain, he has worked in animation for more than ten years, in Spain and in the United States. Seizing the possibility of directing his first independent short film, he asked some of the best artists in their field to take part in this independent project: French animator Bolhem Bouchiba, character designers Carlos Grangel and Sergio Pablos, art director Alfonso Blaas, music composer Mastretta and sound designer Tom Myers.
132596.biography:
Rodrigo Blaas (US) Is a self-taught animator who has worked in animation for more than ten years. He joined Blue Sky Studio in 2000 where he worked on his first feature film, “Ice Age” (2002). He was an animator at Pixar for six years, and worked on projects such as “Finding Nemo” (2003), “The Incredibles” (2004), “Cars” (2006), „Ratatouille“ (2007) and “Wall-E” (2008). In 2007, Rodrigo decided to direct his first short film, “Alma”, with an
international team. Artists from Spain, France and the US took part in this project.

132625.name: Logorama
132625.authors: Hervé de Crecy, Francois Alaux, Ludvovic Houplain, Autour de Minuit, H5
132625.description:
“Logorama”, is a 3D mash-up of corporate imagery, irreverent humor and break-neck Hollywood action. Spectacular car chases, an intense hostage crisis, wild animals rampaging through the city, and even more in “Logorama”!
“Logorama” has been praised by international audiences for its thrill-ride story and its special take on society’s obsessions with brands. The first short film (17 min.), directed by H5, “is created entirely out of real-world logotypes and brand characters. In it, you’ll see the Michelin Man, the Haribo Kid, Bob’s Big Boy, Mr. Pringle and Ronald McDonald, but in some very unfamiliar roles playing the classic movie archetypes of good guys, bad guys and foils.” (Ann-Christine Diaz, Creativity Online)
132625.credits:
Written and directed by H5 (François Alaux, Hervé de Crécy, Ludovic Houplain); Production: Autour de Minuit, France. http://www.logorama-themovie.com
http://blog.autourdeminuit.com/production/logorama/
132625.biography: H5 (François Alaux, Hervé de Crécy, Ludovic Houplain) (FR) “Logorama” was directed within the collective H5 by François Alaux, Hervé de Crécy and Ludovic Houplain, who have directed many music videos and are regularly invited to exhibitions for their artistic talents. “Logorama” is their first short film.

132661.name: Nokta .
132661.description:
“Nokta .” (Dot .) is an abstract short film project which has a creative, distinctive style of production and is an improvisation of organic pieces while considering themes such as power, control and luck. Using low-budget equipment and with the combination of actual camera shooting, 2D and 3D animation techniques, the film alters the reality and physics of the real world using liquid and dynamic simulations.
Even though the film is not produced according to Amos Funkenstein’s text on harmony, this is nevertheless a convenient statement for the stylistic and representational behavior of the film. “I see some correspondence between the foundation of universal harmony on an elliptical orbit and the predilection for the elliptic forms in Baroque architecture. In both cases harmony is still defined as unity within multiplicity, but it ceased to be static, namely, harmony expressed in one ideal geometrical form, and became so to speak dynamic. What was previously regarded as the deviation from the ideal form, was comprehended for the first time as an integral part of the form, or form of forms, which are capable of endless transitions one into another.“ (Amos Funkenstein, “The Dialectical Preparation of Scientific Revolutions: On the Role of Hypothetical Reasoning in the Emergence of Copernican Astronomy and Galilean Mechanics.”)
132661.credits: Art Direction, Design, Animation, Compositing: Onur Senturk, Turkey; Music, Soundfx: Echolab | Gavin Little, Ireland; http://www.echolab.tv
132661.biography:
Onur Senturk (TR) is a freelance designer and director. He studied traditional painting and figure
drawing followed by a traditional animation degree as his BFA. He took part in several international and national collaborative exhibitions with works in both print and time-based media. He co-directed Iskat, which won the Best Experimental Short Film Award in 13th International Golden Cocoon Film Festival in 2006.

132680.name: Ormie
132680.description:
Ormie is a pig with a problem. Ormie likes cookies . . . if only he could reach them! Can anything stand in the way between a pig and his sweet obsession? Find out in the latest short sensation from Starz Animation.
Early in the production of “Ormie”, clear aesthetic goals were established by spending time sketching and storyboarding the character’s subtle and extreme actions. This made for a smooth and appealing transition from the hand-drawn designs into 3D animation. Computer-generated characters and props are composed over abstract watercolor paintings used to frame the action and support the illusion of Ormie’s surreal world. Through his escalating emotional performance, Ormie demonstrates squash-and-stretch deformation, clean storytelling poses, comedic timing as well as the inventive imaginations of the team behind the character.
