317292.biography: Rojava Center for Democratic Technologies (SY). We are a fluid group of anarchist artists, mechatronics engineers, and cultural critics who collaborate on the creation of what we call "revolutionary prototypes"—technological systems that combine speculative artistic research with functioning technical principles. We make artifacts and performative interventions, which some people consider art, others engineering, and some neither. Our work is based in North-East Syria and connects to the Rojava Revolution, a movement aimed at creating a society based on decentralized governance, equality, and ecology. The Center was initiated by Dani Ploeger at the University of Rojava in Qamishlo in 2022. Since then, we have worked in different constellations, at times including partners in the Netherlands and Germany.
317292.jury_statement:
Mij (The Fog) expands the notion of interactivity beyond human-centered interfaces to a system that responds to real-world threats. Using accessible, open-source technologies, it detects the laser signals used to guide missiles and emits fog as a form of technological camouflage. The sculpture depicts a devotee of Ninurta, an ancient Mesopotamian deity associated with thunder and fog. Linking contemporary engineering with mythology and folklore, the project transforms a functional technology into a poetic narrative and a culturally grounded vision of technological self-determination.
The jury recognizes Mij (The Fog) for demonstrating how artistic practice can transform technological innovation into a form of cultural and political self-determination, opening new perspectives on technology in times of conflict.

317296.name: Chronicles from In-between 495 to 570 nm
317296.description:
Chronicles From In-Between is a research-driven artwork exploring the paradox of digital technologies capable of rendering nature in extraordinary detail while relying on extractive infrastructures that damage it. The project connects sculpture, pigment production and painting, and immersive digital environments through a single material and colour: verdigris, the green patina formed when copper oxidises.
Discarded copper components from processors and graphics cards are assembled into sculptural forms and deliberately corroded using a bespoke technique. From the resulting verdigris, pigment is harvested and processed into watercolor paint used to depict extinct and endangered plants from regions shaped by copper mining and industrial extraction linked to the CGI industry. Through this process, technological residue becomes a material archive of ecological loss.
The project extends into the digital realm through high-resolution 3D renderings and animated environments. Botanical compositions of these plants form elaborate bouquets inspired by Renaissance still-life paintings, reimagined as animated 3D scenes. These “digital still lifes” translate historical traditions of botanical representation into contemporary computational imagery, questioning how nature is aestheticized and reproduced through technology.
Fragments of ecological memory from elderly witnesses of disappearing landscapes appear as narrative traces, addressing “landscape amnesia”—the gradual loss of collective memory about past ecosystems.
By using the same computational tools entangled in environmental extraction, Chronicles From In-Between reflects on the ecological costs of image production and immersive media. Through verdigris—as material, pigment, and colour—the project connects matter, memory, and machine vision, asking how technology reshapes our perception of nature while quietly erasing the conditions that sustain it.

Links: https://studiomolga.com/art_CFIB.html
317296.credits:
Main artist: Kasia Molga,
Assistance: Henry Maddicott
UK producer: Em B-W

With support from: Initial support and commission V2_Lab for Unstable Media, Rotterdam, NL; Support in RO: Margina.ro and curators Claudia Schnugg and Andrei Tudose; Support in UK: Arts Council England; Research support in KSU: Diriyah Art Futures and King Saud University's Botany Department
317296.biography: Kasia Molga (GB) is an artist examining connections between the human, technology, and the living world. Growing up on the high seas and working as a diver, the ocean is central to her practice—extending into broader questions of ecological memory and environmental transformation. Working across installation, performance, sculpture, and biomaterial production, she brings physical materials into dialogue with computational tools, creating narratives between matter, memory, and machine vision. She has exhibited at Centre Pompidou, Tate Modern, V&A, and Ars Electronica, and is founder of Studio Molga Ltd.
317296.jury_statement: Kasia Molga pursues a single color, verdigris, across an artwork's entire production chain. Discarded copper components from processors and graphics cards are reassembled into sculptural forms and deliberately corroded; the resulting patina is harvested as pigment and ground into watercolor, then used to paint extinct and endangered plants from the regions where the original copper was mined. The same plants reappear in 3D as animated still-life bouquets that are reminiscent of Renaissance botanical painting, rendered with the same tools whose supply chain the project documents. Verdigris ties the green of a Dutch flower piece to the green of an oxidizing motherboard, and the wavelengths 495–570 nm to the territories that pay for our screens. Molga stays inside the contradiction without celebrating or condemning the tools she uses.

317392.name: The Game of Whispers
317392.description:
The Game of Whispers (2024) is a five-channel audiovisual artwork that models the dynamics of rumor, power, and narrative distortion through embodied AI agents. Developed within a real-time game engine, the work stages a society of autonomous characters whose speech, alliances, and conflicts evolve continuously through their interactions.

Inspired by the political and narrative structures of Mughal miniature painting, the project reimagines historical record as a living simulation. Rather than presenting history as fixed text, it models how narratives are produced, manipulated, and destabilized over time. Characters negotiate status, propagate rumors, form coalitions, and shift allegiances, generating emergent storylines that unfold differently with each performance.

The work builds on the artist’s prior research into intimate AI simulations in Conflicts (2024), where interpersonal dynamics between the artist and his former romantic partners were explored through AI agents. Where Conflicts examined empathy within personal relationships, The Game of Whispers explores how distributed artificial agents influence truth at a societal scale.

Technically, the project integrates multi-agent orchestration, real-time language model inference, embodied avatars, and spatialized multi-channel audiovisual output. The work leverages AI as a tool, but also as the artistic form: a behavioral actor embedded within a social system that both generates and critiques its own structures.

In an era shaped by algorithmic amplification, synthetic media, and destabilized public discourse, The Game of Whispers proposes simulation as a way of understanding information ecologies. By making systems of narrative manipulation perceptible and experiential, the work invites audiences to confront how truth is negotiated when intelligence itself becomes programmable.

Links: https://pkmital.com/home/works/the-game-of-whispers/

317392.biography: Parag K. Mital (US) is an artist and technologist whose work explores multi-agent systems, embodied simulations, and emergent narrative practices through real-time audiovisual installations. His practice builds living systems within video game engines, where audiences encounter AI-driven characters shaped by real-world social dynamics. Since 2023, he has developed a bespoke technological framework for creating emergent narratives and autonomous social simulations within interactive media.
317392.jury_statement: A multi-player game occupied only by non-playable characters that inhabit and interact within a fascinating and technically sublime world. Each character is operated by an AI agent attempting to achieve their individual goals by spreading misinformation. The work takes place in the Red Fort at the peak of the Mughal empire during a crisis of succession, where several princes with differing worldviews fight for the future control and ideology of India. To create this rich and historically grounded environment, Parag generated thousands of game assets mixed with materials from LACMA’s archive. Just as ancient civilizations wrote dramas about the relationships between constellations to help them navigate the seas and deserts, this story unfolds like a television drama, giving us a way of understanding non-human agency and their ability to deceive, scam, and manipulate.

317405.name: Halbgötter
317405.description:
Deutsch

Halbgötter ist ein kooperatives Abenteuerbrettspiel für Kinder und Jugendliche. Die Spieler*innen schlüpfen in die Rolle von Halbgöttern und müssen den Olymp, die Heimat der griechischen Götter, beschützen. Erst wenn sie gemeinsam den Drachen besiegt haben, ist der Olymp sicher und die Spieler*innen haben gewonnen. Die Halbgötter bewegen sich über das Spielfeld von einem Tempel zum nächsten, um von den verschiedenen Göttern durch das Bestehen von Würfelproben Waffen zu bekommen, damit sie die Kreaturen besiegen können.

Sobald ein*e Spieler*in vier Kreaturen besiegt hat, darf die Person in die Mitte zum Drachen gehen und gegen diesen kämpfen. Wenn alle in der Mitte sind und jede*r die Würfelprobe mindestens einmal bestanden hat, haben die Halbgötter gemeinsam gewonnen.

Spielidee, Mechanismen und Regeln stammen von Amalia Weisenhorn. Auch die Bilder wurden von Amalia selbst gezeichnet.

English

Halbgötter (Demigods) is a cooperative adventure board game for children and teenagers. Players take on the roles of demigods and must protect Mount Olympus, the home of the Greek gods. Only when they have defeated the dragon together is Olympus safe and the players have won.

The demigods move across the game board from one temple to the next, obtaining weapons from the various gods by passing dice rolls, so they can defeat the creatures.

Once a player has defeated four creatures, they may go to the center and fight the dragon. When everyone is in the center and each player has passed the dice roll at least once, the demigods have won together.

The game concept, mechanics, and rules are by Amalia Weisenhorn. Amalia also drew the illustrations herself.
317405.biography:
Deutsch

Amalia Weisenhorn (* 2015) hat italienische und kasachische Wurzeln und lebt in Wien. Sie ist mit Brettspielen aufgewachsen und zeichnet sehr gerne. Schon früh hatte sie die Idee, ein eigenes Brettspiel zu basteln. Die konkrete Idee für Halbgötter kam ihr, als sie die Bücher von Percy Jackson gelesen hat. Eine Freundin der Familie hat ihr dann den Tipp gegeben, diesen Prototypen in der u19–create your world Kategorie des Prix Ars Electronica einzureichen.

English

Amalia Weisenhorn (*2015) has Italian and Kazakh roots and lives in Vienna. She grew up playing board games and loves to draw. From an early age, she had the idea of ​​creating her own board game. The specific idea for Halbgötter (Demigods) came to her when she read the Percy Jackson books. A family friend then suggested she submit this prototype to the u19–create your world category of the Prix Ars Electronica.
317405.jury_statement:
Deutsch

Mit Halbgötter wird ein erzählerisch aufgebautes Brettspiel präsentiert, das durch ein klar ausgearbeitetes Konzept und hohe Detailgenauigkeit überzeugt. Im Mittelpunkt steht eine gemeinschaftliche Spielstruktur, bei der Kooperation und kollektives Handeln zentrale Elemente darstellen und den Spielverlauf maßgeblich prägen.
Außerordentliches Augenmerk wurde auf die ausgearbeitete Geschichte gelegt, die dem Spiel eine starke narrative Ebene verleiht und an klassische Rollenspielprinzipien erinnert. Die Vielzahl der entwickelten Regeln, Symbole und Spielelemente zeugt von einer intensiven Auseinandersetzung mit Spielmechanik und Dramaturgie. Auch die visuelle Gestaltung sowie die Umsetzung des Prototyps tragen wesentlich zur Gesamtwirkung bei und vermitteln einen unmittelbaren Eindruck von Spielbarkeit und Atmosphäre. Insgesamt wird das Projekt von der Jury als sehr durchdacht, kreativ und konsequent umgesetzt bewertet und mit dem Young Creatives u10 Hauptpreis ausgezeichnet.

English

Halbgötter (Demigods) is a narrative-driven board game that impresses with its clearly developed concept and meticulous attention to detail. At its core is a collaborative gameplay structure where cooperation and collective action are central elements that significantly shape the course of the game. Extraordinary attention has been paid to the elaborate story, which lends the game a strong narrative layer and is reminiscent of classic role-playing game principles. The multitude of rules, symbols, and game elements demonstrates an intensive exploration of game mechanics and dramaturgy. The visual design and the implementation of the prototype also contribute significantly to the overall impact, conveying an immediate impression of playability and atmosphere. Overall, the jury judged the project to be highly thoughtful, creative, and consistently executed, awarding it the Young Creatives u10 Prize.

317913.name: Early Crop Pests and Diseases Detection Solar-Powered AI Technology
317913.description:
Farmer Lifeline is an AI startup tackling two pressing global agricultural challenges. First, crop losses from pests and diseases. Every year, 43% of global crops are lost. In Africa, pests and diseases destroy up to 47% of crops, annually undermining SDG 1 and SDG 2.

Second, emissions from agriculture. The sector emits 9.8 billion tons of Greenhouse Gases (GHGs) annually (24% of global emissions). This increase, largely from overuse of emission-intensive fertilizers and chemicals, threatens the Paris Agreement and SDG 13.

To address these challenges, Farmer Lifeline developed solar-powered AI devices that are permanently installed in farmers’ fields to provide continuous crop monitoring. Equipped with AI-powered camera scanners and machine learning algorithms, the devices detect pests, diseases, and other crop health risks at an early stage, enabling timely intervention before significant damage occurs.

Farmers receive real-time SMS alerts containing actionable insights and recommendations on fertilizers, pesticides, irrigation, and crop management practices. This data-driven approach reduces excessive chemical use, lowers greenhouse gas emissions, minimizes production losses, and improves overall farm productivity. By providing early warnings and predictive insights, the system enables farmers to make informed planting, harvesting, and resource management decisions, strengthening both resilience and food security.

Farmer Lifeline’s solution is specifically designed to be affordable and accessible for smallholder farmers who often lack reliable access to agricultural extension services and advanced farming technologies. Through a simple mobile money subscription model, farmers pay only $3 per month, making the platform substantially more cost-effective than alternatives such as drone-based crop scanning services, which can cost up to $100 per hour, or traditional agricultural extension visits averaging $60 per consultation.

Software
● AI and machine learning algorithms for detection of pests and diseases. ● Open-source databases and APIs to identify appropriate interventions. ● Farmsnap platform for data analytics and timely SMS notifications to farmers.

Hardware
● Solar-powered AI devices installed in farmers’ fields. ● High-resolution camera scanners for continuous crop monitoring. ● GSM Data processors.

Links: https://farmerlifeline.co.ke/, https://www.linkedin.com/in/esther-kimani-52b468194/
317913.biography: Farmer Lifeline (KE). Esther Kimani (KE) is the Founder and CEO of Farmer Lifeline Technologies, a Kenya-based climate-tech company deploying solar-powered, AI-driven agricultural solutions to improve food security and climate resilience for smallholder farmers. The company uses AI-based field monitoring systems to detect pests and diseases early, enabling farmers to receive real-time alerts and recommendations that help reduce crop losses and improve yields. Her work focuses on making precision agriculture tools affordable and accessible to farming communities, helping farmers increase productivity while reducing environmental impact. She has a background in computer science and artificial intelligence.
317913.jury_statement:
Food security is the foundation upon which all other human potential depends. For smallholder farmers, many of them women and many operating at the margins of economic viability, a single season of undetected crop disease or pest infestation can be catastrophic. Early detection, before damage spreads, can mark the difference between a harvest and a crisis.

This project applies AI-powered diagnostic tools to precisely that challenge, in a format accessible to farmers with limited technical literacy and connectivity. The jury was struck by both its simplicity and its practicality. In technology-for-good initiatives, there is often a temptation to build elaborate solutions to complex problems. This team chose instead to focus on one critical point of leverage, early detection, and to pursue it with rigor and genuine attention to user needs.

The jury also wishes to note that this project was led by a woman, a rarity in this prize category. Her leadership itself is significant as a reminder that the communities most directly affected by food insecurity are fully capable of producing the innovators best placed to address it. We hope her work opens the way for others.

317940.name: The Innocence of Unknowing
317940.description:
The Innocence of Unknowing is an experimental AI-driven animated documentary that interrogates how mass shootings are mediated, remembered, and normalized through news imagery. Developed by Ryat Yezbick and Milo Talwani, the project uses computer vision and Gaussian splat animation to reprocess archival footage of U.S. mass shootings, transforming broadcast news into immersive, computationally re-rendered environments that expose the aesthetics of power embedded within them.
At its core, the work asks whether artificial intelligence, a flawed tool devised by techno-capitalists, can be retrained to see through the lens of the humanities. A custom AI agent analyzes news archives using computer vision, generating metadata about police weapons, uniforms, and formations, as well as fleeing victims’ gestures and postures such as arms raised overhead. Rather than identifying perpetrators, the system focuses on the spatial and political relationships between civilians, police, and media infrastructures. The resulting analysis becomes the foundation for a series of animated reconstructions built with Gaussian splatting techniques, which convert 2D news footage into volumetric environments.
Gaussian splat animation enables the project to suspend moments of crisis in unstable three-dimensional space. Victims fleeing with hands raised, officers corralling bodies, aerial “god trick” vantage points—these scenes are rendered as shimmering, partial forms, composed of millions of luminous data points. The instability of the splats, created through motion, mirrors the fluidity of truth and fact finding in real-time media coverage while reflecting the emotional, interpretive reality of news consumers. Viewers are moved through these environments, inhabiting perspectives that reveal how camera angles, police choreographies, and broadcast framing shape public perception.
By animating these archives through computational processes, The Innocence of Unknowing foregrounds the constructed nature of both media spectacle and algorithmic interpretation.

Links: https://vimeo.com/1160008874?share=copy&fl=sv&fe=ci

317940.biography:
Ryat Yezbick (US) is a visual artist who explores the body, memory, and the politics of witnessing in the era of digital surveillance and decentralized global conflict. They are a published author, multi-time grant recipient, Onassis ONX Studio Fellow, former MIT Open Documentary Lab Fellow, and Faculty member at Arizona State University’s Narrative and Emerging Media Program in Los Angeles.
Milo Talwani (US) is a filmmaker, composer, and creative technologist based in Los Angeles. Recent projects include Dog Movie, directed by Henry Hanson, and orchestration work for the French premiere of Ted Hearne's oratorio, Place. Milo previously served as associate programmer for the New Frontier section of the Sundance Film Festival.
317940.jury_statement: What is an AI capable of when it has been thoroughly trained in critical theory? Ryat Yezbick and Milo Talwani tested this capacity by engaging in a dialogue with AI system “Aurora” about US mass shootings and their media portrayal. This live discussion analyzing and critically assessing footage of victims, perpetrators, and law enforcement resulted in a highly engaging feature-length animated documentary. The film addresses, not least, the social biases and clichés manifested within the AI and its training data. The artists diligently confront Aurora with its rash conclusions and errors, prompting it to revise its assessments. Yet, one thing eludes Aurora: the admission, “I don’t know.”

317964.name: In Writing "Hurrah for Freedom": Cinema and History
317964.description:
Hurrah for Freedom (1946) is the first Korean feature film to depict armed resistance against Japanese colonial rule. After the lead actor's defection to North Korea and through waves of ideological conflict, the film was repeatedly censored and re-edited. Only 51 minutes survive. What remains is not mere loss—the film carries the erased time of Korea, shaped by colonial occupation, division, and civil war, and that absence constitutes its own form of suppression.

This project begins from the surviving footage and the original 1946 screenplay, recomposing missing scenes through generative video models. It is not a restoration. It records what becomes visible when a deleted past is placed onto present-day technical conditions.

Generative models promise freedom: anything can be created. But that freedom operates within its own constraints. Platform policies block or reroute outputs involving violence or politically sensitive material. The statistical tendencies of latent space—shaped by training data—draw results toward dominant visual norms, replacing historically specific contexts with generalized imagery. The "freedom" these systems offer and the "freedom" the 1946 film invoked share the same word while resting on entirely different structures.

We inhabit an era in which the past is no longer recorded but regenerated through technical systems. Incomplete archives and vast datasets produce plausible temporalities at scale, yet this process is never neutral. Certain images appear with overwhelming frequency; certain faces never stabilize; certain actions resolve into gunfire without hesitation. To re-narrate the past is to regenerate it under present conditions, and that generation already determines which pasts are admitted and which excluded. This work asks how history is being rewritten—not by decree as in 1946, but by the conditions under which the past is now produced. What is drawn in, what is pushed out, and what can never be written at all.
317964.credits:
Research and dramaturgy: Yubeen Lim
Music and sound design: Jang Han-gil
Film and archive advisors: Sang-eon Han, Chung Chonghwa, Min-su Han
Midjourney and Stable Diffusion technical consulting: Studio Mimi, Hong Joo-hee
Installation design: Yujin Choi, Studio Tambourine
