320397.biography: Hanna Haaslahti (FI) is a Finnish media artist based in Helsinki, known for interactive, immersive works blending human presence with digital technology. Her installations invite people to participate in social simulations, using tools like real-time face generation, virtual doubles, and projections to explore identity, relationships, and crowd behavior. Her most recent work has focused on exploring narrative possibilities of Digital Doubles.
320397.jury_statement: How would it feel to witness those who have come after you, as an ancestor? What does it mean to share physical space with strangers, only to see your digital self sharing that space and exhibiting behaviors different than your own? Hanna Haaslahti’s Ancestors prompts us to grapple with these questions through her hyper-immersive work. Visitors position themselves in front of a camera, which renders them inside a digital environment alongside rendered counterparts. The work thus reimagines the animation one embodies in real life, pushing it beyond individual control and compelling viewers to decide how the shift feels. Ultimately, Haaslahti invites us to step beyond the regime of possessive individualism and learn to share our presence with others.

320398.name: Ping Pong
320398.description:
Ping Pong is a 3D animated documentary created in Blender, combining pre-designed animation with AI-generated voice dialogue. The film is based on a real conversation between the artist and an AI voice assistant, triggered by memories of a former college friend and the discovery of the friend’s political views on social media.
The project begins with a sense of “political loneliness.” In contemporary China, political discussion often remains difficult even among close friends, gradually replaced by silence and self-censorship. Struggling to understand why a once intimate friend had drifted toward a completely different political position, the author found himself unable to discuss these feelings openly with others. Into this absence entered an AI language model.
When large language models first became widespread, many people shared experiences online of discussing politically sensitive topics with AI. For some, AI became a strangely reliable conversational companion: patient, calm, and always willing to continue listening. In the film, after hearing about the conflict between the author and his old friend, the AI suggests writing him a letter and begins asking questions about their shared memories. The story unfolds through this exchange.
Yet while AI is highly capable of generating language, it still struggles to grasp the complexity of human emotion. The final letter it produces feels awkward, naive, and at times unintentionally funny.
But it is precisely at this moment that the author realizes something important: what moved him was not whether AI had truly “understood” humanity, but the absurd yet sincere interaction itself between a human being and a machine.
The awkward letter does not resolve any real conflict. Yet in an unexpected way, it briefly dissolves the author’s confusion and uncertainty, and ultimately encourages him to reconnect with his old friend once again.
320398.credits:
Director and animation: Tianji Yu
Dialogue: Tianji Yu & ChatGPT
Sound design: Victor Carvalho
Cinematographer: Yifan Wen
With support from: DocNomads Program
320398.biography: Tianji Yu (CN) is a Chinese filmmaker who studied in Europe and New York. He explores the dialogue between technology and storytelling, where reality and imagination overlap. His films unfold like intimate conversations with the universe, shaped by questions, dreams, and quiet reflection. His early work was grounded in observation and lived experience. More recently, his practice has shifted toward computer-based art, expanding into digital media, animation, and hybrid forms between documentary, fiction, and speculative storytelling.
320398.jury_statement: Ping Pong presents an emergent, evolving loop of existentialism. The work centers on a real conversation between the artist and an AI voice assistant. Disappointed by a close friend’s recent political decisions, the protagonist opts for the smooth predictability of an AI over the challenging friction inherent in human interaction. And yet, the AI ultimately prompts a reconsideration of the tension the protagonist experienced. Tianji Yu’s animation is crafted like a moving painting; the simulated wetness of the oil is portrayed viscerally. The sound design compliments the mood; the reverberation of the ping pong ball mirrors the pensive nature of thought. Ping Pong offers a powerful moment to consider what difference truly means.

320399.name: Constellation 2
320399.description:
Constellation 2 consists of three elements: a ring-shaped projection machine, a sourced rock, and a single strip of 16 mm film. On the body of the machine, four analog projectors are mounted, through which the film runs in a perfect continuous loop. At the center of the ring, a rock is placed on a narrow pedestal. Onto its imperfect surface, a distorted 360-degree portrait is projected from four angles simultaneously.

Up close, the portrayed person’s head appears to spin around its own axis. The images flicker, distort, and merge as the four projections wrap around the rock. At times we clearly see the person blinking, gazing into the void, only to morph into something unfamiliar in the next moment.
Stepping back and moving radially away from the center, additional rocks surround both the viewer and the central piece, each placed on tall, narrow metal pedestals. Together, these elements form a spatial and temporal constellation accompanied by the distinct rhythmic beat of the analog film projectors.

Being a part of a larger series of portraits on analog film, the work began with three basic concepts: to portray people who play an important role in the artist’s life while preserving an idea of their nature, to film 360-degree portraits of their heads on 16 mm film, and to select stones as a physical embodiment of each person.

In this intricate arrangement, Constellation 2 merges engineered control and measurement with nature’s fluidity and variation. It endlessly performs the unfolding of time and, through the interplay of its components, offers the intangible: the moving image, the essence of a person, and the futile desire to hold onto a single significant moment. As the viewer is separated from the projection by the machine, it becomes possible to see all parts at once: the film, the projection, and the mechanics. Again, at once, what appears is both an optical illusion and a map to how affection distorts and enhances the mind’s eye.

Links: https://nilsbenediktfischer.com/CONSTELLATION-2, https://vimeo.com/939250145?fl=pl&fe;=vl
320399.credits:
Creation and production: Nils Benedikt Fischer
Film, photography: Konstantin von Sichart, Antonio Castles
Text: My Sjöberg
Research: Valeria Ruiz Mendoza
With support from: Kunstfonds Bonn, NEUSTART-Kultur-Stipendium
320399.biography: Nils Benedikt Fischer (DE) studied Fine Arts at the Berlin University of the Arts and currently lives and works in Berlin. In his practice, he brings together sculpture, film, and engineered mechanisms to create arrangements in which images, materials, and movement enter into dialogue. Through carefully designed machines, he preserves otherwise fragile and ephemeral experiences—such as dreams, memories, and fears— by setting them into continuous loops of repetition. In doing so, he produces spaces where the work speaks through its own internal tensions while inviting viewers to adapt, project, and locate themselves within its unfolding.
320399.jury_statement: Constellation 2 offers a return to the roots of film and animation. Nils Benedikt Fischer’s ingenious mechanical contraption uses four projectors arranged at 90-degree angles. A continuous film strip circulates through these projectors, transforming a stone mounted at the center into a projection screen—or rather, into the object of projection—upon which the images of a human face merge. The projected human head appears to rotate around its own axis, pulling faces and opening and closing its eyes, all while the stone remains fixed in place. The inanimate object is thus brought to life and animated by the light.

320400.name: Dancing Plague
320400.description:
Dancing Plague is a video work based on a custom modification for the video game Grand Theft Auto V. The mod overwrites the workings of Los Santos—a fictional city based on the real world Los Angeles—with a simple alteration in the game mechanics: when the player presses the H key, all male NPCs are forced to dance uncontrollably. These feverish movements interrupt the default behavioral scripts of the game, which often focus on crime and violence. As drivers, construction workers, bankers, and airplane pilots abandon their routines, the system around them falls into a dystopian state of disarray.

The concept originates from a discovery the artists made in the game’s animation library: almost all of GTA V’s dance movements are reserved for female performers, often sex workers. Therefore, an NPC that has its gender boolean set to male will never attempt to execute these animations. By forcefully transferring them onto masculine figures, the work exposes the gendered assumptions embedded in the game’s system. Movements coded as seductive or decorative suddenly become uncanny when performed by male bodies, revealing how identity is constructed through gestures. The resulting choreography creates a visual language where masculinity is both liberated and challenged.

The video’s soundtrack is scored by Azu Tiwaline, a French-Tunisian musician known for blending contemporary electronic music with sub-Saharan trance traditions. Her track “Magnetic Service” underlines the mod’s themes of ritual, trance, and liberation. These associations are also evoked by the video’s title, which draws connections to the historical phenomenon of dancing plagues. Such manias occurred mostly throughout medieval Europe, where groups of people danced uncontrollably for extended periods, sometimes until death. By referencing these events, the work suggests a collective loss of control within rigid codes. It indulges in moments of hysteria and contagion, where subversive movement spreads, challenging both the logic of the game and the cultural norms it reproduces.

Links: https://2girls1comp.xyz
320400.credits:
Dancing Plague (2024) by 2girls1comp (Marco De Mutiis & Alexandra Pfammatter)
Music: Magnetic Service (Extended Version) composed & produced by Azu Tiwaline featuring Cinna Peyghamy with the authorization of Livity Sound & Cylid Publishing.
Created with: Grand Theft Auto V (2013), Rockstar Games
320400.biography: 2girls1comp is a modding duo founded in 2023 by Marco De Mutiis (IT) and Alexandra Pfammatter (CH). Their work changes the logic of video games as an act of creative counter-play, revealing the social and economic fabric in which they are immersed: from reclaiming global digital infrastructures to commenting on free labor within the capitalist ideologies of the gaming industry.
320400.jury_statement:
Dancing Plague is not a video game nor a machinima; it is an artist mod: a radical intervention into the architecture of Grand Theft Auto V. By modifying one of the most globally influential hypermasculine cultural artifacts of the twenty-first century, Marco De Mutiis and Alexandra Pfammatter, working collectively as 2girls1comp, queer the logic of the game from within.
Once infected by the “Dancing Plague,” male non-player characters abruptly abandon the behavioral scripts that structure the game’s performance of masculinity. They stop driving cars, cease acts of aggression, leave behind the spectacle of places like Muscle Beach, and instead begin performing stylized, feminized pole-dance choreographies. Through this viral disruption, the mod destabilizes the gendered codes, fantasies of dominance, and militarized masculinities embedded within the game’s world.
By introducing artistic modding as both a critical and aesthetic practice, 2girls1comp expands the political possibilities of game culture and digital art alike. Dancing Plague stands as one of the most incisive and subversive artist mods of its kind: playful yet deeply challenging the normative structures of digital masculinity.

320401.name: Deer Hunter
320401.description:
Deer Hunter is an assemblage of archival footage, family home videos, and a speculative form of documentary produced using generative AI. The work explores masculinity across past, present, and future through the artist's relationship to the men in his family: Italian immigrants fleeing fascism, who arrived in America in the early twentieth century, his terminally ill godfather, and his newborn son. By returning to Italy to film in the geography his ancestors once departed, the work traces a circular movement between origin and destination. The promise of America — once pursued through migration — reappears as both inheritance and burden, revealing how displacement, aspiration, and nationalism shape inherited notions of masculinity.

The film experiments with a hybrid form of generative filmmaking in which a synthetic animal is introduced into documentary landscape footage. An American white-tailed deer is generated using a custom model trained specifically on the species, then composited into the first and last frames of an existing shot. AI reconstructs the intervening sequence, interpolating the animal across frames while preserving the original camera movement, lighting, and environment. Generative sequences place the deer within Rome's Eur district — known for its monumental Fascist-era architecture — introducing a species that does not belong to the filmed environment and producing moments of ecological fiction: scenes that appear observational yet are constructed through machine learning.
The white-tailed deer occupies a central position throughout the film — at once an object of regarded beauty and a target for violence, particularly among men. Its seeming ubiquity in the United States makes it a subject almost every American has a relationship to. These generative sequences are juxtaposed with footage from a 1970 National Rifle Association film featuring an "American Hunter" reading from José Ortega y Gasset's Meditations on Hunting (1942) — a text ideologically at odds with the organization using it, deployed to lend intellectual cover to over a century of lobbying for gun access, at a cost that has left the United States with a gun homicide rate twenty-six times higher than that of other high-income countries. The voice and likeness of the "American Hunter" are used to generate additional sequences that weave historical and contemporary temporalities together. Passages chosen and assembled by the artist trace a search for closeness made possible only through violence. Calm and assured, the "American Hunter" narrates his own demise — his bravado and assumed mastery of the natural order intact — while his very existence is produced by a technology accelerating toward environmental and humanitarian catastrophe.
The artist's childhood home videos form the film's emotional core, connecting the viewer to a real landscape and a real deer. In them, men in the artist’s family document themselves through the technologies of their time, tracking a whitetail through forests. The artist's own childhood voice can be heard as he reaches toward a hunting tradition that stretches across his lineage — drawn into a performance of masculinity that the film simultaneously inhabits and undoes.
What the film ultimately asks is whether inheritance can be witnessed without being repeated. In staging this inquiry through generative AI, Deer Hunter knowingly implicates its own methods — the technology that reconstructs the deer, resurrects the hunter, and interpolates the past is the same technology reshaping ecological and social futures. Moving between the documentary and the generated, the remembered and the reconstructed, the film traces the distance between men through the performance of masculinity, a country and its myth, a deer in the forest, and a deer that was never there. It does not stand outside this condition, it—and by association— we, do not receive absolution, only responsibility.

Links: https://www.andrewherzog.com/
320401.credits: This video work was made possible through an Affiliated Artist Fellowship at the American Academy in Rome awarded by the Savannah College of Art and Design. Technological production support was provided by the Krea AI platform. Sound design by Tomas Ornelas. Musical composition by Spurge Carter.
320401.biography: Andrew Herzog (US) is an interdisciplinary artist whose medium-agnostic practice examines the constructed boundaries between humanity and the natural world — engaging the perceived liminal space between human and nonhuman life across personal and species-level temporalities. Fatherhood and caregiving have increasingly shaped his practice, informing investigations into masculinity and its role in the compartmentalization of human life from the natural world — traced through lineage, history, and the ecological conditions of the Anthropocene. Drawing on a background in creative technology and design, he develops accessible formal and conceptual languages through familiar materials and circular methodologies. His projects invite audiences to reconsider their relationship to one another and to the natural world.
320401.jury_statement:
One of the fault lines in democracies now descending toward collapse is nationalism: its exceptionalism, supremacist logic, delusions of grandeur, and the militarization and weaponization of patriotism. These political effects are precisely what propel the world’s largest democracy through increasingly fascistic mechanisms, accelerating its fragmentation. In Deer Hunter, Andrew Herzog channels this historical tension through a deeply personal lens. His grandfather fled Mussolini’s Italy for the United States, and the film traces a return to Rome, specifically to the Palazzo della Civiltà Italiana, the monumental architectural symbol of Italian Fascism.
Using AI-generated imagery, archival material, and family footage, Herzog stages a haunting portrait of a white-tailed deer wandering through the stark white facades of the palazzo and its surrounding landscape. In the film, a representative of the National Rifle Association introduces the animal as an “Ambassador to Italy,” positioning it as the face of America itself. Poetic, restrained, and quietly radical, the work becomes both a human and animal study of masculinity and nationalist mythmaking. AI functions here not merely as a tool, but as a conceptual bridge, linking fascist Italy with the authoritarian imaginaries of the contemporary United States through the symbolic figure of the white-tailed deer.

Exceptionally precise, politically incisive, and artistically elegant, Deer Hunter confronts the cyclical return of authoritarianism while turning its gaze across both America and Europe. The film captures the present moment with unusual clarity, reaffirming the enduring warning that “America’s chickens come home to roost.”

320402.name: Endangered Gestures
320402.description:
Endangered Gestures is a short film showing hand gestures for concepts currently under threat by authoritarian shifts around the world. Pairing censored words with gestures proposed by AI, the results sit somewhere between speculative sign language and technical error. The hands that appear are almost-but-not-quite-human, their unreliable digits forming gestures that hover at the edge of meaning.
The words corresponding to each gesture belong to a list of phrases that started disappearing from U.S. government websites, documents, and archives in March 2025. Ideas related to diversity, climate change, and social issues were no longer deemed acceptable and removed by hand or algorithm. Ironically, a large portion of the censored words read like a wishlist for a humane and equitable society.
Asking generative imaging technology to create hand gestures for these words is an ultimately absurd attempt at finding a language of resistance within the ideological constraints of the technology. The increasingly improbable gestures may leave the viewer wondering what strategies and contortions will be required of us to protect these achievements in the age of tech-enabled authoritarianism. Endangered Gestures is a reminder of things worth fostering and celebrating, rendered by the intelligence complicit in their erosion.

Links: https://eesly.xyz/endangered-gestures
320402.credits:
Written and directed by: Bruce Eesly
Voice actors: Lisette Poivre, Bruce Eesly
320402.biography: Bruce Eesly (DE) is a visual artist based in Berlin, Germany. Working with photography, archives, and generative imaging technologies, he examines how photographic images, classification systems, and technological infrastructures shape our understanding of reality. His approach employs humor and a blurring of fact and fiction to question narratives of technological progress and assumptions of photographic truth. Eesly’s work is held in institutional collections and was exhibited at the Rencontres d'Arles, Biennale Némo, and Hebbel am Ufer, among others. He was named a Foam Talent in 2026.
320402.jury_statement: Endangered Gestures arrives at a precisely urgent historical moment. Bruce Eesly notes that the words disappearing from US government archives in 2025, terms associated with diversity, climate change, and social justice, now read like a vanished wishlist for a more humane society. To prompt generative AI to embody these endangered words through hand gestures is an act of deliberate contradiction and absurdity: seeking a language of resistance within the very technological system implicated in their erasure. What lingers most, are the hands themselves. For years, fingers remained one of the last thresholds AI image generators could not convincingly cross, a marker separating synthetic imagery from photography. These imperfect fingers may represent one of the last visible traces of imperfection as a sign of the human. Their contorted gestures reaching for concepts under ideological threat feel deeply honest. Endangered Gestures emerges at the moment when every image must become suspect, interrogated not only for what it depicts, but for the systems that produce it. The work captures this threshold with remarkable clarity and timeliness.

320403.name: Exhibition³
320403.description:
Exhibition³: An artistic dialogue in virtual space and a search for new ways of presenting art in the digital age.

Visual Layer
Exhibition³ is an anaglyph 3D animation, experienced with anaglyph 3D glasses. Visitors enter a three-dimensional virtual exhibition, making the space tangibly perceptible. We (Sabine Hertig and Dirk Koy) engage in a dialogue, moving along the virtual x-, y-, and z-axes. At the core lies the interplay between naturalness and artificiality—the interweaving of real and virtual worlds.
From the very beginning, Exhibition³ is based on artworks, and the architecture is developed around them—custom-tailored and continuously evolving to meet their needs. The spectrum ranges from concrete, possible exhibition scenarios to abstract, utopian architectural spaces that can only exist digitally. By recontextualizing our own artistic works within a purpose-built virtual exhibition space, and shaping the form and atmosphere of the spaces surrounding the artworks, we not only take on a curatorial role but also seek a format where architecture and art merge into a total work of art. At the same time, the film reveals the process of reflecting on and staging the artworks, involving viewers in the dialogue between the artists.

Sound Layer
Just like in the visual space, various analog and digitally generated sounds collide and overlap in the sound world, forming a new hybrid whole. The acoustic composition is a collage of real and digital sounds. Physical environmental noises are combined with analog instruments like the violin (played by Sabine) and digitally created sounds (developed by Dirk). Here too, an artistic dialogue emerges between analog and digital sound sources. Dirk (digital) and Sabine (analog) deliberately work from their respective strengths but also record analog sounds together and collaboratively develop the composition further in the digital space.

Links: https://sabinehertig.ch, https://www.dirkkoy.com/, https://vimeo.com/1185862872
320403.credits:
Concept and sound: Sabine Hertig, Dirk Koy
3D animation, 3D modeling, compositing: Dirk Koy
With support from: Fachausschuss für Film- & Medienkunst BS /BL; Ernst Göhner Stiftung; GGG Basel
320403.biography:
Sabine Hertig (CH, *1982) is a Basel-based artist. Starting from analogue collage as a mode of thinking, she explores in drawing, painting, photography, and film the relationship between fragment and whole, as well as pictorial space in a digitalized world. She lives and works in Basel and exhibits internationally.
Dirk Koy (CH, *1977) is a Basel-based moving image artist. He blends analog, drawn, and digital elements into hybrid worlds suspended between concrete and abstract representation. His process-driven works focus on motion, traces and transformation, and have been internationally exhibited and awarded.
320403.jury_statement: Exhibition³ by Sabine Hertig and Dirk Koy invites visitors to explore the M. C. Escher-inspired architecture of a museum. The works on display appear to come to life, growing rampantly around the audience, or dissolving into complete entropy. For a long time, people have dreamed that video games would emulate museums, and museums would become like video games. In Exhibition³, these two worlds finally converge. Horror-action adventures and bourgeois media art are ingeniously and multisensorily interwoven in a dazzling audiovisual explosion. Furthermore, Hertig and Koy ensure that each exhibited piece is not merely translated into three dimensions but captivates on its own merits. This exhibition represents the ultimate utopia, even for the Ars Electronica Festival, demonstrating how art can devour its audience.

320404.name: FOREVER MEETINGS
320404.description:
FOREVER MEETINGS is a series of software-driven artworks of endlessly evolving conversations between AI-driven avatars.
Built in custom real-time software, each iteration runs fully locally (offline), foregrounding the tendencies of the model itself. Avatars are given opposing personas, a style of conversation, and a prompt (for instance: “gossip about whether the nuclear family is anti-feminist”), and the dialogue unfolds until the prompts refresh and a new theme begins. The works take form as large-scale projections, sculptural wallworks, and screen-based pieces.
Across the series, conversation itself is the medium. The avatars perform cliche cultural scripts, inhabiting exaggerated personas and rhetorical styles as they attempt to reason through questions drawn from the artist's own curiosities, positions, and lived experiences. Because the system continuously reshuffles prompts the dialogue never resolves, it drifts, repeats, contradicts itself, and evolves over time. The fact that the model is locally stored allows the work to act as a time-capsule of the moment the model was initially trained, with the prompts dredging through its ultimately static knowledge base.
The work highlights that LLMs as conversational partners are trained on human language, and reveals and exaggerates the patterns of discourse of its original training set. In its clichés, it's often ridiculous, but occasionally relatable, which can be equally disturbing as it is comforting: someone else has thought these thoughts before.

Links: https://sarahrothberg.com/FOREVER-MEETINGS
320404.credits:
Lead artist: Sarah Rothberg
AI System engineer: Yotam Mann
Unity development + Generative Animation System: Marpi
Original soundscape: Nailah Hunter
Production assistant: Han Zhang
Physical frame paint finish: Claire Hentschker
With support from: Onassis ONX; bitforms gallery; Jerome Hill Foundation
320404.biography: Sarah Rothberg (US) is an interactive media artist, creating playful, poetic, and usually a-bit-weird experiences that invite you to reconsider your relationships to the world around you. Rothberg's work engages with the impact of new technologies and communication tools, and takes many forms (ranging from installation to performance, software, video, writing, workshops, and experiments with technology). Rothberg is an Assistant Arts Professor at ITP (NYU), an inaugural member of Onassis ONX Studio, and part of collaboratives: MORE&MORE UNLIMITED and IS THIS THING ON?
320404.jury_statement: FOREVER MEETINGS actively resists the easiest interpretation of AI art: the idea that a work about AI, created by AI, often dissolves into its own premise. Instead, Sarah Rothberg’s artist hand remains clearly legible throughout the piece, evident in the construction of the personas, the intricate visual language, and the specific friction each pairing is designed to produce. This visual distinctiveness is what grounds the work. The aesthetic carries a signature that no prompt could reliably reproduce. In a field saturated with artworks exploring AI's inherent aesthetic tendencies, FOREVER MEETINGS retains the essential trace of the artist who made intentional, guiding choices.

320405.name: Le Miroir
320405.description:
Le Miroir is an experimental film exploring the fragmentation of identity through dreamlike mental landscapes shaped by perception, memory, and contemporary image cultures. The film stages my own virtual double, a MetaHuman generated from my physical appearance with whom I interact throughout a shifting psychological landscape. Simultaneously actress, avatar, and projection, I confront an unstable version of myself suspended between embodiment and simulation.
Structured around figures inspired by psychoanalytic archetypes such as the Ego, the Superego, the Id, and the Self, the film unfolds as an introspective journey through evolving perceptual spaces. At the center of this mental architecture, a luminous prism diffuses a hypnotic flow that alters perception, bends time, and blurs the boundaries between reality and imagination.
The project combines real time 3D animation, motion capture, photogrammetry, miniature physical sets, and filmed sequences. By integrating captured bodies into digitally reconstructed environments, the film creates a constant oscillation between material presence and synthetic space. Rather than opposing analog and digital media, Le Miroir explores their coexistence within contemporary regimes of perception.
The soundtrack combines synthesizers, electroacoustic composition, and spatial sound design to create an immersive sensory environment accompanying this psychological traversal. Through this hybrid language between experimental cinema, installation, and simulation, the film examines how technological systems reshape subjectivity, memory, and self-perception.

Links: https://www.camillesauer.com/en/post/le-miroir-1, https://vimeo.com/1102573272/f930804bb1?fl=ip&fe=ec

320405.biography: Camille Sauer (FR) is a visual artist, filmmaker, and composer whose work explores the intersection of sound, cinema, installation, and digital simulation. Combining analog processes, real-time technologies, and immersive environments, she investigates perception, subjectivity, and technological ecologies. A student at Le Fresnoy and a graduate of the École des Beaux-Arts de Paris, she is currently pursuing a PhD on the “Techno-Sensitive Organism” between Le Fresnoy and the University of Lille.
320405.jury_statement: Le Miroir is a compelling experimental animated film that explores identity through the encounter between a physical body and its digital double. Using a MetaHuman avatar derived from the artist’s own likeness and animated through motion capture, Camille Sauer stages a dialogue between embodied presence and algorithmic reconstruction through an introspective journey. Its strength lies in the integration of embodied and computational systems to produce fluid, shifting environments where scale, space, and perception are continuously transformed. It foregrounds animation as a performative and spatial practice, merging performative cinema with real-time animation while critically engaging contemporary relationships to self-image, digital doubles, and consciousness.

320406.name: Micro-Nano Landscape
320406.description:
Micro-Nano Landscape is a video installation derived from laboratory research on magnetically controlled micro-nano robotic collectives. The work is based on high-magnification microscopic recordings of gravity-defying colloidal formations composed of magnetic microparticles. Under a dual-axis oscillating magnetic field, these particles self-assemble, reconfigure, and execute coordinated motion in dynamic equilibrium.
Rather than simulating natural imagery, the project reveals how engineered matter generates emergent visual orders at microscopic scales. The recorded movements—vertical growth, tilt modulation, adaptive locomotion, swarm coordination—are not animated effects but the direct physical outcome of a precisely modulated magnetic control system. The resulting trajectories evoke fluid landscape formations, yet remain grounded in material robotics research.
The work reframes micro-robotics as a form of programmable matter whose agency emerges through collective behavior rather than anthropomorphic design. By enlarging microscopic documentation into a projected cinematic scale, Micro-Nano Landscape destabilizes the hierarchy between the visible and the invisible. The microscopic becomes spatially immersive; scientific documentation becomes perceptual interface.
Drawing from both contemporary robotics research and the philosophical principle of “seeing the small to understand the grand,” the project proposes scale as a cognitive condition. It suggests that technological systems increasingly operate at dimensions beyond direct perception while nonetheless shaping environments, bodies, and future medical applications. The installation positions art as a perceptual mediator between micro-scale technological operations and human sensory understanding.

Links: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yxyzYumk88Y, https://youtu.be/utLpHqNOAD4
320406.credits:
Artist: Suxuan Jiang
Research collaboration: Jiangfan Yu
With support from: Shenzhen Institute of Artificial Intelligence and Robotics for Society, AIRS SciArt Co-lab
320406.biography:
Artist: Suxuan Jiang
Research collaboration: Jiangfan Yu
With support from: Shenzhen Institute of Artificial Intelligence and Robotics for Society, AIRS SciArt Co-lab
320406.jury_statement: Micro-Nano Landscape situates animation in real-time physical phenomena rather than simulation. Its imagery emerges directly from laboratory research: magnetically controlled micro-nano robotic systems observed under high magnification and driven by a precisely programmed magnetic field. The resulting motion forms landscape-like abstractions through measurable forces. The work’s strength lies in treating animation as a process of revealing, not fabricating, as particles self-organize into clusters, continuously reconfiguring and moving in coordinated ways. By scaling microscopic events into an immersive visual field, Suxuan Jiang and collaborator Jiangfan Yu offer a materially grounded, research-driven approach that foregrounds emergence, collective agency, and the aesthetics of otherwise imperceptible technological systems.

320407.name: Spray and Pray
320407.description:
Spray and Pray is a speculative animated documentary that examines monetized disinformation infrastructures known as mushroom websites. These are networks of automatically generated news sites designed to launder misleading content and generate advertising revenue. The project focuses on the human-machine arrangements behind these infrastructures: platform users recruited to spread links for micro-payments, domain operators managing large clusters of websites, advertising intermediaries, and algorithmic systems that amplify circulation. Instead of framing disinformation as a purely technical problem, the film traces how automation, human labor, and economic incentives are entangled in producing scalable influence.

Developed through long-term research since 2023, the project draws on investigative journalism, academic reports, media-monitoring data, and collaboration with machine-learning researchers. Bulgarian-language disinformation content, an underrepresented area in AI-based detection, plays a central role, pointing to regional asymmetries in technological oversight and political exposure. Machine-learning models were applied to analyze headlines collected from mushroom websites, testing machine-generated text detection, disinformation likelihood, and sentiment. These experiments were not intended to provide definitive proof, but to inform the film's structure by foregrounding the limits of automated analysis.

The film adopts a hybrid documentary form in which research material is translated into cinematic situations. Characters are composed from anonymized data and performed roles, while synthetic voices and animation echo the mediated authorship of the systems portrayed. One fictional figure, the mushroom, speaks only through collected headlines, acting as a voice of the network itself.
In Spray and Pray, speculation becomes a form of evidence, tracing opaque infrastructures in which agency, authorship, and responsibility are continuously displaced.

Links: https://venetaandrova.com/spray-and-pray

Sound design: Daniel Windisch

320407.biography: Veneta Androva (BG) is a visual artist and filmmaker based between Berlin and Sofia. Working with CGI-based moving image, documentary research, and speculative forms, she investigates how technological systems shape perception, political reality, and collective imagination. Her works are shown internationally across film festivals and exhibition contexts. In 2026, Spray and Pray premiered at Visions du Réel and is presented as part of the Bulgarian Pavilion at La Biennale di Venezia. Her film AIVA received an Award of Distinction at Prix Ars Electronica 2021.
320407.jury_statement: Fake news and propaganda websites operate with particular ease in Bulgaria: lax legislation has enabled these emerging sites to spring up like mushrooms, becoming a lucrative business for operators and paid armies of trolls. Simultaneously, AI-based detection proves far less effective in Bulgarian than in other languages, allowing mass right-wing propaganda to frequently slip under the radar. With her extraordinary animated documentary, as humorous as its content is repulsive, Veneta Androva explores the human-machine interface. By deploying fictional yet thoroughly researched animated characters, particularly a smug, plum mushroom-man reading utterly absurd headlines, Spray and Pray lays bare the economic and political mechanisms of the lucrative business of anti-democratic subversion.

320409.name: A Cartography of Genocide: Israel's Conduct in Gaza Since October 2023
320409.description:
Since the start of Israel’s military campaign in Gaza in October 2023, Forensic Architecture (FA) has been collecting data related to attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure by the Israeli military, revealing the near-total destruction of civilian life in Gaza. FA has also collected and analyzed evacuation orders issued by the Israeli military, directing Palestinian civilians to areas of Gaza designated as ‘safe’. These orders have resulted in the repeated, large-scale displacement of the Palestinian population across Gaza, often to areas which, despite this designation, have subsequently come under attack.

Mass displacement and attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure converge in the observed targeting of medical practitioners and infrastructure (often doubling as shelters), an ongoing focal point within FA’s work on Gaza, best represented in their investigation into the al-Ahli Hospital blast, When it stopped being a war: The Situated Testimony of Dr Ghassan Abu-Sittah. The project speaks to the multiscalar approach necessary to understand and analyze the relation between incidents and patterns in Gaza, so that testimonies from the ground may be not only elevated but further situated and corroborated within an investigative framework.

FA’s development of a database and interactive platform, composed of many thousands of datapoints, offers a vehicle for understanding the relationship between individual incidents like the al-Ahli hospital blast and wider Israeli strategies for dismantling the fundamental conditions of life in Gaza. Israel's false criminalization of medical staff and their sites of operation has made both seeking and providing medical care in Gaza a liability, and set the stage for the subsequent targeting of all categories of infrastructure, from the urban to the agricultural.

To identify patterns such as this in Israel’s conduct, FA's interactive web platform turns thousands of datapoints into a navigable ‘map’ of Gaza, within which it is possible to define regions, periods in time, and categories of events. Users can filter the data, revealing trends within datasets and relationships between different datasets (for instance, between the military ground invasion and the destruction of medical infrastructure). The patterns observed broadly indicate a systematic and organized campaign to destroy life, conditions necessary for life, and life-sustaining infrastructure. Forensic Architecture’s monitoring and research consists of an interactive cartographic platform and an 827-page text report, which deploy spatial and pattern analysis to observe the ways in which Israel’s military operations entailed widespread civilian harm. The platform is an iterative, live interface that FA continually updates and maintains, while the report was provided to the South African legal team to support their ongoing submissions in the genocide case against Israel at the International Court of Justice in The Hague.

320409.biography:
Forensic Architecture (FA) (GB) is a research agency based at Goldsmiths, University of London, that investigates human rights violations committed by states, police forces, militaries, and corporations. FA works in partnership with institutions across civil society—grassroots activists, legal teams, international NGOs, and media organisations—to carry out investigations with and on behalf of communities and individuals affected by conflict, police brutality, border regimes, and environmental violence.

The interdisciplinary group uses architecture as an optical device to investigate contested incidents, cross-referencing a range of evidentiary sources and methodologies including open-source research, situated witness interviews, remote sensing, digital modelling, and spatial analysis. FA is also credited with the creation of an eponymous new field and form of interdisciplinary investigative practice, and have supported the growth of agencies worldwide that utilize and advance their methods.

FA has undertaken over 100 investigations worldwide, findings from which have been presented across international media, in exhibitions at leading cultural institutions, and in parliamentary inquiries, citizen’s tribunals, and national and international courtrooms, including the International Criminal Court, the International Court of Justice, the European Court of Human Rights, and the United Nations General Assembly.
320409.jury_statement:
The Golden Nica is awarded to A Cartography of Genocide: Israel’s Conduct in Gaza Since October 2023 by Forensic Architecture in recognition of a work whose significance extends far beyond the boundaries of interactive art, while remaining deeply rooted in the critical capacities of artistic practice. The interface has become the dominant form through which people encounter the world and this project retools the interface as a space of public investigation.
For over a decade, Forensic Architecture, led by Israeli born architect Eyal Weizman, has pioneered new methodologies at the intersection of architecture, technology, journalism, human rights research, and visual culture. In this project, the collective brings together vast quantities of spatial, temporal, and evidentiary data to construct an interactive cartography of Israel’s military campaign in Gaza. Through satellite imagery, geospatial analysis, open-source intelligence, witness testimony, and forensic reconstruction, the platform enables users to navigate and interrogate patterns of destruction across territory, infrastructure, and civilian life.
The jury recognized this work for its interface design, information architecture, methodological rigor, and the organization of public knowledge. By transforming thousands of dispersed data points into a publicly accessible and navigable interface, the project demonstrates how interactive media can render complex realities legible without reducing their complexity. In doing so, the work transforms the interface into a civic infrastructure. Through acts of navigation, comparison, and investigation, users become participants in the construction of public knowledge.
The significance of this work lies not only in the urgency of its subject matter, but in the way it transforms evidence into an interactive public resource. It shows how artists, architects, researchers, and designers can deploy advanced technologies in the service of public knowledge, historical documentation, and civic accountability at a moment when technological systems are frequently mobilized for surveillance, extraction, militarization, and disinformation, A Cartography of Genocide offers a radically different model for technological practice: grounded in transparency and accessibility.
This work is especially vital in an era when artistic, cultural, and academic spaces are increasingly subject to censorship and pressures that constrain what can be shown, discussed, or investigated. Projects that rigorously collect, organize, and make evidence accessible help sustain the conditions for public inquiry, critical reflection, and democratic debate.
The jury believes this work represents one of the most significant contemporary examples of how interactive and computational media can intervene meaningfully in urgent political and humanitarian realities. It is an extraordinary achievement whose implications will resonate far beyond the present moment.

The Coordinates of Our Present – Welcome to the World of Irresolvable Conflicts

Statement by Gerfried Stocker

Under the title “Negotiating Humanity,” this year’s festival dedicates itself to a present in which much of what we have long taken for granted is being shaken, and fundamental coordinates of our world are in motion and being renegotiated. Not individual crises stand at the center, but the irreversible shift of those reference systems within which we understand politics, technology, society, and humanity itself.

The geopolitical and hegemonic conflicts that open up along these transformations are escalating and hardening. The effects of climate change that have manifested so far increasingly prove to be harbingers of impacts that reach far beyond the primary physical consequences of global warming. And not least, the development of artificial intelligence has raised questions that touch on the foundations of our self-understanding and challenge our understanding of what it means to be human, the Conditio Humana.

The results of this year’s Prix Ars Electronica reinforce us in this thematic framing. Once again, the Prix Ars Electronica proves itself a seismograph of social and cultural shifts in our present, making visible how clearly a changed understanding of artistic practice has established itself: to view artistic work not only as reflection and statement, but as active intervention, as a field in which the capacity for social impact of art becomes increasingly more important than formal, aesthetic, or individual positions.

In all three main categories of the Prix Ars Electronica as well as in the STARTS Prize of the European Commission, which is announced jointly with the Prix, the international expert juries have ranked projects at the top that uncompromisingly confront the great conflicts and upheavals of our time, and in doing so place our self-understanding of our role as human beings and as humanity up for debate. In highly different forms, with different artistic means, methods, and messages, the awarded projects engage with that field of tension that Ars Electronica has carried in its title since its founding in 1979: Art – Technology – Society.

That this role does not remain an abstract programmatic positioning shows itself this year with particular clarity. For a jury of five international experts has decided, in an extensive and substantive process, to award the Golden Nica of the Prix Ars Electronica 2026 in the category Interactive Art + to the project “A Cartography of Genocide” by Forensic Architecture.

We are aware that the presentation of a project that carries the word “genocide” explicitly in its title triggers deep and opposing reactions in many people: outrage over the massive suffering of the civilian population in Gaza, as well as pain and objection among those who see in this choice of terminology a relativization of the historical singularity of the Holocaust.

We respect the jury’s decision. At the same time, we consider it necessary — precisely from an Austrian perspective — not to leave this decision unchallenged, and to discuss openly the historical, political, and social implications of this decision — not in order to take sides or render a judgment, but in the awareness of our institutional responsibility to give space to openness, diversity, and controversy, to name dissent and not to conceal it.

This also includes the unambiguous and resolute rejection of antisemitism, racism, and every form of disregard for human dignity.

Precisely in times of fundamental upheaval, we see it all the more as the responsibility of a festival for art, technology, and society to keep spaces for dialogue open even under conditions of deep polarization, to strengthen the capacity for conflict and democratic debate, and thus to counter the logic of mutual escalation.

320410.name: R€¥€R$€
320410.description:
Getting closer to the Amazon is like zooming into an immensely complex and abundant system. Diving deeper is confronting, as it leads to the experience that, in fact, one knows nothing.
Laura Colmenares Guerra

R€¥€R$€ delves into the socio-environmental situation of Amazonia. The work is structured in four chapters: immersive real-time 3D environments, built on Unreal Engine, transport the viewer along rivers, through jungle-like landscapes. As the viewer floats above the water, the names of the Indigenous Peoples appear inscribed in the river surface. Naming them was essential: they are the protectors of this territory.

The second chapter interweaves archival footage with the virtual world. The third, at the center of the experience, presents six interactive maps revealing the pressures of extractivism: deforestation, oil and gas blocks, mining, hydroelectric plants, road infrastructure, and fire zones. Viewers navigate these layers, witnessing how extractive pressures accumulate and overlap across nine countries and more than 847 million hectares. The interactive maps are built on open-source geospatial data produced by RAISG, a consortium of civil society organisations across six Amazonian countries, in collaboration with COICA, representing more than 500 Indigenous Peoples across the basin.

The cartographic work explores the territory through hydrological divisions rather than political boundaries. Rivers are sacred, ancestors, the circulatory system of a living world. By structuring the experience around river basins, the work aligns itself with an understanding of territory as unified by water.

R€¥€R$€ is the third chapter of the Ríos Trilogy (2018–2024), exploring the Amazon Basin through language, cartography, and the construction of territory. The Ríos Trilogy does not pretend to speak for Amazonia or its peoples. It examines how colonial systems of representation construct particular narratives about a territory that belongs, first and foremost, to itself, and how human, cultural and environmental dimensions continue to collide with economic and political forces under acute climate stress.

Links: https://ulara.org/selected-work/rios-chapter-n3, https://ulara.org/selected-work/rios-trilogy

320410.biography: Laura Colmenares Guerra (CO/BE) is a Colombian artist based in Brussels. Her practice encompasses installation, sculpture, and digital 3D narratives, including animation, virtual reality, and ceramics 3D printing. Working from a research-based approach, she explores the relationships between contemporary Western societies and living ecosystems, questioning constructions of nature, territory, and technology as mediations of reality. Her work often transforms environmental data and topographic information into immersive, sensor-based experiences that connect audiences to distant ecological realities. Recent projects address themes of environmental fragility, interspecies transformation, and the entanglement between extractivist systems and vulnerable territories.
320410.jury_statement:
With R€¥€R$€, Laura Colmenares Guerra has created an aesthetically compelling immersive work that introduces viewers to the complexity of one of the world’s most fascinating yet endangered ecosystems: the Amazon region. Through virtual reality and interactive cartographies, the project exposes the entanglement of ecological fragility with political and economic forces, pointing out the devastating impact of extractivism and deforestation.
R€¥€R$€ highlights the fatal connection between colonialism and capitalism, which is a central theme of the artwork. By using symbols such as gold, raw materials, or algorithmic processes, the artist draws attention to the historical exploitation of the Amazon region. It immediately becomes clear that this exploitation continues to follow the logic of resource extraction. Virtual reality makes this critique particularly effective by making the power structures palpable.
The fact that the challenges facing the Amazon region do not stop at political borders was subtly conveyed through a curatorial decision regarding the division of the areas to be explored: rather than following the logic of national borders, the exhibition is divided into twenty-one sections, corresponding to the headwaters of the Amazon’s major tributaries—across nine countries and more than 847 million hectares.

320411.name: Adventures of the Witch's Garden
320411.description:
Adventures of the Witch’s Garden (AWG) is an adventure game designed with the purpose of fostering play as care, while preserving African stories of communal growth and resistance. The project is based on real stories gathered through research conducted in Ghana to examine technological surveillance as violence and power that creates inequalities in motion, illustrated through the lives of three friends. The game’s narrative follows the story of a fictionalized non-binary traditional priest who is on a journey of renewal, after experiencing spiritual depletion due to violent political events and extreme surveillance against gendered minorities in their country. AWG makes the connection with Ghanaian traditional spirituality within a world where the encroaching forces of modern technology are represented by dark creatures, choking wires and dense, and brutalist architecture.

I began designing the game as an experiment to advance technological experiences based on what communities shared in solidarity rather than what is forcefully extracted. In times of overwhelming struggles for digital rights technologists and activists, I asked, what kind of connections and technologies could become a playful outlet, allowing us to reflect, laugh, and tend to each other through solidarity?

To create AWG I closely learned how community gardening practices can be used to design technical infrastructures that embody digital societies based on care, shared support, and social benefit. Just like many community gardens, the project centers play as a subversive and imaginative medium that reclaims our digital public spaces as joyful, while protecting vulnerable communities and our knowledge.
Each challenge within the game reflects regrowth, and renewal, through planting, spiritual guides, and destroying artefacts of surveillance and extraction.

They run the Flowers and Gardening Studio, co-creating communal technology infrastructures and archiving knowledge through play, creative data work, and visual imagery. Their work is guided by collective calculated refusals against regimes of surveillance and extraction. Mardiya has received grant awards from Mozilla/ GIZ, APC, and the University of San Diego's Kroc Institute of Peace and Justice, and has been featured in Bloomsbury Press, Feminist Africa, and Chatham House.
320411.jury_statement: Adventures of the Witch’s Garden (AWG) uses subversive play as a communal channel to unveil the impact of surveillance technologies on sexual minority communities. The Garden is metaphorical for imaginaries around queer opacities centered on healing, joy, and repair. This is a counterbalance to an onslaught of digital media flooded with dehumanizing stories of queer individuals. Grounded in speculative non-fiction called the Sexuality of Technology, Ghanaian traditional spirituality clashes with a brutalist environment of digital surveillance infrastructures. Adventures of the Witch’s Garden is open access, accessible offline, and does not collect any data, embodying queer practices of survival and thereby reclaiming a sense of self in a heavily surveilled digital ecosystem.

320412.name: Built to Go Live: Taking the Signal Back | Blokada INFO
320412.description:
Blokada INFO is a student-led newsroom and media infrastructure project combining participatory governance, ethical journalism, and technical resilience to safeguard public visibility and knowledge mobility during periods of social tension. It emerged during the student protests in Serbia, shaped by the movement’s motto “Institutions must do their work,” to provide reliable, on-the-ground public information amid widespread distrust in legacy state media.
We launched on 1 February 2025 in Novi Sad with a 24-hour live broadcast. Uninterrupted real-time reporting is both an editorial and a technological choice: it shortens the distance between citizens and events, hugely reduces space for misinformation, and creates an accessible public archive of what happened and when.
It emerged from cross-faculty collaboration among students at the University of Novi Sad. Students from diverse disciplines formed what we believe is Serbia’s first student newsroom dedicated to a live TV format distributed through digital platforms. From the outset, we adopted a plenary decision-making model, a characteristic of the broader student movement, where decisions and editorial responsibility are shared across the entire team.
Our work is entirely volunteer-based and funded only through citizen donations. With extremely limited resources, we developed low-budget, open-source solutions, including a device/workflow that bonds multiple cellular connections so that livestreams remain stable under network congestion.
Despite constant pressure in the field, Blokada INFO has endured. Our archive documents multiple incidents, including equipment theft and damage involving pro-government groups and, at times, police. Some cases were recorded on the EFJ/MFRR Mapping Media Freedom platform and hence we received the Marina Kovačev Award for integrity and perseverance.
Since 1 February 2025, we have covered all major protests in Serbia, multiple local elections, and the cyclists’ ride to Strasbourg.

Links: https://link.blokada.info, https://blokada.info, https://link.blokada.info/github, https://link.blokada.info/youtube, https://link.blokada.info/facebook, https://link.blokada.info/instagram
320412.credits:
Blokada INFO exists thanks to Serbia’s student movement and its direct-democratic plenary model, which inspired our collective way of working. We are grateful to the professors, mentors, journalists, and individuals who constantly help us learn and improve. Above all, we thank all past, current, and future volunteers who, despite growing pressure on journalists in Serbia, continue to give their time, skills, and courage to keep the public informed.

With support from: Blokada INFO is entirely volunteer-run and sustained primarily through community solidarity rather than institutional funding. Our work was made possible by early technical support from N1, a regional media outlet, which lent equipment and shared production advice, and from a local DJ studio, which introduced us to livestreaming basics. A local datacenter continues to provide free server capacity for internal systems and livestream distribution. We have also received financial, professional, fundraising, and equipment support from NDNV (Independent Journalists’ Association of Vojvodina), NUNS (Independent Journalists’ Association of Serbia), the trade union at RTV (Radio Television of Vojvodina), civic initiatives “Podrži Studente,” and “IT Blokada”. Above all, the project is sustained by citizens of Serbia and its diaspora through direct financial support and/or donated equipment.
320412.biography: Blokada INFO (RS) is a student collective from Serbia formed during 2024/25 student protests, when it became clear that major public events were not being made visible enough through traditional media outlets. Starting at the University of Novi Sad and later expanding through cooperation with students from other Serbian university centers, it brought together reporting, design, live production, communications, logistics, and engineering. Since its first 24-hour broadcast on 1 February 2025, it has produced 100+ livestreams documenting real-time events, reaching 320,000+ YouTube watch hours, 14.6 million Facebook views, and nearly 40 million Instagram views at the time of writing.
320412.jury_statement: The Blokada INFO is a student-led newsroom and media infrastructure project launched at the beginning of 2025 in Novi Sad. It began with a 24-hour live broadcast of the dramatic events unfolding in Serbia. Its aim was to provide reliable, on-the-ground public information amid widespread distrust in legacy state media. The movement advocates participatory governance, ethical journalism, and technical resilience to safeguard public visibility and knowledge mobility during periods of social tension. Given the rise of Gen Z movements across the world, Blokada INFO deserves attention because it offers an educative case study of how to democratize broadcasting with a low-cost, but sophisticated and ingenious stack of DIY technologies. They demonstrate how high-quality, mobile streaming need no longer be an exclusive domain of major TV networks.

320413.name: Margi – India’s one stop against online harms
320413.description:
At CDF, we factor the incentives, power imbalances, systemic inequities, and user autonomy limitations that shape the current tech ecosystem, into our information literacy projects. We translate the jargon and complexities to fun, creative, and easily accessible solutions to make them effective and engaging.
In 2025, there was a 24% spike in cybercrime, and Indians have lost over Rs. 22,495 crore to online scams. Between 2020 and 2024, the NCRP recorded a 118% rise in online crimes against women and children. When faced with various forms of online harms—harassment, scams, privacy breaches, manipulation, sextortion, child sexual abuse, and mental health challenges—people look online for answers. But solutions are mostly siloed, scattered, and inaccessible.
Margi (prototype) was created as a simple ‘one-stop’ solution, mapping free and open-access preventive resources and responsive solutions in India that tackle a range of techno-social harms. Margi (meaning ‘traveller’) was designed for people to easily find local or national resources and solutions in their language of preference, and reach there in under 3 clicks. The prototype’s homepage allows casual as well as intentional browsers to search using location, language, by harm or content format. The key distinguishing factor is the preventive and responsive approaches; the former guides users like reserachers, educators, and journalists find information literacy resources, mental health toolkits, games, videos, and other methods to help inoculate communities against harms, and the latter helps victims address immediate harm through reporting and redressal mechanisms.
Once complete and accessed and used by digital Indians, the traffic to Margi will help build insights on the types and nodes of various forms of harm across States in India, and help governments plan policy, and allocate funds and resources efficiently to tackle or prevent them.

Links: https://margiindia.in, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vrOyIeOEZtY

Nidhi has been recognized among 100 Brilliant Women in AI Ethics™ 2024.

320413.jury_statement: Margi is a platform designed to serve as a one-stop resource against online harms. When faced with scams, sexual abuse etc. people often turn to the internet for answers. However, advice is mostly siloed, scattered, or inaccessible. Margi helps citizens to find local or national resources and solutions in their language of preference with just a few clicks. It tackles issues such as (1) online scams and fraud providing resources to help users avoid financial loss; (2) harassment and privacy breaches—addressing issues such as gender-based violence; (3) misinformation and AI Harms—educating users on the risks associated with AI. It was created by Nidhi Sudhan, co-founder of Citizen Digital Foundation, an Indian nonprofit dedicated towards making digital technologies safer, more responsible, and equitable.

320414.name: The Planetary Compendium:    Case Studies on Planetary Governance
320414.description:
The Planetary Compendium is an evolving ‘Wunderkammer’ of planetary governance. This living archive maps the shifting architectures, imaginaries, and experiments shaping how life on Earth may be organized, sustained, and represented.
Co-developed by Berggruen Institute (BI) and Dark Matter Labs (Dm), the Compendium brings together ten case studies—historic precedents, emerging experiments, and speculative futures—in a audio-visual multi-format knowledge repository.

Each case is a window into the infrastructures that shape our collective planetary future: from lunar governance and rights of nature to the ethics of geoengineering, transboundary risk mitigation, and interspecies communication. Together, the compendium gathers fragments of how we have tried, and might yet try, to inhabit a planet unfettered by the boundaries of nations, systems, and species.

320414.biography:
Anahat Kaur (IN) is a visual communication and UI designer at Dark Matter Labs. She creates beautiful and effective design solutions for digital and print platforms. She holds a Master's degree in Design from The Basel School of Design in Switzerland and has worked for a diverse range of clients and companies across Europe and India. Her creative process is non-linear and informed by a cross-pollination of ideas from different topics and personal experiences. With years of experience in brand design and development, she creates powerful narratives and believes in using her skills to bring important issues to light.

Arianna Smaron (PL) is an interdisciplinary designer working across visual research, art direction, product design, and storytelling. The practice focuses on visual sense-making and design infrastructures for cultural organisations, civic bodies, and research-led initiatives across Europe and North America, spanning digital platforms, physical materials, and research contexts. With experience across art museums, universities, and public institutions, Arianna was previously Director of the educational programme at La Scuola Open Source, an experimental school rooted in collaborative and non-linear learning processes.
320414.jury_statement: The Planetary Compendium is an evolving, multi-sensory intellectual tool created to reimagine planetary governance. Arianna Smaron and Anahat Kaur have created a rich learning platform with a growing digital atlas of essays, artifacts, and case studies that explore how life on Earth can be organized and represented. Based on the framework of “planetary civics,” the key features of the Compendium are: (1) a living archive, which is an evolving resource that documents imaginaries and experiments related to planetary governance, and (2) a space for collaborative knowledge, that brings together thinkers, practitioners, and domain experts from around the world to identify new pathways for research and collaboration. The jury sees in it a scalable educational tool that can engage students in investigating systemic changes in finance, culture, technology, and policy needed to address the entangled crises of our time.

320415.name: Repeat as necessary: Performance Operating System (2026)
320415.description:
The body is technology. The most ancient, the most democratic, the most universally shared.
Performance art has long carried a structural problem. Every preservation model leans on something outside the work: a foundation that outlives the artist, a body that remembers, a certificate in custody, a chain that breaks when someone forgets.
Operator built a different answer. The Performance Operating System is an open on-chain architecture that holds every parameter needed to regenerate a live performance: choreography, music, notation, costume, motion data, conservation manual. The performance can happen again indefinitely, without the artists, without an institution, without permission.

Repeat as necessary is its first instantiation. A 31-minute ritual guiding audience-participants through collective nervous-system states: threshold, entrainment, dissolution, return. Premiered in Bodrum in 2025 with seven dancers, it uses repetitive movement, breath, and tuned sound frequencies until the bodies of audience and performer sync.
The system's registry contract indexes nine data contracts. A 1/1 HTML NFT fires events, assembles state, and renders the architecture live. The artist’s voice lives on-chain, prompting dancers. A charcoal afterimage tracks presence across 40 formations. When a wallet holds one token from each chapter, entrainment is achieved, and the artwork shifts state.

This is Operator's second architecture for choreographic preservation and transactability. The first, the Operator Generative Choreography Method (2023), encoded movement. The Performance Operating System encodes everything a live performance depends on.
This work refuses the impossible choice performance has historically forced: be collected and frozen, or remain alive and unsustained. Repeat as necessary can be restaged anywhere by anyone; that openness makes ownership meaningful. What is collected is not documentation of a past performance but an engine for future ones. The system is the work.

320415.biography: Operator (US), (est. 2016), is the artist duo of Ania Catherine, a choreographer and performance artist, and Dejha Ti, a multimedia artist and technologist. The practice develops critical and conceptual approaches to experience, engineering medium-agnostic work that joins environments, technology, and the body. On View, (SCAD Museum of Art, 2019), opened an ongoing inquiry into privacy and extractive technologies; Human Unreadable (2023-2026) introduced on-chain generative works that made choreography collectable; Repeat as necessary (2025-2026) built the Performance Operating System, an architecture holding everything required to regenerate a live performance, indefinitely. Awards: 2 Lumen Prizes, Prix Ars Electronica, ADC Gold Cube, S+T+ARTS, MediaFutures.
320415.jury_statement: Operator’s Repeat as necessary proposes a quiet inversion: technology appears not as an external layer, but as circuitry already inscribed in the body. Framed as a Performance Operating System, the work treats performance and its system as one organism, designed from the outset to be both experience and infrastructure. Every parameter needed to regenerate the piece—notations, frequencies, costumes, choreographic directions, even intended nervous-system states—lives permanently across a network of smart contracts on-chain and open for access. Despite a conceptual density that occasionally risks overdetermining the viewer/participant's experience, it articulates a powerful proposition: digital systems can serve as vessels for the shared preservation of lived presence, human memory, and collective sensation. Ultimately, the blockchain serves not as a ledger of ownership, but as a functional engine for future reactivation in a more resilient art eco-system.

320416.name: Sabot - Riding the Algorithm
320416.description:
Riding the Algorithm is a research and design project that repurposes delivery workers' data to create a 'digital commons'—a collective repository of information owned and governed by the riders themselves. The project emerges from a collaboration between the artist, delivery workers in South London, the Independent Workers of Great Britain (IWGB) union (London) and RidersXDerechos (Spain). It responds to the 'black-boxing' of management algorithms. Currently, platforms extract real-time data from workers making profit of their labor, and of the mapping of such labor.
The project centers on Sabot, an open-source mobile application designed to subvert this power asymmetry. While platform apps isolate workers by concealing their colleagues and optimizing value from their repeated actions, Sabot repurposes data collection to inform riders' decisions, to contribute to the community of care on the road and generate greater capacity to collectively organize. By treating social and collective knowledge as a shared resource, the project challenges the extractive logic of surveillance capitalism and seeks to allow riders to become active agents who ride the algorithm to their own advantage.
A prototype was developed in conversation with riders in 2022, who defined its features, experimenting and questioning new forms of political organization under datafied and distributed workspaces. As a tool, but also in the process of its development, Sabot calls for political engagement with the social relations that underpin automated management. This requires an active effort dismantling and reimagining the social and political structures from which platform capitalism emerges, and to design alternative forms of technology rooted in collective autonomy.

Links: https://github.com/julianueno/sabot, https://www.fabrikzeitung.ch/riding-the-algorithm-repurposing-delivery-workers-data-into-a-digital-commons/#, https://blogfundacion.arquia.es/2024/10/el-chisme-algoritmico/, https://julianueno.xyz/

320416.biography: Júlia Nueno Guitart (ES) is a researcher and engineer. Her work explores the computational systems that organize life and the spaces we inhabit, with the goal of developing new ways of understanding and acting with and through them. She is currently a member of the Forensic Architecture team and is pursuing her PhD at the Centre for Research Architecture at Goldsmiths (University of London), where she also teaches on the master's program in the same discipline. She is the editor of Genocidios. Una lectura Forense (Galaxia Gutenberg, 2025), and her articles and opinion columns have appeared in Der Spiegel, The Guardian, VICENews, SpringerIn, FabrikZeitung, and VersoBlog.
320416.jury_statement: Sabot is an app-based project that rethinks the role of data within the gig economy. Built in collaboration with delivery workers, it transforms self-generated data into a shared resource, countering platform models that isolate individuals and maximize productivity. By aggregating real-time information on routes, demand, and working conditions, the app enables forms of collective awareness and coordination that challenge algorithmic management. Rather than optimizing individual performance, Sabot fosters a distributed intelligence grounded in cooperation. In doing so, it proposes a digital commons where data becomes a tool for negotiation and agency, pointing toward new forms of worker-led infrastructures within platform economies.

320417.name: The Animated Book of Genocides: An animated VR experience Girl Earth Fire Time and Between the Wall and the Sides
320417.description:
The Animated Book of Genocides, a multimedia interactive installation, features the Virtual Reality animation *Girl Earth Fire Time*, the 2D animation Between the Wall and the Sides, and The Book of Genocides, the interactive-art-installation-turned-disaster-comic that birthed these animations.
Using multiple layers of scientific|artistic interaction—ranging from images drawn into the surface of a mid-20th-century zoology textbook to the latest digital innovations of VR— the installation moves genocide beyond massacre to focus on its remediable systemic roots. It exposes the patterns of dehumanization, settler colonialism, and profit that lie at the root of genocide as it empowers users/viewers to act to end, prevent, and collectively heal from these atrocities.

The VR experience Girl Earth Fire Time reconnects the user to our natural propensity for love and compassion through weaving together the story of artist and author Dana Mashoian Walrath’s grandmother Oghidar during the Armenian genocide and her encounters in the ancestral realm, where she meets victims and perpetrators of other genocides including those in Southern Africa, the Holocaust, and Palestine. Between the Wall and the Sides traces the dehumanization of genocide and connects the UN Genocide Convention’s failure today back to the rejection of the 1951 “We Charge Genocide” petition Black Americans filed against the US government once the convention was established. The installation also provides the opportunity for participants to alter destructive authoritative texts, a process integral to the creation of the installation, and to interact with digitally rendered turn-the-flap sections of the disaster comic. The installation’s continuum between the physical and the virtual aims to spark dialogue and to empower participants to enact the systemic changes vital for humanity’s collective survival.

Links: https://www.bookofgenocides.com/, https://www.danawalrath.com/girl-earth-fire-time, https://canva.link/qokwa2r4qqmhgks
